optionExplanations: G6PD deficiency affects all cells, but symptoms are most prominent in RBCs; G6PD A- is not localized specifically to the liver.
In G6PD A-, the enzyme is kinetically normal but has a shortened half-life. Younger cells (reticulocytes) have enough activity to survive, meaning hemolysis stops once old cells are destroyed.
Mature erythrocytes do not have mitochondria or alternate NADPH sources like the malic enzyme, which is why they are uniquely sensitive to G6PD defects.
Large deletions in G6PD are usually lethal and not identified in clinical populations; both A- and Mediterranean are typically missense mutations.
Both variants involve enzyme instability or altered kinetics, but the primary clinical difference is the degree of residual activity in young versus old cells.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 145 (Book Page): G6PD A- is the prototype of the moderate (Class III) form of the disease. The red cells contain an unstable but kinetically normal G6PD, with most of the enzyme activity present in the reticulocytes and younger erythrocytes... The oldest cells, therefore, have the lowest level of enzyme activity.

category: Enlist the components of balanced diet and elaborate the importance of each component
statement: In calculating the total daily energy expenditure of a patient, a dietician must account for the metabolic caloric value of different macronutrients. Which of the following provides the highest amount of metabolic energy per gram consumed?
options: Proteins
Ethanol
Dietary Fiber
Fats
Carbohydrates
correctOption: Fats
optionExplanations: Proteins yield only 4 kcal/g.
Ethanol is intermediate, yielding 7 kcal/g, which is less than fat.
Fiber provides very little usable metabolic energy for humans as it is mostly non-digestible.
Fats are the most energy-dense macronutrient, yielding approximately 9 kcal per gram, which is more than double that of carbohydrates or protein.
Carbohydrates yield only 4 kcal/g.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 359 (Book Page): [Note that the energy content of fat is more than twice that of carbohydrate or protein... fat (9 kcal/g), protein (4 kcal/g), and carbohydrate (4 kcal/g).]

category: Elaborate the structure of ATP synthase (complex V)
coreConcept: Respiratory Control and Complex V Blockade
statement: A 10-month-old infant presents with developmental delay, hypotonia, and lactic acidosis. Genetic testing reveals a mutation in the mitochondrial DNA specifically affecting a subunit of the membrane-spanning domain of ATP synthase, rendering it unable to rotate. Metabolic profiling indicates that despite a high proton gradient across the inner mitochondrial membrane, ATP production is negligible. Which of the following best describes the physiological state of this patient's mitochondria?
options: Rapid dissipation of the pH gradient through the mutated Fo domain channel.
Increased oxygen consumption due to the high electrical gradient in the intermembrane space.
Induction of nonshivering thermogenesis to compensate for the lack of chemical energy.
Maximal ATP synthesis driven by the failure of the respiratory control mechanism.
Stopped electron transport due to the inability to pump protons against an undissipated gradient.
correctOption: Stopped electron transport due to the inability to pump protons against an undissipated gradient.
optionExplanations: A mutation that prevents Fo rotation would stop the flow of protons through the channel, meaning the pH gradient would remain high rather than being dissipated.
Oxygen consumption would actually decrease because electron transport stops when the proton gradient becomes too steep and cannot be dissipated.

Nonshivering thermogenesis is mediated by Uncoupling Protein 1 (UCP1) in brown fat, not as a direct compensatory mechanism for a mutated ATP synthase in all tissues; it requires its own specific induction path.
ATP synthesis would be negligible because the mechanical coupling between the Fo proton flow and the F1 conformational change is broken.

Oxidative phosphorylation is tightly coupled. If the Fo domain cannot rotate and allow protons back into the matrix, the gradient becomes so steep that the ETC can no longer pump protons, halting oxygen use.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 78 (Book Page): Because the pH and electrical gradients cannot be dissipated in the presence of this drug [or a functional block of Fo], electron transport stops because of the difficulty of pumping any more protons against the steep gradients. This dependency of cellular respiration on the ability to phosphorylate ADP to ATP is known as respiratory control.

category: Enlist symptoms and signs
statement: A mother introduces fruit juice to her 6-month-old infant for the first time. Within hours, the child develops vomiting and shows signs of severe hypoglycemia. Physical examination reveals jaundice and hepatomegaly. What biochemical event is directly responsible for the hypoglycemia and hepatic dysfunction in this condition?
options: Osmotic diarrhea caused by unabsorbed disaccharides in the gut
Excessive accumulation of sorbitol in the lens and liver cells
Failure of the liver to produce glucose from glycogen via phosphorylase
Elevation of blood galactose leading to galactitol production
Intracellular trapping of fructose 1-phosphate and depletion of ATP
correctOption: Intracellular trapping of fructose 1-phosphate and depletion of ATP
optionExplanations: Osmotic diarrhea occurs in disaccharidase deficiencies like lactase deficiency, but doesn't explain the acute systemic symptoms like jaundice and hypoglycemia.
Sorbitol accumulation is associated with chronic diabetic complications in the lens and nerves, not acute post-prandial hypoglycemia in an infant.
While glycogenolysis is affected, it is the depletion of phosphate/ATP due to the specific enzyme block (Aldolase B) that is the primary mechanism cited in the text for HFI.
Galactitol production is the hallmark of galactosemia, which occurs with milk ingestion, not fruit juice which is rich in fructose.

In Hereditary Fructose Intolerance (aldolase B deficiency), the trapping of fructose 1-phosphate depletes intracellular phosphate and ATP, which are necessary for gluconeogenesis and glycogenolysis, thus causing severe hypoglycemia.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 130 (Book Page): Fructose 1-phosphate accumulates, resulting in a drop in the level of inorganic phosphate (Pi) and, therefore, of ATP... The decreased availability of hepatic ATP affects gluconeogenesis (causing hypoglycemia with vomiting).

category: Calculate the energy yield of TCA
statement: Which of the following describes a 'proton leak' in the inner mitochondrial membrane and its subsequent effect on the calculated energy yield of the TCA cycle?
options: It prevents the dissociation of the F1 domain from the Fo domain.
It increases the P:O ratio by allowing more protons to flow through ATP synthase.
It results in the capture of energy as heat rather than ATP.
It decreases the concentration of ADP available in the matrix.
It stops the TCA cycle by inhibiting the reduction of NAD+.
correctOption: It results in the capture of energy as heat rather than ATP.
optionExplanations: Oligomycin prevents proton flow through Fo, but a 'leak' is the opposite—it is an alternative pathway for protons.
A proton leak decreases the P:O ratio because the proton gradient is dissipated without driving ATP synthesis.

Uncoupling proteins (UCPs) allow protons to bypass ATP synthase. While the TCA cycle and ETC continue (often at a faster rate), the energy released is not captured as ATP but is dissipated as heat (nonshivering thermogenesis).
Uncoupling usually leads to an increase in ADP because ATP is being used but not regenerated by the mitochondria.
The TCA cycle actually speeds up because the lack of ATP causes an increase in the availability of NAD+ and ADP (loss of respiratory control).
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 79 (Book Page): These carrier proteins create a “proton leak,” that is, they allow protons to re-enter the mitochondrial matrix without energy being captured as ATP... The energy is released as heat.

category: Elaborate key features of various transport systems for entry of glucose into cells
statement: Which of the following describes the energy requirement of the SGLT system found in renal tubules?
options: It directly hydrolyzes ATP at the transporter site (Primary Active).
It is a passive system requiring no energy.
It is driven by the high concentration of glucose in the tubular lumen.
It utilizes the pH gradient created by the electron transport chain.
It uses the energy of the sodium gradient maintained by the Na+-K+ ATPase (Secondary Active).
correctOption: It uses the energy of the sodium gradient maintained by the Na+-K+ ATPase (Secondary Active).
optionExplanations: While active, SGLT is secondary active transport; it doesn't hydrolyze ATP itself but relies on the Na+ gradient.
SGLT is an active transport system, distinguishing it from the passive GLUT family.
If it were driven by the high concentration in the lumen, it would be passive; SGLT exists specifically to transport glucose when luminal concentrations are low.
The pH gradient from the electron transport chain is used in mitochondria for ATP synthesis, not for SGLT transport.
SGLT uses the energy stored in the sodium gradient (created by the Na+-K+ pump) to pull glucose into the cell against its gradient.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 97 (Book Page): This system is a carrier-mediated process in which the movement of glucose is coupled to the concentration gradient of Na+, which is transported into the cell at the same time.

category: Elaborate key features of various transport systems for entry of glucose into cells
coreConcept: SGLT Function in Intestine and Kidney
statement: A neonatal patient presents with severe osmotic diarrhea and failure to thrive. Genetic testing reveals a mutation in a sodium-dependent transporter located in the renal tubules and intestinal epithelial cells. Which physiologic feature of glucose transport is most likely compromised in this patient?
options: Down-gradient facilitated diffusion into the portal blood
Up-gradient transport coupled to the Na+ concentration gradient
Bidirectional transport during the fasting state
Hexokinase-mediated trapping of glucose in the cytosol
Insulin-stimulated glucose storage in the liver
correctOption: Up-gradient transport coupled to the Na+ concentration gradient
optionExplanations: Facilitated diffusion into the portal blood is mediated by GLUT-2 on the basolateral membrane, which is Na+-independent and unaffected by SGLT mutations.

The SGLT system moves glucose into the intestinal cell or renal tubule cell against its gradient by coupling it with sodium. A defect leads to glucose remaining in the lumen, causing osmotic diarrhea or glycosuria.
Bidirectional transport is a hallmark of GLUT-2 in the liver, kidney, and beta cells; SGLT transporters are generally unidirectional, moving glucose into the cell.
Hexokinase mediates the phosphorylation of glucose to trap it, but the question describes a defect in the transporter protein itself, which precedes the action of hexokinase.
Glucose storage in the liver involves GLUT-2 and is regulated by insulin's effects on intracellular enzymes, not by a sodium-dependent cotransporter.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 89 (Book Page): This is an energy-requiring process that transports glucose “against” a concentration gradient... This system is a carrier-mediated process in which the movement of glucose is coupled to the concentration gradient of Na+... The carrier is a sodium-dependent–glucose transporter or SGLT. This type of transport occurs in the epithelial cells of the intestine, renal tubules...

category: Elaborate the regulation and importance of gluconeogenesis
statement: A chronic alcoholic patient is found unconscious after several days of binge drinking and minimal food intake. His blood glucose is 35 mg/dl (profoundly hypoglycemic). The inhibition of gluconeogenesis in this patient is primarily due to an increase in the cytosolic NADH/NAD+ ratio. How does this high ratio specifically prevent glucose synthesis?
options: It blocks the transport of pyruvate into the mitochondria
It causes the competitive inhibition of Fructose 1,6-bisphosphatase
It prevents the activation of Pyruvate Carboxylase by Acetyl CoA
It inhibits the enzyme Glucose 6-phosphatase directly
It shifts the equilibrium from oxaloacetate toward malate, depleting gluconeogenic precursors
correctOption: It shifts the equilibrium from oxaloacetate toward malate, depleting gluconeogenic precursors
optionExplanations: Pyruvate transport is not the primary block; rather, any pyruvate available is converted to lactate due to the high NADH, further depleting gluconeogenic substrates.
Fructose 1,6-bisphosphatase is regulated by AMP and Fructose 2,6-bisphosphate, not by the NADH/NAD+ ratio.
Acetyl CoA levels may actually be high due to ethanol metabolism, but the high NADH/NAD+ ratio is the dominant factor in the OAA/malate equilibrium shift.
NADH does not have a direct inhibitory effect on Glucose 6-phosphatase; the issue is upstream with precursor availability.

The metabolism of ethanol produces excess NADH. This high NADH/NAD+ ratio forces the malate dehydrogenase reaction to favor malate, thereby 'trapping' oxaloacetate and preventing it from being used for gluconeogenesis.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 116 (Book Page): The increase in NADH as ethanol is oxidized, will decrease the availability of OAA because the reversible oxidation of malate to OAA by malate dehydrogenase... is driven in the reverse direction by the high availability of NADH.

category: Discuss the metabolic fates of pyruvate
statement: A 35-year-old worker at a pesticide manufacturing plant is admitted with severe neurological disturbances. It is determined that he has been exposed to trivalent arsenic (arsenite). This toxin specifically targets a coenzyme required for the oxidative decarboxylation of pyruvate. Which part of the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex is directly inhibited by this mechanism?
options: The FAD-binding site of dihydrolipoyl dehydrogenase in E3.
The lysine residue of the biotin-carrier protein.
The thiol groups of lipoic acid in E2.
The magnesium-binding site of PDH phosphatase.
The reactive carbon of thiamine pyrophosphate in E1.
correctOption: The thiol groups of lipoic acid in E2.
optionExplanations: While E3 uses FAD to reoxidize lipoic acid, the direct inhibitory binding of arsenic occurs on the lipoic acid substrate/cofactor itself.
Biotin is involved in pyruvate carboxylase; arsenic poisoning affects alpha-keto acid dehydrogenases that utilize lipoic acid.
Arsenite binds covalently to the vicinal sulfhydryl groups of lipoic acid in the E2 (transacetylase) component, preventing the transfer of the acetyl group and halting the complex.
Arsenic does not primarily target the regulatory phosphatase; its toxicity stems from inhibiting the catalytic core by sequestering lipoic acid thiol groups.
TPP is used by E1 for decarboxylation but is not the primary target for trivalent arsenic covalent binding.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 103 (Book Page): Arsenite (the trivalent form of arsenic) forms a stable complex with the thiol (–SH) groups of lipoic acid, making that compound unavailable to serve as a coenzyme. When it binds to lipoic acid in the PDH complex, pyruvate (and consequently lactate) accumulates.

category: Discuss the metabolic fates of pyruvate
statement: Pyruvate carboxylase, which catalyzes the conversion of pyruvate to oxaloacetate, requires which of the following coenzymes for its catalytic activity?
options: Biotin
Flavin adenine dinucleotide (FAD)
Pyridoxal phosphate (PLP)
Niacin (NAD+)
Thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP)
correctOption: Biotin
optionExplanations: Biotin is covalently bound to pyruvate carboxylase and acts as a carrier of activated CO2 to convert the three-carbon pyruvate into four-carbon oxaloacetate.
FAD is used in the E3 subunit of the PDH complex as an electron carrier, but it is not involved in the pyruvate carboxylase reaction.
PLP is the coenzyme for transaminases and glycogen phosphorylase, but it is not utilized in the carboxylation of pyruvate.
NAD+ is an electron acceptor in the oxidative decarboxylation of pyruvate by PDH, but it is not a coenzyme for pyruvate carboxylase.
TPP is required by decarboxylases like the E1 subunit of the PDH complex, not by the carboxylase that adds CO2 to pyruvate.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 105 (Book Page): Carboxylation of pyruvate to oxaloacetate (OAA) by pyruvate carboxylase is a biotin-dependent reaction.

category: Enlist various types of glycogen storage diseases (GSDs)
statement: What metabolic consequence is expected in Type VI GSD (Hers disease) that helps distinguish it from Type V GSD (McArdle syndrome)?
options: Failure of blood glucose to rise after glucagon administration.
Massive glycogen accumulation specifically in the lysosomes.
Hyperuricemia and gouty arthritis.
Lactic acidosis due to impaired aerobic glycolysis.
Presence of abnormal limit dextrins in the skeletal muscle.
correctOption: Failure of blood glucose to rise after glucagon administration.
optionExplanations: Hers disease involves liver glycogen phosphorylase. Since the liver cannot break down glycogen in response to glucagon, blood glucose will not rise. McArdle syndrome affects muscle phosphorylase and would not affect the hyperglycemic response to glucagon.
Lysosomal accumulation is only seen in Type II (Pompe disease).
Hyperuricemia is a feature of Von Gierke disease (Type Ia) due to phosphate depletion and reduced glucose 6-phosphatase activity, not the hallmark of Hers disease.
Lactic acidosis is characteristic of Von Gierke disease (Type Ia), while McArdle syndrome actually shows a *lack* of lactate production during exercise.
Limit dextrins are associated with Type III (Cori disease), which affects the debranching enzyme, not the phosphorylase.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 121 (Book Page): [Deficiency of the liver isozyme causes Type VI: Hers disease with mild fasting hypoglycemia... Type V: McArdle syndrome... Skeletal muscle affected; liver enzyme normal]

category: Calculate the energy yield of TCA
statement: A patient with a history of dieting is admitted for severe hyperthermia and metabolic acidosis after ingesting 2,4-dinitrophenol (DNP). In this patient, what is the most likely effect on the P:O ratio and the total energy yield during the complete mitochondrial oxidation of pyruvate to CO2?
options: P:O ratio remains 3:1; yield decreases to 5 ATP
P:O ratio decreases to 0; yield decreases to 1 ATP
P:O ratio decreases to 1:1; yield remains 15 ATP
P:O ratio increases to 4:1; yield increases to 20 ATP
P:O ratio remains 3:1; yield remains 15 ATP
correctOption: P:O ratio decreases to 0; yield decreases to 1 ATP
optionExplanations: If the P:O ratio were 3:1, the yield would be 15 ATP, but uncoupling specifically prevents this ratio from being achieved.

DNP dissipates the proton gradient, making the P:O ratio 0 for the ETC. The only ATP/GTP generated is from substrate-level phosphorylation in the TCA cycle (1 GTP), resulting in a net yield of 1 ATP per pyruvate.
Uncoupling doesn't just lower the ratio; it effectively reduces the P:O of the ETC to zero, as the gradient required for ATP synthase is lost.
Uncouplers decrease, never increase, the efficiency of ATP synthesis.
DNP uncouples oxidation from phosphorylation, so the P:O ratio cannot remain at 3:1 and ATP yield cannot be maintained.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 79 (Book Page): This uncoupler causes electron transport to proceed at a rapid rate without establishing a proton gradient... energy is released as heat rather than being used to synthesize ATP. Page 106 (Book Page): a total of 15 ATPs are produced from the complete mitochondrial oxidation of pyruvate to CO2.

category: Explain the significance of Cori cycle and glucosealanine cycle
statement: Where does the first irreversible step of gluconeogenesis, the conversion of pyruvate to oxaloacetate, occur within the cell as part of the Cori and Glucose-Alanine cycles?
options: Endoplasmic reticulum
Lysosomes
Golgi apparatus
Mitochondria
Cytosol
correctOption: Mitochondria
optionExplanations: The endoplasmic reticulum is the site of the final step of gluconeogenesis (glucose 6-phosphatase), not the first step.
Lysosomes are involved in the degradation of glycogen (Pompe disease) but not in the gluconeogenic conversion of pyruvate.
The Golgi apparatus is involved in protein modification and lactose synthesis, not the conversion of pyruvate to glucose.
The enzyme pyruvate carboxylase is located exclusively in the mitochondrial matrix, requiring oxaloacetate to be converted to malate for export to the cytosol.
While many steps of gluconeogenesis are cytosolic, the initial carboxylation of pyruvate is mitochondrial.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 110 (Book Page): [Note: This reaction occurs in the mitochondria of liver and kidney cells, and has two purposes: to provide an important substrate for gluconeogenesis, and to provide OAA that can replenish the TCA cycle intermediates]

category: Define and classify nutrients into macro and micronutrients
statement: A patient is consuming high-potency micronutrient supplements and fortified foods. To ensure the patient does not exceed the threshold beyond which the potential risk of adverse health effects increases, which Dietary Reference Intake (DRI) standard must be consulted?
options: Tolerable Upper Intake Level (UL).
Estimated Average Requirement (EAR).
Recommended Dietary Allowance (RDA).
Adequate Intake (AI).
Acceptable Macronutrient Distribution Range (AMDR).
correctOption: Tolerable Upper Intake Level (UL).
optionExplanations: Correct. The UL is the specific standard established to protect individuals from the adverse effects of excessive nutrient intake, especially from supplements.
The EAR is used to estimate requirements for 50% of a group and is not intended to provide guidance on safety or toxicity upper limits.
The RDA is the intake target for nutritional adequacy (covering 98% of the population) rather than the safety ceiling for toxicity.
Adequate Intake (AI) is used as a recommended intake target when evidence is insufficient for an RDA; it does not define the upper safety limit.
The AMDR refers to the percentage distribution of macronutrients (carbs, fats, proteins) to prevent chronic disease, not to individual micronutrient toxicity.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 358 (Book Page): The UL is the highest average daily nutrient intake level that is likely to pose no risk of adverse health effects to almost all individuals in the general population. As intake increases above the UL, the potential risk of adverse effects may increase.

category: Enlist symptoms and signs
statement: A 3-year-old child presents with a history of recurrent, severe bacterial infections. Biopsy of a persistent skin lesion reveals the formation of granulomas. Which specific diagnostic sign is associated with the underlying enzyme deficiency in this case?
options: Low levels of serum ceruloplasmin
Absence of the 'respiratory burst' in activated leukocytes
Accumulation of glycogen in vacuoles
Increased blood levels of lactic acid after exercise
Detection of Heinz bodies in erythrocytes
correctOption: Absence of the 'respiratory burst' in activated leukocytes
optionExplanations: Low ceruloplasmin is associated with Wilson's disease (copper metabolism), which is unrelated to the bactericidal functions of neutrophils.
CGD is caused by a deficiency in NADPH oxidase, meaning leukocytes cannot produce superoxide, leading to a negative respiratory burst test.
Vacuolar glycogen accumulation is characteristic of Pompe disease, a lysosomal storage disorder, not a phagocytic defect.
Lactic acid increases in McArdle syndrome are absent; increased lactic acid is common in Von Gierke or during anaerobic exercise.
Heinz bodies are a sign of G6PD deficiency, where oxidative stress denatures hemoglobin, not a sign of CGD.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 142 (Book Page): Genetic deficiencies in NADPH oxidase cause chronic granulomatous disease (CGD) characterized by severe, persistent infections. and the formation of granulomas... The rapid consumption of molecular oxygen that accompanies formation of superoxide is referred to as the respiratory burst.

category: Suggest a simple method for estimation of caloric requirements of sedentary adults, moderately active adults, and very active adults
statement: What is the recommended simple approximation for the daily caloric intake required to maintain body weight in a healthy sedentary adult?
options: 30 kcal/kg/day
35 kcal/kg/day
20 kcal/kg/day
25 kcal/kg/day
40 kcal/kg/day
correctOption: 30 kcal/kg/day
optionExplanations: According to simple approximations for energy requirements, sedentary adults require 30 kcal/kg/day to maintain current body weight, providing a baseline for clinicians to estimate nutritional needs.
35 kcal/kg/day is the specific approximation used for moderately active adults rather than sedentary ones.
20 kcal/kg/day is significantly below the estimated requirement for weight maintenance in a healthy sedentary adult and would likely result in weight loss over time.
25 kcal/kg/day is a lower estimate than the 30 kcal/kg standard provided for sedentary maintenance, potentially reflecting a caloric deficit rather than maintenance.
40 kcal/kg/day is the approximation designated for very active individuals, representing a higher metabolic demand than sedentary lifestyles.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 358 (Book Page): For example, sedentary adults require about 30 kcal/kg/day to maintain body weight; moderately active adults require 35 kcal/kg/day; and very active adults require 40 kcal/kg/day.

category: Describe the transport of pyruvate from cytosol to mitochondria
statement: The inner mitochondrial membrane is described as being unusually rich in which component, accounting for its role in specialized transport and oxidative phosphorylation?
options: Triglycerides
Protein
Glycolipids
Cholesterol
Phospholipids
correctOption: Protein
optionExplanations: Triglycerides are energy storage molecules found in droplets or adipocytes; they are not structural components of the mitochondrial membranes.
The high protein content (approximately 75-80% by weight) reflects the density of respiratory chain complexes and specialized transport systems like the pyruvate carrier.
Glycolipids are primarily found on the outer leaflet of the plasma membrane for cell signaling and are not the dominant feature of the inner mitochondrial membrane.
The inner mitochondrial membrane is actually relatively low in cholesterol compared to the plasma membrane, which contributes to its specific permeability properties.
While phospholipids form the bilayer, the 'unusual' characteristic of the inner membrane is its exceptionally high protein-to-lipid ratio.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 74 (Book Page): The inner mitochondrial membrane is unusually rich in protein, half of which is directly involved in electron transport and oxidative phosphorylation.

category: Enlist the hormones that play important roles in regulating carbohydrate metabolism
statement: A patient is prescribed a medication that significantly increases prolactin levels as a side effect. Which hormonal mechanism directly explains how this could lead to the production of the 'milk sugar' in the mammary gland?
options: Activation of UDP-hexose 4-epimerase to generate glucose
Induction of the synthesis of alpha-lactalbumin (Protein B)
Competitive inhibition of galactosyltransferase (Protein A)
Repression of the gene for UDP-glucose pyrophosphorylase
Phosphorylation of glucose 6-phosphate translocase
correctOption: Induction of the synthesis of alpha-lactalbumin (Protein B)
optionExplanations: The epimerase converts UDP-glucose to UDP-galactose; while necessary, its activation is not the specific mechanism by which prolactin triggers lactose synthesis.

Prolactin induces the synthesis of alpha-lactalbumin (Protein B). Protein B binds to Protein A (galactosyltransferase), changing its specificity so that it uses glucose as a substrate to synthesize lactose.
Protein B does not inhibit Protein A; it modifies its substrate specificity. Without Protein B, Protein A normally synthesizes N-acetyllactosamine.
Lactose synthesis requires UDP-glucose/UDP-galactose; repressing the pyrophosphorylase would inhibit, not stimulate, the pathway.
Glucose 6-phosphate translocase is involved in gluconeogenesis and glycogenolysis in the liver/kidney, not the terminal step of lactose synthesis.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 134 (Book Page): [Protein B is found only in lactating mammary glands. It is alpha-lactalbumin, and its synthesis is stimulated by the peptide hormone, prolactin.]

category: Infer the key biochemical and clinical features of various GSDs from the respective enzyme deficiencies
statement: Which of the following describes the fundamental structural defect in the glycogen molecule found in patients with Andersen disease (Type IV GSD)?
options: Highly branched with extremely short outer chains.
Presence of long, unbranched outer chains due to lack of α(1→6) linkages.
Composed exclusively of glucose 6-phosphate monomers.
Limit dextrins with single glucose residues at branch points.
Structurally normal but trapped in lysosomal vacuoles.
correctOption: Presence of long, unbranched outer chains due to lack of α(1→6) linkages.
optionExplanations: Glycogen with extremely short outer chains (limit dextrins) is characteristic of Cori disease (Type III), not Andersen disease.

Branching enzyme creates α(1→6) linkages. Its deficiency results in the synthesis of 'amylopectinosis', where glycogen has very few branches and long outer chains, which the immune system attacks as foreign.
Glycogen is a polymer of glucose, not glucose 6-phosphate; the phosphate is removed during degradation or added only at the first carbon as G1P.
This describes the structure seen in Cori disease (debranching enzyme deficiency) following the action of phosphorylase.
Normal glycogen trapped in lysosomes is the description of Pompe disease (Type II).
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 121 (Book Page): [Note: A GSD can also be caused by defects in branching enzyme... resulting in Type IV: Andersen disease and causing death in early childhood.]

category: Calculate the energy yield of TCA
statement: A 45-year-old male is brought to the emergency department after suspected exposure to arsenite. Arsenite is known to inhibit enzymes requiring lipoic acid, such as the alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase complex. In this patient, what would be the calculated net ATP yield from the aerobic metabolism of a single molecule of Acetyl CoA entering the TCA cycle?
options: 6 ATP
0 ATP
9 ATP
12 ATP
3 ATP
correctOption: 3 ATP
optionExplanations: 6 ATP would assume two NADH-producing steps occurred; however, only one (Isocitrate to alpha-ketoglutarate) precedes the block.
0 ATP is incorrect because the initial step of the TCA cycle (Isocitrate Dehydrogenase) occurs before the alpha-ketoglutarate step and produces NADH.
9 ATP would require three NADH-producing steps, but the second and third NADH-producing steps are blocked or follow the block.
12 ATP is the normal yield, which is impossible here due to the inhibition of a key rate-limiting multienzyme complex by arsenite binding to lipoic acid units in E2 subunits (Page 111).

If alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase is inhibited, the cycle stops there. The only energy-yielding step prior to this is Isocitrate Dehydrogenase, which produces 1 NADH (3 ATP). The subsequent steps (Succinate thiokinase, etc.) cannot occur.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 103 (Book Page): Arsenite... forms a stable complex with the thiol (–SH) groups of lipoic acid... When it binds to lipoic acid in the PDH complex, pyruvate (and consequently lactate) accumulates.

category: Define body mass index (BMI)
statement: According to nutritional standards, a sedentary adult requires approximately 30 kcal/kg/day to maintain their current Body Mass Index (BMI). If an 80 kg man wishes to maintain his weight, what is his approximate total daily caloric requirement?
options: 2,800 kcal
4,000 kcal
2,400 kcal
1,800 kcal
3,200 kcal
correctOption: 2,400 kcal
optionExplanations: 2,800 kcal would be the requirement if he were moderately active (35 kcal/kg * 80 kg).
4,000 kcal is far in excess of the maintenance requirements for a sedentary individual of 80 kg.
Calculation: 80 kg * 30 kcal/kg = 2,400 kcal/day. This represents the total calories needed for a sedentary individual of this weight to maintain their BMI.
1,800 kcal is the approximate RMR for a 70 kg man, not the total maintenance calories for an 80 kg man.
3,200 kcal would be the requirement if he were very active (40 kcal/kg * 80 kg).
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 351 (Book Page): [sedentary adults require about 30 kcal/kg/day to maintain body weight]

category: Enlist the components of complex I, II, III, and IV
statement: A research scientist is studying the effect of an experimental toxin that prevents the reversible conversion of cytochrome iron from the ferric (Fe3+) to the ferrous (Fe2+) state. This toxin would effectively inhibit the function of which group of ETC components?
options: Coenzyme Q
Nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD+)
Iron-sulfur centers only
Cytochromes
Flavin mononucleotide (FMN)
correctOption: Cytochromes
optionExplanations: Coenzyme Q (ubiquinone) is a quinone derivative that carries hydrogen atoms (electrons + protons), not involving iron valency changes.
NAD+ is a coenzyme that accepts hydride ions (2 electrons and 1 proton), not via an iron-valency change.
While iron-sulfur centers also undergo redox changes, the specific mechanism of reversible conversion between Fe3+ and Fe2+ within a porphyrin/heme ring is the hallmark of cytochromes.
Cytochromes (found in Complexes III, IV, and the mobile Cytochrome c) use the iron atom within their heme group to carry single electrons by switching between Fe3+ and Fe2+.
FMN is a flavin derivative that accepts two hydrogen atoms to become FMNH2; it does not contain iron.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 76 (Book Page): Unlike the heme groups of hemoglobin, the cytochrome iron is reversibly converted from its ferric (Fe3+) to its ferrous (Fe2+) form as a normal part of its function as a reversible carrier of electrons.

category: Infer the key biochemical and clinical features of various GSDs from the respective enzyme deficiencies
coreConcept: Ischemic exercise test findings in McArdle Syndrome
statement: A patient with suspected McArdle syndrome undergoes an ischemic exercise test. Which of the following physiological responses would confirm the biochemical diagnosis of this specific GSD?
options: Failure of the blood pH to drop despite strenuous muscular contraction
Excessive production of ketone bodies by the liver
Hyperinsulinemia following the cessation of exercise
Detection of high levels of α(1→6)-glucosidase in the plasma
A rapid rise in blood glucose levels during exercise
correctOption: Failure of the blood pH to drop despite strenuous muscular contraction
optionExplanations: In normal individuals, anaerobic glycolysis produces lactate, which drops the pH. In McArdle syndrome, muscle glycogen cannot be converted to glucose 1-phosphate, preventing glycolysis and the subsequent rise in lactate. Thus, the pH fails to drop as expected.
Ketone body production is a feature of fasting or fat metabolism, not a diagnostic test for muscle phosphorylase deficiency.
Insulin levels do not specifically diagnose GSD Type V.
α(1→6)-glucosidase is a debranching enzyme activity; its plasma level is not used to diagnose McArdle syndrome.
Blood glucose levels are maintained by the liver in McArdle syndrome, so a 'rapid rise' is not a diagnostic feature of the muscle defect.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 121 (Book Page): [TYPE V: McARDLE SYNDROME] ...No rise in blood lactate during strenuous exercise. Page 95 (Book Page): [Lactate formation in muscle] ...during intense exercise, lactate accumulates in muscle, causing a drop in the intracellular pH...

category: Elaborate the concept and importance of Balanced Diet
statement: A nutrition committee is establishing a dietary reference standard for a healthy 25-year-old male. If the requirement for a specific nutrient is normally distributed and the Estimated Average Requirement (EAR) is known, which parameter is calculated to ensure a 97% to 98% probability of adequacy for the individual?
options: Adequate Intake (AI)
Acceptable Macronutrient Distribution Range (AMDR)
Tolerable Upper Intake Level (UL)
Recommended Dietary Allowance (RDA)
Estimated Energy Requirement (EER)
correctOption: Recommended Dietary Allowance (RDA)
optionExplanations: Adequate Intake (AI) is utilized only when sufficient scientific evidence is unavailable to calculate an EAR and RDA, based on observed average intakes.
The Acceptable Macronutrient Distribution Range (AMDR) refers to the percentage of total energy that should be derived from fats, proteins, and carbohydrates to reduce chronic disease risk.
The Tolerable Upper Intake Level (UL) is not a goal for adequacy; rather, it is the highest average daily intake likely to pose no risk of adverse health effects in almost all individuals.
The Recommended Dietary Allowance (RDA) is specifically set at two standard deviations above the EAR to ensure it covers nearly the entire population (97-98%).

The Estimated Energy Requirement (EER) is used to predict the average dietary energy intake needed to maintain energy balance in a healthy adult, not the requirements for specific vitamins or minerals.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 357 (Book Page): [Recommended Dietary Allowance (RDA): The RDA is the average daily dietary intake level that is sufficient to meet the nutrient requirements of nearly all (97–98%) the individuals in a life stage and gender group.]

category: Define basal metabolic rate (BMR)
statement: A comparison between a 70-kg man and a 50-kg woman reveals a difference in their standard Resting Metabolic Rates (1,800 kcal vs 1,300 kcal). Which physiological factor is most consistent with this variation in RMR?
options: Men spend more energy on ion transport per cell than women.
Women have a higher thermic effect of food per kilogram.
The RMR is independent of gender and height.
Differences in body composition and weight determine the energy required for maintenance functions.
Women do not require energy for cellular integrity at rest.
correctOption: Differences in body composition and weight determine the energy required for maintenance functions.
optionExplanations: There is no evidence in the text suggesting that the rate of ion transport per individual cell differs between genders; the total requirement differs based on size.
The text does not state that the thermic effect of food differs by gender per kilogram; the RMR difference is cited based on total mass and gender.
The text explicitly states that energy requirements (including RMR) are predicted based on age, gender, height, and weight.
RMR is influenced by gender and mass; men generally have a higher RMR than women, largely due to differences in body composition (e.g., muscle mass) and overall weight.
All living organisms require energy for cellular integrity; this is a core component of RMR for both genders.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 350 (Book Page): Differences in the genetics, body composition, metabolism, and behavior of individuals make it difficult to accurately predict a person’s caloric requirements... Page 351 (Book Page): In an adult, the RMR is about 1,800 kcal for men (70 kg) and 1,300 kcal for women (50 kg).

category: Elaborate the structure of ATP synthase (complex V)
statement: In the structural elaboration of Complex V, which of the following best describes the spatial relationship and permeability of the Fo and F1 domains within the inner mitochondrial membrane?
options: F1 provides the proton channel through the cristae, while Fo is located in the intermembrane space.
Fo and F1 are both mobile carriers that move between Complex III and Complex IV.
Fo resides in the matrix to bind ADP, while F1 spans the membrane to capture protons.
Fo acts as a specialized channel within the membrane, while F1 resides entirely within the matrix.
Both domains are highly permeable to small ions and span the entire lipid bilayer.
correctOption: Fo acts as a specialized channel within the membrane, while F1 resides entirely within the matrix.
optionExplanations: This is a reversal of roles; Fo provides the channel and is in the membrane, while F1 is catalytic and in the matrix.
Mobile carriers are coenzyme Q and cytochrome c; Complex V is a large, multi-subunit stationary protein complex.
This reverses the structural roles; Fo handles membrane proton transport while F1 handles the binding and phosphorylation of ADP in the matrix.
Structural analysis shows the Fo domain is integrated into the membrane to facilitate proton transport, while the F1 domain is the extramembranous catalytic unit in the matrix.
The inner membrane is generally impermeable to ions; only the Fo domain provides a specific, controlled channel for protons.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 74 (Book Page): Complex V is a protein complex that contains a domain (F o ) that spans the inner mitochondrial membrane, and a domain (F 1 ) that appears as a sphere that protrudes into the mitochondrial matrix.

category: Define gluconeogenesis and enumerate gluconeogenic substrates (precursors)
statement: Metabolic intermediates that yield only specific molecules upon degradation are classified as ketogenic. Which of the following compounds is excluded from serving as a precursor for gluconeogenesis for this reason?
options: Glycerol
Alpha-Ketoglutarate
Leucine
Lactate
Pyruvate
correctOption: Leucine
optionExplanations: Glycerol is a key glucogenic substrate derived from triacylglycerol hydrolysis and enters the pathway as DHAP.
Alpha-ketoglutarate is an alpha-ketoacid derived from glucogenic amino acids that can enter the TCA cycle to form oxaloacetate, a direct precursor for glucose synthesis.
Leucine is an exclusively ketogenic amino acid because it is metabolized to acetyl CoA, which cannot be converted back to pyruvate due to the irreversibility of the PDH reaction.
Lactate is one of the most important gluconeogenic precursors, often recycled via the Cori cycle.
Pyruvate is the immediate starting point for the gluconeogenic pathway after it is carboxylated to oxaloacetate.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 110 (Book Page): Acetyl coenzyme A (CoA) and compounds that give rise only to acetyl CoA (for example, acetoacetate and amino acids such as lysine and leucine) cannot give rise to a net synthesis of glucose.

category: Diagnose G6PD (glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase) deficiency based on given data
statement: In contrasting the diagnostic features of G6PD A- and G6PD Mediterranean variants, which observation regarding the hemolytic episode is characteristic of the G6PD A- variant?
options: Hemolysis is more severe because the enzyme has decreased catalytic activity in all cells
Hemolysis is chronic and occurs in the absence of any oxidative stressors
Hemolysis is self-limiting as older erythrocytes are replaced by younger cells with sufficient enzyme activity
Hemolysis only occurs upon the ingestion of fava beans and never with pharmacological triggers
The enzyme is kinetically abnormal even in reticulocytes, leading to early death of all red cells
correctOption: Hemolysis is self-limiting as older erythrocytes are replaced by younger cells with sufficient enzyme activity
optionExplanations: G6PD Mediterranean (Class II) is typically more severe than G6PD A- because the enzyme stability is much lower, affecting a larger portion of the cell population.
Chronic hemolysis is associated with Class I mutations, whereas G6PD A- is a Class III mutation that requires a trigger for episodic hemolysis.
In G6PD A-, the enzyme is unstable and loses activity as the cell ages. Younger cells and reticulocytes have near-normal activity, making the hemolytic crisis self-limiting.
G6PD A- can be triggered by infection, fava beans, or various medications (AAA: Antibiotics, Antimalarials, Antipyretics), not just dietary factors.
In G6PD A-, the reticulocytes have relatively normal enzyme activity; it is the age-related decline in activity that causes the older cells to lyses preferentially.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 145 (Book Page): G6PD A- is the prototype of the moderate (Class III) form of the disease. ... most of the enzyme activity present in the reticulocytes and younger erythrocytes ... The anemia is self-limited because the older, vulnerable population of erythrocytes is replaced by younger RBCs with sufficient G6PD activity

category: Elaborate key features of various transport systems for entry of glucose into cells
statement: In the physiological regulation of blood glucose, the 'glucose sensor' in pancreatic beta cells allows the secretion of insulin only when blood glucose levels are high. Which feature of the transport system in these cells facilitates this sensing mechanism?
options: Insulin-dependent recruitment of GLUT-4
High-affinity transport by GLUT-1
Active transport against a gradient by SGLT-1
High-capacity, high-Km transport by GLUT-2
Specific fructose transport by GLUT-5
correctOption: High-capacity, high-Km transport by GLUT-2
optionExplanations: GLUT-4 is the result of insulin action, not the cause of insulin secretion. Beta cells must sense glucose to release insulin before GLUT-4 can be activated in peripheral tissues.
GLUT-1 has a low Km, meaning it is saturated at normal fasting glucose levels and cannot accurately 'sense' the magnitude of hyperglycemia.
SGLT-1 is an active transporter in the intestine; beta cells utilize facilitated diffusion (GLUT) to equilibrate intracellular glucose with the blood for sensing purposes.

GLUT-2 has a high Km, ensuring that glucose entry into beta cells is proportional to blood glucose levels over a wide range. This allows the beta cell to 'sense' hyperglycemia and initiate the insulin secretion cascade via subsequent phosphorylation by glucokinase.
GLUT-5 handles fructose, which does not serve as the primary physiological signal for insulin release in the pancreatic beta cell sensing loop.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 90 (Book Page): In β cells, glucokinase functions as the glucose sensor, determining the threshold for insulin secretion... [Note: GLUT-2 is also found in pancreatic β cells.] ...Glucokinase differs from hexokinase in several important properties. For example, it has a much higher Km, requiring a higher glucose concentration for half-saturation.

category: Enlist various types of glycogen storage diseases (GSDs)
statement: A deficiency in the amylo-α(1→4)→α(1→6)-transglucosidase enzyme leads to which specific GSD type and glycogen structure?
options: Type I (Von Gierke disease); normal glycogen structure with excessive accumulation.
Type V (McArdle syndrome); normal glycogen structure with skeletal muscle restriction.
Type II (Pompe disease); normal glycogen structure sequestered in lysosomes.
Type III (Cori disease); short outer branches and increased solubility.
Type IV (Andersen disease); long, unbranched glucose chains with reduced solubility.
correctOption: Type IV (Andersen disease); long, unbranched glucose chains with reduced solubility.
optionExplanations: Type I (Von Gierke) affects the release of glucose from glucose 6-phosphate; the glycogen synthesized and stored is structurally normal.
Type V (McArdle) is a phosphorylase deficiency; it prevents the degradation of glycogen but does not alter the synthesis or structure of the stored glycogen.
Type II involves a lysosomal enzyme defect; the structure of the glycogen synthesized in the cytosol is unaffected and remains normal.
Type III (Cori) involves a debranching deficiency, which leaves the branches intact but very short (limit dextrins) because phosphorylase cannot degrade them.

Type IV (Andersen disease) involves a deficiency in the branching enzyme, which normally creates α(1→6) bonds. Without it, the glycogen is relatively linear (amylose-like), making it less soluble and often leading to cirrhosis.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 121 (Book Page): Type IV: Andersen disease... deficiency in branching enzyme... resulting in Type IV: Andersen disease and causing death in early childhood.

category: Infer the consequences of deficiency and excess of these hormones
statement: Under the influence of the peptide hormone prolactin, which specific biochemical modification occurs in the lactating mammary gland to facilitate the synthesis of 'milk sugar'?
options: Induction of Protein A to transfer galactose to N-acetyl-D-glucosamine.
Stimulation of Protein B (alpha-lactalbumin) synthesis to alter the sugar specificity of Protein A.
Direct activation of galactokinase by insulin-like growth factor-1.
Competitive inhibition of beta-galactosidase to prevent the immediate hydrolysis of lactose.
Decreased transcription of the gene encoding UDP-hexose 4-epimerase.
correctOption: Stimulation of Protein B (alpha-lactalbumin) synthesis to alter the sugar specificity of Protein A.
optionExplanations: Protein A (galactosyltransferase) is already present in many tissues to synthesize N-acetyllactosamine; prolactin specifically stimulates Protein B to change Protein A's behavior.
Prolactin induces the synthesis of alpha-lactalbumin (Protein B), which binds to galactosyltransferase (Protein A) in the Golgi, lowering its Km for glucose and enabling the production of lactose.
The text does not mention IGF-1 as a regulator of galactokinase in the context of lactose synthesis; the key hormonal driver is prolactin acting on the B subunit.
Beta-galactosidase (lactase) is an intestinal enzyme; its inhibition in the mammary gland is not the mechanism for lactose synthesis.
UDP-hexose 4-epimerase is necessary to produce UDP-galactose from UDP-glucose for lactose synthesis; it would not be decreased during lactation.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 134 (Book Page): Protein B is alpha-lactalbumin, and its synthesis is stimulated by the peptide hormone, prolactin. Protein B forms a complex with the enzyme, protein A, changing the specificity of that transferase so that lactose... is produced.

category: Elaborate the concept and importance of Balanced Diet
coreConcept: Physiological Effects of Omega-3 Fatty Acids
statement: Regarding the metabolic utilization of dietary fats, which statement correctly identifies the cardioprotective mechanism associated with omega-3 (ω-3) polyunsaturated fatty acids found in fish oils?
options: They behave like saturated fats by increasing the risk of coronary heart disease.
They primarily function by significantly increasing the plasma concentration of LDL.
They lower plasma cholesterol by specifically inhibiting the absorption of all dietary protein.
They reduce serum triacylglycerols and suppress cardiac arrhythmias.
They act as the primary source of trans-fatty acids in commercial baked goods.
correctOption: They reduce serum triacylglycerols and suppress cardiac arrhythmias.
optionExplanations: Unlike saturated fats, omega-3 fatty acids are highly protective against CHD and reduce the risk of sudden cardiac death.
Omega-3 fats have little effect on LDL levels; they do not increase them.
Omega-3 fats do not interfere with protein absorption; their benefits are mediated through lipid and cardiovascular pathways.
The unique benefits of fish oils (EPA/DHA) include triacylglycerol reduction and stabilization of cardiac rhythm, which are distinct from the LDL-lowering of omega-6 oils.
Trans-fatty acids are primarily formed during the industrial hydrogenation of vegetable oils, not from natural fish oils.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 364 (Book Page): Dietary ω-3 polyunsaturated fats suppress cardiac arrhythmias, reduce serum triacylglycerols, decrease the tendency for thrombosis, lower blood pressure, and substantially reduce risk of cardiovascular mortality.

category: Define gluconeogenesis and enumerate gluconeogenic substrates (precursors)
coreConcept: Renal vs. Hepatic Gluconeogenesis in Starvation
statement: A 45-year-old male is trapped in a remote area without food for 10 days, consuming only water. He is currently in a state of prolonged fasting. In this specific physiological state, which of the following accurately describes the organ-specific contribution to the total glucose production via gluconeogenesis?
options: The skeletal muscle becomes the primary site of glucose release into the blood.
The brain begins to synthesize its own glucose from fatty acid backbones.
The liver provides 100% of the glucose as the kidneys cannot perform gluconeogenesis.
The kidneys contribute approximately 40% of the total glucose production.
The pancreas initiates gluconeogenesis to support insulin-independent tissues.
correctOption: The kidneys contribute approximately 40% of the total glucose production.
optionExplanations: Skeletal muscle lacks glucose 6-phosphatase and cannot release free glucose into the blood.
The brain requires a continuous supply of glucose from the blood; it cannot synthesize its own glucose.
The kidneys are capable of gluconeogenesis and their contribution increases significantly during starvation.
During prolonged starvation (as in a 10-day fast), the renal contribution to gluconeogenesis rises to nearly 40% of the total output.
The pancreas is not a gluconeogenic organ; the liver and kidneys are the primary sites.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 109 (Book Page): During an overnight fast, approximately 90% of gluconeogenesis occurs in the liver, with the kidneys providing 10% of the newly synthesized glucose molecules. However, during prolonged fasting, the kidneys become major glucose-producing organs, contributing an estimated 40% of the total glucose production.

category: Define basal metabolic rate (BMR)
coreConcept: Contribution of RMR to Total Energy Expenditure
statement: In a sedentary adult, what is the typical percentage of total daily energy expenditure (TEE) accounted for by the Resting Metabolic Rate (RMR)?
options: Over 90%
optionExplanations: The majority of energy used by a sedentary person (50-70%) is dedicated simply to maintaining basic life functions (RMR).
5% to 10% is the contribution of the thermic effect of food to the total energy expenditure.
45% to 65% is the AMDR for carbohydrates, not the TEE percentage for RMR.
20% to 35% is the Acceptable Macronutrient Distribution Range (AMDR) for fat, not the TEE percentage for RMR.
While RMR is the largest component, physical activity and the thermic effect of food ensure it is rarely over 90% of TEE.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 359 (Book Page) / 531: From 50–70% of the daily energy expenditure in sedentary individuals is attributable to the RMR.

category: Describe the TCA cycle along with regulation & significance
statement: A researcher is studying the regulation of the Pyruvate Dehydrogenase (PDH) complex. They find that the addition of specific compounds leads to the inactivation of the E1 component through phosphorylation. Which of the following sets of mitochondrial signals most likely stimulates the kinase responsible for this inhibition?
options: High Calcium and Low NADH
High Pyruvate and High Calcium
High Pyruvate and High ADP
Low ATP and High NAD+
High ATP, High Acetyl CoA, and High NADH
correctOption: High ATP, High Acetyl CoA, and High NADH
optionExplanations: Calcium is a strong activator of PDH phosphatase, which dephosphorylates and activates the complex, the opposite of the described inhibition.
Both pyruvate and calcium act as inhibitors of the kinase or activators of the phosphatase, respectively, ensuring the PDH complex remains active to process fuel.
Pyruvate is a potent inhibitor of PDH kinase; its presence would keep the complex active by preventing phosphorylation. High ADP is a low-energy signal that does not activate the kinase.
Low ATP and high NAD+ are signals of energy depletion that would favor the active, dephosphorylated state of the PDH complex to increase energy production.

High levels of ATP, Acetyl CoA, and NADH indicate a high-energy state. These molecules allosterically activate PDH kinase, which then phosphorylates the E1 subunit, rendering the PDH complex inactive.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 103 (Book Page): The cyclic AMP-independent PDH kinase phosphorylates and, thereby, inhibits E1... The kinase itself is allosterically activated by ATP, acetyl CoA, and NADH. Therefore, in the presence of these high-energy signals, the PDH complex is turned off.

category: Delineate special nutritional requirements during pregnancy, lactation, growth, and old age
statement: An 18-month-old child is brought to a clinic in a developing region. The mother states the child was weaned 6 months ago to a diet of native cereal gruels. On examination, the child is irritable, has an enlarged fatty liver, and displays significant abdominal and peripheral edema. Which nutritional deficiency syndrome and associated laboratory finding are most consistent with this presentation?
options: Von Gierke disease; characterized by hyperlacticacidemia and hyperuricemia
Scurvy; characterized by hemorrhage and impaired collagen synthesis
Marasmus; characterized by markedly decreased weight for height
Kwashiorkor; characterized by severely decreased serum albumin
Essential fatty acid deficiency; characterized by scaly dermatitis and hair loss
correctOption: Kwashiorkor; characterized by severely decreased serum albumin
optionExplanations: Von Gierke disease is a glycogen storage disease. While it presents with hepatomegaly and hypoglycemia, it is not a result of weaning-induced protein malnutrition.
Scurvy results from Vitamin C deficiency and causes bruising and gum issues, but does not typically present with the protein-deficient edema and fatty liver seen in this child.
Marasmus is caused by an overall calorie deficiency and is characterized by extreme muscle wasting (emaciation) without the edema or fatty liver seen here.

The clinical picture of edema (caused by low oncotic pressure from hypoalbuminemia) and a fatty liver (due to reduced apolipoprotein synthesis) after weaning onto a low-protein diet is the classic presentation of Kwashiorkor.
Essential fatty acid deficiency does cause skin issues, but it would not explain the severe edema or the specific weaning history described.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 361 (Book Page): Kwashiorkor occurs when protein deprivation is relatively greater than the reduction in total calories. Typical symptoms include stunted growth, edema, skin lesions, depigmented hair, anorexia, enlarged fatty liver, and decreased plasma albumin concentration.

category: Describe the TCA cycle along with regulation & significance
statement: In the regulation of the pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDH) complex, which mechanism describes the inhibitory effect of high mitochondrial ATP levels?
options: Allosteric inhibition of the E1 decarboxylase subunit by ATP
Activation of PDH kinase, which phosphorylates and inactivates the E1 subunit
Competitive inhibition of dihydrolipoyl transacetylase by ADP
Direct cleavage of the thiamine pyrophosphate coenzyme
Dephosphorylation of the E1 subunit by PDH phosphatase
correctOption: Activation of PDH kinase, which phosphorylates and inactivates the E1 subunit
optionExplanations: ATP does not act as a direct allosteric inhibitor of the E1 subunit; its inhibitory effect is mediated through the action of a specific regulatory kinase.
High levels of ATP allosterically activate PDH kinase. Once activated, this kinase phosphorylates the E1 subunit (pyruvate dehydrogenase), rendering the entire complex inactive.
Dihydrolipoyl transacetylase (E2) is inhibited by its product, acetyl CoA, rather than being competitively inhibited by ADP, which is a low-energy signal.
Thiamine pyrophosphate is a tightly bound coenzyme for E1; its physiological regulation does not involve direct enzymatic cleavage or destruction.
PDH phosphatase is responsible for dephosphorylating and thus activating the PDH complex, often in response to calcium signals, which is the opposite of the effect of ATP.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 103 (Book Page): Covalent modification by the two regulatory enzymes that are part of the complex alternately activate and inactivate E1 (PDH). The cyclic AMP-independent PDH kinase phosphorylates and, thereby, inhibits E1 (PDH)... The kinase itself is allosterically activated by ATP, acetyl CoA, and NADH.

category: Enlist the hormones that play important roles in regulating carbohydrate metabolism
statement: A 24-year-old male is fasting for a religious observance. Which of the following hormonal signals is primarily responsible for increasing intracellular cyclic AMP (cAMP) levels to initiate hepatic glycogenolysis?
options: Cortisol
Thyroxine
Glucagon
Somatostatin
Insulin
correctOption: Glucagon
optionExplanations: Cortisol is a steroid hormone that acts via nuclear receptors to influence gene transcription (like PEPCK) rather than acutely raising cAMP levels.
Thyroxine generally increases the basal metabolic rate but does not serve as the primary acute messenger for cAMP-mediated glycogenolysis in the fasting state.

Glucagon binds to its G protein-coupled receptor (GPCR) on hepatocytes, activating adenylyl cyclase which converts ATP to cAMP, the primary second messenger for activating protein kinase A and subsequent glycogen degradation.
Somatostatin is a paracrine inhibitor that typically inhibits the release of both insulin and glucagon, but it does not directly stimulate glycogenolysis via cAMP.
Insulin is a tyrosine kinase receptor-linked hormone that lowers cAMP levels by activating phosphodiesterase, thereby inhibiting glycogenolysis.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 124 (Book Page): Binding of glucagon or epinephrine to their specific hepatocyte GPCR, or of epinephrine to specific myocyte GPCR, results in the G protein-mediated activation of adenylyl cyclase. This enzyme catalyzes the synthesis of cAMP, which activates cAMP-dependent protein kinase A (PKA).

category: Elaborate the regulation and importance of gluconeogenesis
statement: A medical student is studying the importance of gluconeogenesis during the transition from an overnight fast to prolonged starvation. Which of the following best describes the physiological significance of this pathway during an extended period without dietary carbohydrate intake?
options: It allows the skeletal muscle to release free glucose into the systemic circulation.
It prevents the production of ketone bodies by diverting acetyl CoA into glucose synthesis.
It utilizes acetyl CoA derived from fatty acid oxidation as a direct carbon precursor for glucose.
It enables the liver and kidneys to synthesize glucose to meet the needs of the brain and erythrocytes.
It serves as the primary source of glucose for the first 10–18 hours of fasting.
correctOption: It enables the liver and kidneys to synthesize glucose to meet the needs of the brain and erythrocytes.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. Muscle lacks glucose 6-phosphatase and therefore cannot release free glucose into the blood; it uses its glycogen stores internally for glycolysis.
Incorrect. Gluconeogenesis does not prevent ketone body production; in fact, both pathways are active during fasting as the liver processes fatty acids.
Incorrect. Acetyl CoA cannot be used for net synthesis of glucose in humans due to the irreversible nature of the pyruvate dehydrogenase reaction.
Correct. The brain and erythrocytes have an absolute requirement for glucose. During prolonged fasting, gluconeogenesis in the liver and kidneys provides this essential fuel.
Incorrect. Liver glycogen is the essential postprandial source of glucose for the first 10–18 hours; gluconeogenesis becomes the dominant source only after these stores are depleted.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 109 (Book Page): [Some tissues, such as the brain, red blood cells, kidney medulla, lens and cornea of the eye, testes, and exercising muscle, require a continuous supply of glucose as a metabolic fuel... During a prolonged fast, however, hepatic glycogen stores are depleted, and glucose is formed from precursors... by a special pathway, gluconeogenesis.]

category: Enlist the hormones that play important roles in regulating carbohydrate metabolism
statement: Which hormone primarily initiates the signaling cascade that increases the synthesis of glucokinase, phosphofructokinase, and pyruvate kinase in the liver during the well-fed state?
options: Insulin
Glucagon
Thyroxine
Cortisol
Epinephrine
correctOption: Insulin
optionExplanations: Insulin acts as an anabolic signal in the well-fed state, promoting the transcription of genes for key regulatory enzymes of glycolysis to facilitate glucose utilization.
Glucagon acts in opposition to insulin, decreasing the transcription and synthesis of these key glycolytic enzymes during fasting states.
Thyroxine increases overall metabolic rate and some glucose uptake, but it is not the primary hormone cited for the specific coordinated induction of the three key glycolytic kinases.

While cortisol influences metabolism, it is typically associated with the induction of gluconeogenic enzymes rather than a direct, primary role in the induction of these three specific glycolytic regulators.
Epinephrine primarily acts to mobilize fuels during stress and inhibits insulin secretion; it does not promote the long-term synthesis of glycolytic enzymes in the liver.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 97 (Book Page): [Regular consumption of meals rich in carbohydrate or administration of insulin initiates an increase in the amount of glucokinase, phosphofructokinase, and pyruvate kinase in liver. These changes reflect an increase in gene transcription, resulting in increased enzyme synthesis.]

category: Define basal metabolic rate (BMR)
statement: What is the formal biochemical definition of the resting metabolic rate (RMR), which was historically referred to as the basal metabolic rate?
options: The energy expended during the maximum rate of physical exertion.
The total daily caloric intake minus the energy used for physical activity.
The minimum number of calories needed to maintain nitrogen balance during growth.
The heat produced specifically during the digestion and absorption of macronutrients.
The energy required to carry out normal body functions in a resting, postabsorptive state.
correctOption: The energy required to carry out normal body functions in a resting, postabsorptive state.
optionExplanations: Energy expended during maximum exertion is related to physical activity levels, not the resting or basal state.
Total daily energy expenditure includes RMR, the thermic effect of food, and physical activity; subtracting only activity leaves both RMR and the thermic effect of food.
Nitrogen balance is a measure of protein metabolism, whereas RMR is a measure of total energy expenditure.
This describes the thermic effect of food (diet-induced thermogenesis), not the resting metabolic rate.
The RMR is defined as the energy required for basic maintenance of life (respiration, blood flow, etc.) in a resting, postabsorptive individual.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 359 (Book Page): The energy expended by an individual in a resting, postabsorptive state is called the resting (formerly, basal) metabolic rate (RMR).

category: Elaborate key features of various transport systems for entry of glucose into cells
statement: Which of the following describes the thermodynamic direction of glucose movement during facilitated diffusion mediated by the GLUT protein family?
options: Coupled to the efflux of potassium ions from the cell.
From high extracellular concentration to lower intracellular concentration.
Independently of the glucose concentration gradient.
Against the concentration gradient using ATP hydrolysis.
From low concentration to high concentration via a sodium symport.
correctOption: From high extracellular concentration to lower intracellular concentration.
optionExplanations: Glucose transport via GLUTs is not coupled to ion gradients; it is the transporter's conformational change that moves the sugar.
Facilitated diffusion uses a carrier protein to allow a polar molecule like glucose to move down its chemical concentration gradient without energy input.
Facilitated diffusion is entirely dependent on the concentration gradient; transport stops once equilibrium is reached.
Active transport moves molecules against a gradient; facilitated diffusion is a passive process that does not use ATP.
Moving from low to high concentration via a sodium symport is the mechanism of SGLT, not the GLUT facilitated diffusion family.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 89 (Book Page): In facilitated diffusion, glucose movement follows a concentration gradient, that is, from a high glucose concentration to a lower one.

category: Elaborate key features of various transport systems for entry of glucose into cells
statement: A 45-year-old male with type 2 diabetes and a BMI of 34 kg\/m2 presents for a follow-up. He has high fasting blood glucose. His physician explains that his muscle cells are not effectively 'clearing' glucose from his blood because of impaired signaling for a specific transporter. Which physiological process is most likely defective in this patient?
options: Activation of the SGLT-1 transporter in the renal tubules
The export of glucose from the liver via GLUT-2 during the postprandial state
Insulin-induced translocation of GLUT-4 from intracellular vesicles to the plasma membrane
The high-affinity binding of glucose to GLUT-1 in the blood-brain barrier
Fructose-specific transport in the small intestine via GLUT-5
correctOption: Insulin-induced translocation of GLUT-4 from intracellular vesicles to the plasma membrane
optionExplanations: SGLT-1 in the renal tubules is responsible for glucose reabsorption from the urine, but its defect would lead to glucosuria, not necessarily the peripheral insulin resistance seen in Type 2 Diabetes.
Hepatocytes do not use GLUT-4; they use GLUT-2. Furthermore, in the postprandial state, the liver should be taking up glucose for glycogen synthesis, not exporting it.

In skeletal muscle and adipose tissue, GLUT-4 is stored in intracellular vesicles. Insulin signaling normally triggers these vesicles to fuse with the plasma membrane. In insulin resistance (Type 2 diabetes), this translocation is impaired, leading to hyperglycemia.
GLUT-1 in the blood-brain barrier is insulin-independent and provides a basal supply of glucose to the brain. It is not responsible for the massive postprandial glucose clearance required by muscle.
GLUT-5 is specific for fructose transport. While fructose metabolism can be related to metabolic syndrome, the primary defect in blood glucose clearance in diabetes involves GLUT-4 and glucose.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 97 (Book Page): GLUT-4 is abundant in adipose tissue and skeletal muscle. [Note: The number of GLUT-4 transporters active in these tissues is increased by insulin.]

category: Suggest dietary advice for patients suffering from diabetes mellitus, hypertension, obesity, renal disease, lactose intolerance, gluten enteropathy, hypercholesterolemia, and hemorrhoids
coreConcept: Pathophysiological Contrast of PEM: Kwashiorkor vs. Marasmus
statement: When comparing the two extreme forms of protein-energy malnutrition (PEM), which pathophysiological distinction is most characteristic of Kwashiorkor as opposed to Marasmus?
options: A high glycemic response due to a diet composed exclusively of complex polysaccharides.
A severe reduction in visceral protein synthesis resulting in hypoalbuminemia and edema.
The absence of skin lesions and depigmented hair commonly found in calorie-deprived infants.
The presence of extreme muscle wasting and emaciation due to a total calorie deficiency.
Maintenance of the immune system's ability to resist secondary bacterial infections.
correctOption: A severe reduction in visceral protein synthesis resulting in hypoalbuminemia and edema.
optionExplanations: Glycemic response is a measure of postprandial glucose rise and is irrelevant to the differentiation of PEM types based on visceral protein synthesis.
Kwashiorkor is characterized by a selective protein deficiency. This leads to decreased hepatic synthesis of albumin, resulting in a loss of plasma oncotic pressure and subsequent systemic edema.
Kwashiorkor actually features skin lesions and depigmented hair, whereas Marasmus lacks these specific inflammatory/nutritional indicators.
Extreme muscle wasting and emaciation are the hallmarks of Marasmus, where there is a global deficiency of both protein and total calories.
Both forms of PEM lead to a depressed immune system; neither maintains the ability to resist secondary infections effectively.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 361 (Book Page): Kwashiorkor occurs when protein deprivation is relatively greater than the reduction in total calories. Protein deprivation is associated with severely decreased synthesis of visceral protein... Typical symptoms include... edema... and decreased plasma albumin concentration.

category: Elaborate key features of various transport systems for entry of glucose into cells
statement: In the intestinal epithelium, the transport of glucose from the lumen into the mucosal cell occurs against a concentration gradient. What is the immediate energetic requirement for this specific transport mechanism?
options: The presence of a high-affinity fructose binding site
Passive movement through aquaporin-like channels
Coupling with the downward concentration gradient of Sodium (Na+)
Direct hydrolysis of ATP by the transporter protein
Facilitated diffusion through a conformational change in GLUT-2
correctOption: Coupling with the downward concentration gradient of Sodium (Na+)
optionExplanations: Fructose uptake in the intestine is mediated by GLUT-5, which is a sodium-independent facilitated diffusion system, not a secondary active transport system.
Glucose is a polar molecule and cannot pass through passive channels or the lipid bilayer; it requires specific carrier proteins like SGLTs or GLUTs.
The sodium-monosaccharide cotransporter (SGLT) uses the potential energy of the sodium gradient (high outside, low inside) to drag glucose into the cell against its own chemical gradient.
The SGLT system does not use direct ATP hydrolysis (primary active transport); instead, it utilizes the ion gradient established by the Na+/K+ ATPase.
GLUT-2 is involved in the facilitated diffusion of glucose out of the mucosal cell into the portal circulation, not the initial uptake from the intestinal lumen against a gradient.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 97 (Book Page): This system is a carrier-mediated process in which the movement of glucose is coupled to the concentration gradient of Na+, which is transported into the cell at the same time. The carrier is a sodium-dependent–glucose transporter or SGLT.

category: Describe the reactions, regulation, and biomedical importance of uronic acid pathway and sorbitol pathway
statement: A sugar alcohol is chemically characterized by which of the following modifications to a standard monosaccharide?
options: Oxidation of the aldehyde group to a carboxyl group.
Phosphorylation of the carbon 6 position.
Reduction of the aldehyde or ketone group to a hydroxyl group.
Replacement of a hydroxyl group with an amino group.
Formation of a glycosidic bond between two anomeric carbons.
correctOption: Reduction of the aldehyde or ketone group to a hydroxyl group.
optionExplanations: Oxidation of the aldehyde group to a carboxyl group produces an aldonic acid (like gluconic acid), not a sugar alcohol.
Phosphorylation at carbon 6 creates a sugar phosphate (like glucose 6-phosphate), which is an intermediate of glycolysis, not a polyol.
A polyol or sugar alcohol (like sorbitol) is produced when the carbonyl group (aldehyde in glucose) is reduced to a hydroxyl group.
Replacing a hydroxyl with an amino group creates an amino sugar (like glucosamine), not a sugar alcohol.
A glycosidic bond between two anomeric carbons forms a non-reducing disaccharide (like sucrose), not a polyol.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 131 (Book Page): An alternate mechanism for metabolizing a monosaccharide is to convert it to a polyol (sugar alcohol) by the reduction of an aldehyde group, thereby producing an additional hydroxyl group.

category: Enlist the components of balanced diet and elaborate the importance of each component
statement: A strict vegan is planning a diet and is concerned about the protein quality of plant-based sources. They decide to combine wheat and kidney beans in their meals. Why is this specific combination considered to have a higher biological value than eating either food alone?
options: Combining them prevents the denaturation of plant proteins during the digestion process.
Wheat is rich in methionine and poor in lysine, while beans are rich in lysine and poor in methionine.
Wheat is rich in lysine and poor in methionine, while beans are rich in methionine and poor in lysine.
The fiber in the beans increases the bioavailability of the essential amino acids found in wheat.
Wheat and beans both contain all essential amino acids in proportions identical to human tissue.
correctOption: Wheat is rich in methionine and poor in lysine, while beans are rich in lysine and poor in methionine.
