citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 126 (Book Page): Binding of epinephrine to hepatocyte alpha-1-adrenergic G protein-coupled receptors activates a phospholipid-dependent cascade... results in movement of Ca2+ from the ER... activates hepatic phosphorylase kinase b. [Note: Epinephrine at beta-adrenergic receptors signals through a rise in cAMP, not calcium.]

category: Enlist the components of balanced diet and elaborate the importance of each component
statement: In the context of macronutrient energy content, which of the following substances provides the highest caloric density per gram when metabolized in a calorimeter?
options: Purified plant starch
Soluble dietary fiber
Triacylglycerols
Ethanol
Animal-derived protein
correctOption: Triacylglycerols
optionExplanations: Starch is a carbohydrate and yields approximately 4 kcal/g.
Fiber provides very little energy (approaching 0 to 2 kcal/g depending on fermentation), far less than the other macronutrients.
Fats (triacylglycerols) are the most energy-dense macronutrient, yielding 9 kcal/g due to their highly reduced chemical structure.
Ethanol yields 7 kcal/g, which is higher than carbohydrates but lower than fats.
Proteins yield approximately 4 kcal/g, similar to carbohydrates.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 359 (Book Page): Note that the energy content of fat is more than twice that of carbohydrate or protein, whereas the energy content of ethanol is intermediate between those of fat and carbohydrate.

category: Diagnose G6PD (glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase) deficiency based on given data
statement: When distinguishing between the various genetic variants of G6PD deficiency, which clinical or biochemical contrast is characteristic of the G6PD Mediterranean (Class II) variant compared to G6PD A- (Class III)?
options: The Mediterranean variant is associated with chronic nonspherocytic anemia even without triggers.
The Mediterranean variant results in a much lower residual enzyme activity due to severe instability.
G6PD A- is more severe because it affects reticulocytes and young erythrocytes equally.
The Mediterranean variant shows normal enzyme stability but decreased catalytic affinity.
Only the Mediterranean variant is triggered by fava beans, while G6PD A- is not.
correctOption: The Mediterranean variant results in a much lower residual enzyme activity due to severe instability.
optionExplanations: Chronic nonspherocytic anemia is the hallmark of Class I mutations; Class II (Mediterranean) usually presents with episodic hemolysis triggered by stress.
G6PD Mediterranean is a Class II mutation with <10% residual activity, whereas G6PD A- is Class III with 10-60% activity, making the Mediterranean variant significantly more severe.
In G6PD A-, the younger cells (reticulocytes) have nearly normal activity, which is why the hemolysis is self-limiting; this is less true for the Mediterranean variant.
The Mediterranean variant is specifically characterized by decreased stability of the enzyme protein, leading to a rapid loss of activity as the cell ages.
While 'favism' is more common in the Mediterranean variant, both can theoretically be affected by severe oxidative stress; the primary distinction is the level of residual activity.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 145 (Book Page): G6PD Mediterranean is the prototype of a more severe (Class II) deficiency in which the enzyme has decreased stability resulting in decreased enzymic activity.

category: Differentiate between Kwashiorkor and Marasmus based on the given data
statement: When comparing the clinical behavioral and dietary presentation of Protein-Energy Malnutrition, which set of features is characteristic of Marasmus?
options: Alert and irritable mood with a good appetite
Listless behavior with a preference for carbohydrate gruels
Lethargic behavior with no interest in feeding
Irritable only when picked up with a poor appetite
Apathetic mood with a poor appetite
correctOption: Alert and irritable mood with a good appetite
optionExplanations: Children with Marasmus are typically alert and irritable, and because their primary deficiency is calories, they maintain a vigorous appetite and are often eager to eat.
While they may eat carbohydrate gruels, the behavioral description of 'listless' specifically fits the visceral protein deprivation found in Kwashiorkor.
Lethargy and lack of interest in feeding (anorexia) are common in the severe protein deprivation of Kwashiorkor rather than the calorie hunger of Marasmus.
The description of being irritable when picked up but apathetic otherwise describes the classic mood of a child with Kwashiorkor.
An apathetic mood and poor appetite (anorexia) are clinical hallmarks of Kwashiorkor, not Marasmus.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 358 (Book Page): CHARACTERISTIC... MARASMUS... Mood: Alert, irritable... Appetite: Good

category: Clearly differentiate between upper body obesity and lower body obesity
statement: Which of the following is the most significant clinical outcome associated with lower body obesity compared to upper body obesity?
options: Stronger correlation with hypertension
Higher risk of developing Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus
Increased risk of hepatic steatosis
Lower risk of metabolic complications
Higher incidence of Metabolic Syndrome
correctOption: Lower risk of metabolic complications
optionExplanations: Hypertension is one of the components of Metabolic Syndrome and is more strongly correlated with upper body obesity.
The risk of Type 2 Diabetes is much higher in upper body (android) obesity due to insulin resistance.
Hepatic steatosis (fatty liver) is linked to the high flux of FFAs through the portal vein from visceral (upper body) fat.

Lower body fat (gynoid) is relatively metabolically 'stable' and does not release inflammatory mediators or FFAs into the portal vein as aggressively as visceral fat, resulting in lower metabolic risk.
Metabolic Syndrome is primarily driven by central/visceral adiposity, not lower body fat.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 342 (Book Page): Lower body obesity (gynoid, pear-shaped, or peripheral)... is associated with a much lower risk of metabolic complications.

category: Describe the TCA cycle along with regulation & significance
coreConcept: Energy Yield of the TCA Cycle
statement: What is the total net yield of high-energy phosphate bonds produced directly through substrate-level phosphorylation during one complete turn of the tricarboxylic acid cycle?
options: Twelve ATP
Two ATP
One GTP (or ATP)
Zero
Three NADH
correctOption: One GTP (or ATP)
optionExplanations: Twelve ATP is the total yield per acetyl CoA after oxidative phosphorylation is completed in the ETC, but only one of those is produced 'directly' by the cycle itself.
While two carbons enter the cycle, they only produce one direct high-energy phosphate bond. The rest of the energy is captured as reduced coenzymes.
One turn of the TCA cycle produces exactly one GTP (equivalent to one ATP) at the succinate thiokinase step via substrate-level phosphorylation.
The TCA cycle does produce energy directly at one specific step, so the yield is not zero.
Three NADH are produced, but these are reduced coenzymes that require the electron transport chain to produce ATP; they are not themselves high-energy phosphate bonds.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 105 (Book Page): The generation of GTP by succinate thiokinase is another example of substrate-level phosphorylation... The total yield of ATP from the oxidation of one acetyl CoA is [Page 113 (Book Page)] 12 ATP... [but only] 1 GTP comes from substrate level phosphorylation.

category: Describe the effect of arsenic poisoning on carbohydrate metabolism and ATP production
coreConcept: Contrast between Arsenate Glycolytic Bypass and Arsenite Enzyme Inhibition
statement: A biochemist is analyzing the effects of different arsenic oxidation states on cellular respiration. In contrast to arsenate’s effect on glycolysis, how does trivalent arsenite specifically disrupt the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle?
options: By inhibiting the reoxidation of FADH2 at Complex II
By uncoupling oxidative phosphorylation at the F0 domain of ATP synthase
By acting as a competitive inhibitor of oxaloacetate at the citrate synthase step
By forming a stable complex with the lipoic acid coenzyme of alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase
By preventing the transport of pyruvate across the inner mitochondrial membrane
correctOption: By forming a stable complex with the lipoic acid coenzyme of alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase
optionExplanations: Complex II (succinate dehydrogenase) contains FAD and iron-sulfur centers but does not rely on lipoic acid. Arsenite's primary mechanism involves thiol binding on lipoic acid-dependent complexes, which does not include Complex II.

While arsenic can replace phosphate in the F1 domain of ATP synthase to form ADP-arsenate, this is an effect of pentavalent arsenic (arsenate) or general arsenic poisoning, not the specific mechanism by which trivalent arsenite inhibits TCA cycle dehydrogenases.

Oxaloacetate binding to citrate synthase is a regulated step, but arsenic does not compete with oxaloacetate. Arsenic toxicity is primarily centered on enzymes requiring lipoic acid or phosphate mimetic reactions.

Alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase is a multienzyme complex analogous to pyruvate dehydrogenase. Trivalent arsenite binds strongly to the sulfhydryl groups of the lipoic acid cofactor in the E2 subunit of this complex, effectively stopping the TCA cycle at this step.

Pyruvate enters the mitochondria via a specific transporter. Arsenic toxicity occurs once pyruvate is already in the matrix (via PDH inhibition) or in the cytosol (via G3PDH bypass), but it is not known to inhibit the pyruvate transporter itself.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 103 (Book Page): “Arsenic poisoning” is, however, due primarily to inhibition of enzymes that require lipoic acid as a coenzyme, including E2 of the PDH complex, ( -ketoglutarate dehydrogenase (see below)... Arsenite (the trivalent form of arsenic) forms a stable complex with the thiol (–SH) groups of lipoic acid, making that compound unavailable to serve as a coenzyme.

category: Define basal metabolic rate (BMR)
statement: In the physiological maintenance of a healthy adult, which mechanistic processes are primarily powered by the energy expenditure accounted for in the resting metabolic rate?
options: Digestion of complex carbohydrates and emulsification of dietary fats.
Respiration, blood flow, ion transport, and maintenance of cellular integrity.
Muscular contraction required for heavy physical labor or athletic performance.
Bile acid synthesis and hydroxylation of vitamin D in the kidney.
Synthesis of glycogen and triacylglycerol during the fed state.
correctOption: Respiration, blood flow, ion transport, and maintenance of cellular integrity.
optionExplanations: Energy used for digestion and absorption is classified as the thermic effect of food (TEF), which is distinct from the RMR.
These are the essential 'housekeeping' functions of the body that continue at a baseline rate even when the body is at rest, comprising the RMR.
Physical activity provides the greatest variation in total energy expenditure but is an addition to, not a part of, the RMR.

While these are metabolic functions, the definition specifically highlights respiration, blood flow, and ion transport as the representative housekeeping functions of RMR energy use in the reference text. Option C is the direct definition from the text provided for BMR/RMR components.
Glycogen and fat synthesis are anabolic processes largely occurring postprandially; RMR measures energy used for maintenance in the postabsorptive state.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 359 (Book Page): It represents the energy required to carry out the normal body functions, such as respiration, blood flow, ion transport, and maintenance of cellular integrity.

category: Clearly differentiate between substrate level phosphorylation and oxidative phosphorylation
statement: During anaerobic glycolysis in a mature erythrocyte, the cell remains viable despite the absence of mitochondria. This viability is entirely dependent on which bioenergetic principle?
options: The utilization of the malate-aspartate shuttle to move reducing equivalents into the matrix.
The capture of free energy from substrate-level phosphorylation at the phosphoglycerate kinase and pyruvate kinase steps.
The production of heat through the action of uncoupling proteins in the inner membrane.
The conversion of lactate to pyruvate to regenerate ATP via oxidative phosphorylation.
The oxidation of NADH by the electron transport chain to produce 3 ATP per glucose.
correctOption: The capture of free energy from substrate-level phosphorylation at the phosphoglycerate kinase and pyruvate kinase steps.
optionExplanations: The malate-aspartate shuttle requires a mitochondrial matrix and the ETC to function, neither of which is present in a mature red blood cell.

In anaerobic glycolysis, the cell nets 2 ATP solely through substrate-level phosphorylation (at the steps of PGK and PK). This provides the essential energy needed to maintain ionic gradients and cell shape.
Uncoupling proteins generate heat by dissipating a proton gradient in mitochondria. Without mitochondria, erythrocytes cannot utilize this mechanism.
In anaerobic conditions, pyruvate is converted TO lactate (via LDH) to regenerate NAD+ for glycolysis. The cell cannot oxidize lactate to pyruvate for energy because it lacks the TCA cycle and ETC.
Erythrocytes lack mitochondria and thus cannot perform oxidative phosphorylation or use the electron transport chain to oxidize NADH.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 96 (Book Page): 1. Anaerobic glycolysis: Two molecules of ATP are generated for each molecule of glucose converted to two molecules of lactate (Figure 8.22). There is no net production or consumption of NADH. Page 94 (Book Page): [Erythrocytes] lack mitochondria and [are] therefore completely dependent on glycolysis for production of ATP... fueling the pumps necessary for the maintenance of the biconcave, flexible shape.

category: Enlist causes and types of Protein Energy Malnutrition (PEM)
statement: In the pathophysiology of Kwashiorkor, which underlying biochemical mechanism is primarily responsible for the characteristic development of peripheral edema?
options: Increased capillary hydrostatic pressure due to cardiac failure
Increased vascular permeability caused by systemic inflammatory cytokines
Decreased plasma albumin concentration resulting from impaired visceral protein synthesis
Excessive intake of sodium leading to water retention
Chronic renal failure leading to decreased glomerular filtration of water
correctOption: Decreased plasma albumin concentration resulting from impaired visceral protein synthesis
optionExplanations: While heart failure can cause edema, the primary cause in Kwashiorkor is the lack of oncotic pressure, not a primary pump failure.
Inflammatory cytokines can cause edema in sepsis, but in Kwashiorkor, the mechanism is the steady-state lack of protein substrates for albumin synthesis.
The severe lack of dietary protein leads to a marked decrease in the synthesis of visceral proteins like albumin, lowering plasma oncotic pressure and causing fluid to leak into the tissues (edema).
Kwashiorkor is defined by protein deprivation, not primary sodium toxicity; water retention occurs because the low oncotic pressure cannot keep fluid in the vessels.
Though renal function can be impacted in late-stage PEM, the hallmark edema is specifically tied to the oncotic pressure drop from hypoalbuminemia.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 361 (Book Page): Edema results from the lack of adequate plasma proteins to maintain the distribution of water between blood and tissues.

category: Enlist the components of complex I, II, III, and IV
statement: In the structural classification of the mitochondrial respiratory chain, all members are protein complexes except for which ubiquitous mobile component?
options: NADH dehydrogenase
Coenzyme Q
Cytochrome a
Cytochrome c1
Succinate dehydrogenase
correctOption: Coenzyme Q
optionExplanations: NADH dehydrogenase is a large protein complex (Complex I) consisting of multiple subunits including flavoproteins and iron-sulfur proteins.
Coenzyme Q (ubiquinone) is a non-protein quinone derivative with a hydrophobic isoprenoid tail, distinguishing it as the only non-protein member of the chain.
Cytochrome a is a protein subunit of Complex IV (Cytochrome oxidase) containing a heme group.
Cytochrome c1 is a protein component of Complex III (Cytochrome bc1 complex) and is not a non-protein lipid-soluble derivative.
Succinate dehydrogenase is a protein complex (Complex II) that serves as an enzyme in both the TCA cycle and the electron transport chain.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 74 (Book Page): With the exception of coenzyme Q, all members of this chain are proteins.

category: Diagrammatically illustrate the organization of electron transport chain (ETC) depicting the flow of electrons
statement: A researcher is comparing the mechanisms of electron entry into the respiratory chain. Which of the following best describes the functional contrast between Coenzyme Q and Cytochrome c within the organization of the electron transport chain?
options: Coenzyme Q accepts electrons only from Complex I, while Cytochrome c accepts only from Complex II.
Both are embedded within the inner membrane lipid bilayer as stationary prosthetic groups.
Coenzyme Q is a fixed protein complex, whereas Cytochrome c is a mobile lipid-soluble carrier.
Coenzyme Q reacts directly with molecular oxygen, while Cytochrome c reacts with water.
Coenzyme Q is a mobile lipid-soluble carrier, whereas Cytochrome c is a mobile peripheral protein.
correctOption: Coenzyme Q is a mobile lipid-soluble carrier, whereas Cytochrome c is a mobile peripheral protein.
optionExplanations: Coenzyme Q is a collection point for electrons from both Complex I and Complex II (as well as others); Cytochrome c receives electrons specifically from Complex III.
Both are mobile carriers, not stationary groups. This mobility is essential for transferring electrons between the large, relatively immobile protein complexes (I, III, and IV).
Coenzyme Q is actually mobile and lipid-soluble due to its long isoprenoid tail, while Cytochrome c is the protein component.
Neither of these carriers reacts with oxygen; only the Cytochrome a+a3 complex (Complex IV) has the coordination site to bind and reduce oxygen to water.

Correct. Coenzyme Q (ubiquinone) is a non-protein, lipid-soluble quinone that moves within the hydrophobic interior of the membrane. Cytochrome c is a water-soluble protein located on the outer surface (cytosolic side) of the inner mitochondrial membrane.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 75 (Book Page): CoQ is a mobile carrier and can accept hydrogen atoms both from FMNH2... and from FADH2... Page 76 (Book Page): [Note: Cytochrome c is associated with the outer face of the inner membrane and, like CoQ, is a mobile carrier of electrons.]

category: Delineate special nutritional requirements during pregnancy, lactation, growth, and old age
statement: A 32-year-old woman, currently lactating and weighing 60 kg, requires a dietary assessment. Based on the specialized nutritional requirements for her current physiological state, what is the total recommended daily protein intake to support both her maintenance and milk production?
options: 48 g/day
60 g/day
78 g/day
90 g/day
120 g/day
correctOption: 78 g/day
optionExplanations: 48 g/day (60 kg x 0.8) only covers the basal requirement for a non-pregnant, non-lactating adult female.
60 g/day is 1.0 g/kg, which is an arbitrary figure that does not account for the specific +30 g/day supplement required for lactation.
The calculation involves the basal adult RDA (60 kg x 0.8 g/kg = 48 g/day) plus the specialized lactational requirement of 30 g/day, totaling 78 g/day.
90 g/day is an overestimation and does not follow the specific RDA calculations provided in the standard chief examiner reference material.
120 g/day is excessively high and may lead to increased urinary calcium and risk of nephrolithiasis as discussed in the text regarding excess protein consumption.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 364 (Book Page): The RDA for protein is computed for proteins of mixed biologic value at 0.8 g/kg of body weight for adults... Women who are pregnant or lactating require up to 30 g/day in addition to their basal requirements.

category: Elaborate the effect of oligomycin and uncouplers on ATP production
coreConcept: Dissipation vs. Steepening of the Proton Gradient
statement: Which of the following describes the fundamental biochemical difference in the mitochondrial proton gradient when comparing the effects of an uncoupler to the effects of oligomycin?
options: Both agents result in a complete loss of the electrical gradient
Uncouplers block the gradient formation, while oligomycin has no effect on the gradient
Both agents result in a maximally steep pH gradient
Uncouplers dissipate the gradient, while oligomycin increases it
Uncouplers increase the gradient, while oligomycin dissipates it
correctOption: Uncouplers dissipate the gradient, while oligomycin increases it
optionExplanations: Only uncouplers result in the loss of the electrical gradient by providing an alternate path for protons.
Oligomycin has a profound effect by causing the gradient to become undissipated; it does not have 'no effect'.
Only oligomycin results in a maximally steep gradient; uncouplers do the opposite.

Uncouplers increase the permeability of the inner membrane to protons, dissipating the gradient. Oligomycin blocks the reentry of protons through ATP synthase, causing the gradient to reach its maximum possible steepness until electron transport stalls.
This is incorrect; uncouplers allow protons to leak across the membrane, thus removing the gradient, while oligomycin prevents their return, making the gradient steeper.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 78 (Book Page)-87: Because the pH and electrical gradients cannot be dissipated in the presence of [oligomycin]... This uncoupler [2,4-dinitrophenol] causes electron transport to proceed at a rapid rate without establishing a proton gradient.

category: Categorize individuals into underweight, normal, overweight, obese, and morbidly obese based on theirs BMI values
statement: A 12-month-old child from a low-income region presents with severe muscle wasting, a BMI-for-age z-score indicating extreme underweight (estimated equivalent BMI of 11.5 kg/m²), and an 'old man' facial appearance. Which pathophysiological state is most consistent with this presentation?
options: Obese Class III due to rapid growth spurts.
Standard Normal Weight for the 1-year age group.
Kwashiorkor due to high carbohydrate, zero protein intake.
Overweight due to excessive cereal gruel consumption.
Marasmus due to chronic deficiency of both total calories and protein.
correctOption: Marasmus due to chronic deficiency of both total calories and protein.
optionExplanations: Obese Class III is the opposite of this presentation, requiring a BMI far above the normal for age.
The normal BMI-for-age is much higher; a value of 11.5 represents severe malnutrition.
Kwashiorkor (Page 377) is characterized by edema (swollen belly) and may have a relatively higher BMI due to water retention; this child shows wasting (emaciation).
Excessive cereal consumption would provide calories; Marasmus is defined by a lack of both calories and protein.

A BMI equivalent of 11.5 in a child is a life-threatening underweight state. The combination of emaciation and a 'wizened' face is classic for Marasmus, where there is a chronic deficit of all macronutrients and calories.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 369 (Book Page): Marasmus occurs when calorie deprivation is relatively greater than the reduction in protein... Typical symptoms include arrested growth, extreme muscle wasting (emaciation), weakness, and anemia.

category: Diagrammatically illustrate the organization of electron transport chain (ETC) depicting the flow of electrons
statement: During the transfer of electrons through the respiratory chain, why does the reduction of oxygen at Complex IV represent the final step in the physiological flow of electrons?
options: Complex IV contains copper atoms that facilitate the only direct reaction with molecular oxygen.
Complex IV is the only site where proton pumping does not occur.
Oxygen has the most negative standard reduction potential in the chain.
Oxygen is the only component that can spontaneously reduce the cytochromes.
The reduction of oxygen is an endergonic process requiring ATP hydrolysis.
correctOption: Complex IV contains copper atoms that facilitate the only direct reaction with molecular oxygen.
optionExplanations: Cytochrome a + a3 (Complex IV) contains heme iron and copper atoms. It is the only complex with a specific coordination site capable of binding molecular oxygen directly, allowing for its four-electron reduction to water.
Proton pumping does occur at Complex IV; Complex II is the only major complex that does not pump protons across the inner membrane.
Oxygen actually has the most positive standard reduction potential (+0.82 V) in the chain, making it the most avid electron acceptor, not a negative one.
Oxygen does not reduce cytochromes; rather, it is reduced by cytochrome oxidase (Complex IV) after cytochromes have been reduced by preceding carriers.
The reduction of oxygen to water is a highly exergonic reaction, releasing a large amount of free energy used to drive oxidative phosphorylation, rather than requiring it.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 76 (Book Page): This cytochrome complex is the only electron carrier in which the heme iron has an available coordination site that can react directly with O2, and so also is called cytochrome oxidase.

category: Clearly differentiate between substrate level phosphorylation and oxidative phosphorylation
statement: A researcher is studying an isolated mitochondrial preparation. She observes that even when the inner membrane is made permeable to protons, the preparation continues to produce a small amount of ATP/GTP when supplied with succinyl-CoA. This is best explained by:
options: The reversal of the ATP synthase complex due to high substrate availability.
The activation of oxidative phosphorylation by high concentrations of succinate.
The reduction of oxygen by Succinate Dehydrogenase in the absence of a gradient.
The fact that substrate-level phosphorylation is independent of the transmembrane electrochemical gradient.
The coupling of the TCA cycle to the outer mitochondrial membrane transporters.
correctOption: The fact that substrate-level phosphorylation is independent of the transmembrane electrochemical gradient.
optionExplanations: In the absence of a proton gradient, ATP synthase would actually hydrolyze ATP to try and restore the gradient, rather than synthesize it.
If the membrane is permeable to protons, oxidative phosphorylation cannot occur because the chemiosmotic gradient required to drive ATP synthase is dissipated.
Succinate dehydrogenase is Complex II and transfers electrons to CoQ; it does not react with oxygen directly nor does it produce ATP in the absence of a gradient.

Correct. Substrate-level phosphorylation (such as the GTP produced from succinyl-CoA by succinate thiokinase) is a purely enzymatic reaction occurring in the matrix. It does not require a proton gradient or the ETC, unlike OxPhos.
The TCA cycle occurs in the matrix and its SLP step is not coupled to membrane transporters; it is a soluble enzyme reaction.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 105 (Book Page): The generation of GTP by succinate thiokinase is another example of substrate-level phosphorylation... The cycle does not involve net consumption or production of oxaloacetate.

category: Elaborate the reaction catalyzed by pyruvate dehydrogenase complex (PDH) along with regulation and significance
statement: The activity of the pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDH) complex is strictly regulated by covalent modification through the actions of PDH kinase and PDH phosphatase. Which of the following metabolic signals acts as a potent allosteric activator of PDH kinase, thereby leading to the inhibition of the complex?
options: Acetyl CoA
Adenosine diphosphate (ADP)
Pyruvate
Calcium ions (Ca2+)
Nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD+)
correctOption: Acetyl CoA
optionExplanations: Acetyl CoA is a product of the PDH reaction. High levels signal energy abundance and allosterically activate PDH kinase, which phosphorylates E1 and inhibits the complex to prevent overproduction.
ADP generally signals a low-energy state and does not activate the PDH kinase; the kinase is specifically activated by the 'energy-rich' signals like ATP.
Pyruvate is a potent inhibitor of PDH kinase. By inhibiting the kinase, pyruvate ensures that the PDH complex remains in its active (dephosphorylated) form to process the available substrate.
Calcium ions are strong activators of PDH phosphatase, which dephosphorylates and activates the PDH complex; they do not activate the inhibitory PDH kinase.
NAD+ is the oxidized form of the coenzyme. It is NADH (the reduced form) that acts as a signal of high energy to activate the PDH kinase, not the oxidized NAD+ molecule.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 103 (Book Page): The kinase itself is allosterically activated by ATP, acetyl CoA, and NADH. Therefore, in the presence of these high-energy signals, the PDH complex is turned off.

category: Suggest a simple method for estimation of caloric requirements of sedentary adults, moderately active adults, and very active adults
coreConcept: Caloric Factor for Very Active Adults
statement: What is the approximated caloric requirement per kilogram of body weight for a 'very active' adult to maintain their weight?
options: 30 kcal/kg/day
35 kcal/kg/day
25 kcal/kg/day
40 kcal/kg/day
50 kcal/kg/day
correctOption: 40 kcal/kg/day
optionExplanations: 30 kcal/kg is the estimation factor for sedentary adults.
35 kcal/kg is the estimation factor for moderately active adults.
25 kcal/kg is used for weight loss or individuals with very low metabolic rates, not for the 'very active' population.
The standard simplified factor for estimating the caloric needs of a very active adult is 40 kcal per kilogram of body weight per day.
50 kcal/kg is not a standard factor in the simplified classification of sedentary, moderately active, and very active adults.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 358 (Book Page): ...very active adults require 40 kcal/kg/day.

category: Explain how ethanol consumption causes hypoglycemia and fatty liver
statement: In the context of ethanol-induced hypoglycemia, the elevated NADH levels in the liver cause a shift in the malate dehydrogenase reaction equilibrium. What is the direct consequence of this shift regarding the availability of gluconeogenic precursors?
options: Decreased transport of malate to the cytosol
Accumulation of oxaloacetate in the mitochondrial matrix
Activation of pyruvate carboxylase to replenish oxaloacetate
Depletion of oxaloacetate as it is reduced to malate
Increased conversion of malate to oxaloacetate
correctOption: Depletion of oxaloacetate as it is reduced to malate
optionExplanations: Malate transport actually increases because malate is being produced in excess in the mitochondria to be shuttled out, though this does not help gluconeogenesis as the cytosol also lacks the NAD+ to re-oxidize it.
Oxaloacetate does not accumulate; it is rapidly consumed in the production of malate due to the high concentration of the reducing agent NADH.

While pyruvate carboxylase is activated by acetyl-CoA, ethanol consumption also depletes its substrate (pyruvate) by shifting it to lactate, so OAA cannot be effectively replenished through this route during ethanol metabolism.

According to Le Chatelier's principle, the high cytosolic and mitochondrial NADH/NAD+ ratio produced by ethanol metabolism forces the malate dehydrogenase reaction to favor malate formation, thus sequestering oxaloacetate and preventing its entry into the gluconeogenic pathway.
Increased conversion of malate to oxaloacetate occurs only when NAD+ levels are high; ethanol metabolism depletes NAD+ and provides excess NADH, driving the reaction toward malate.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 116 (Book Page): The increase in NADH as ethanol is oxidized, will decrease the availability of OAA because the reversible oxidation of malate to OAA by malate dehydrogenase of the TCA cycle is driven in the reverse direction by the high availability of NADH.

category: Enlist the components of complex I, II, III, and IV
coreConcept: Complex II as a Diagnostic Marker for Myopathies
statement: A 12-year-old patient presents with muscle weakness and exercise intolerance. A biopsy of skeletal muscle reveals 'ragged-red fibers.' Histochemical staining shows abnormal mitochondrial proliferation, particularly staining positive for an enzyme that utilizes FAD as a coenzyme and contains Fe-S centers but does not pump protons. Which complex is most likely being highlighted by this stain?
options: Complex IV (Cytochrome c oxidase)
Complex III (Cytochrome bc1)
Complex V (ATP synthase)
Complex II (Succinate dehydrogenase)
Complex I (NADH dehydrogenase)
correctOption: Complex II (Succinate dehydrogenase)
optionExplanations: Complex IV is often deficient in certain mitochondrial disorders (like Leigh syndrome), but the proliferation of mitochondria themselves is traditionally visualized using the Complex II stain.
Complex III consists of cytochrome b and c1 and Fe-S centers, but it is not the specific target used for identifying mitochondrial proliferation in ragged-red fiber pathology.

Complex V is the ATP synthase and, while essential for energy, is not the enzymatic marker (Succinate dehydrogenase) referred to for diagnostic staining of mitochondrial proliferation in this clinical context.

Complex II (succinate dehydrogenase) is the only complex in the ETC that is encoded entirely by nuclear DNA and is used as a histochemical marker for mitochondria because it is embedded in the inner membrane and its activity reflects mitochondrial mass.
Complex I uses FMN and Fe-S centers and is a major proton pump; it is not the standard enzyme used for the histochemical hallmark staining in mitochondrial myopathies.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 80 (Book Page): Muscle fibers from a patient with a mitochondrial myopathy show abnormal mitochondrial proliferation when stained for succinate dehydrogenase, an enzyme of Complex II.

category: Differentiate between Kwashiorkor and Marasmus based on the given data
statement: In the metabolic management of Protein-Energy Malnutrition, why is the administration of high-carbohydrate, low-protein gruels considered 'protein-wasting' in a child with Marasmus?
options: Carbohydrates inhibit the absorption of essential amino acids in the jejunum.
Excessive carbohydrate intake induces the rapid renal excretion of albumin.
Carbohydrate-only diets increase the thermic effect of food beyond safe limits.
High carbohydrate intake stimulates insulin, which prevents muscle protein breakdown.
Lack of dietary carbohydrate forces the body to use proteins for gluconeogenesis.
correctOption: Lack of dietary carbohydrate forces the body to use proteins for gluconeogenesis.
optionExplanations: Carbohydrates do not inhibit amino acid absorption; the issue is the lack of amino acid intake and the metabolic diversion of internal proteins.
The lack of carbohydrate does not cause renal albumin excretion; the hypoalbuminemia of Kwashiorkor is due to decreased hepatic synthesis.
The thermic effect of food is a normal physiological response (5-10% expenditure) and is not the cause of protein wasting in these conditions.
Insulin actually inhibits muscle breakdown; the metabolic crisis in Marasmus is driven by low insulin and high cortisol, promoting catabolism.
In Marasmus, a lack of calories (including carbohydrates) forces the body to deaminate its own tissue proteins to provide carbon skeletons for gluconeogenesis to maintain blood glucose for the brain.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 361 (Book Page): If carbohydrate intake is less than 130 g/day, substantial amounts of protein are metabolized to provide precursors for gluconeogenesis.

category: Describe the glycolytic pathway along with its regulation and significance
statement: Which of the following sets of products is generated during the anaerobic conversion of one molecule of glucose to lactate in a mature erythrocyte?
options: 2 Lactate, 2 NADH, 4 ATP
2 Pyruvate, 2 NADH, 2 ATP
2 Lactate, 2 ATP, and zero net NADH
1 Pyruvate, 1 Acetyl CoA, 1 ATP
2 Lactate, 2 NAD+, 2 ATP
correctOption: 2 Lactate, 2 ATP, and zero net NADH
optionExplanations: The gross production is 4 ATP, but 2 are consumed in the energy investment phase, leaving a net of 2 ATP. Also, there is no net NADH.
This describes aerobic glycolysis before the entry into the TCA cycle, but in erythrocytes, which lack mitochondria, lactate is the required end product.

Anaerobic glycolysis yields a net of 2 ATP per glucose. The NADH produced in the oxidation of glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate is consumed in the reduction of pyruvate to lactate, resulting in no net change in NADH/NAD+ concentrations.
Acetyl CoA production requires mitochondria and aerobic conditions, which are absent in mature erythrocytes.

While 2 lactate and 2 ATP are produced, the NAD+ produced in the lactate dehydrogenase step is recycled back to the glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate dehydrogenase step, meaning there is no 'net' production.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 96 (Book Page): Two molecules of ATP are generated for each molecule of glucose converted to two molecules of lactate. There is no net production or consumption of NADH.

category: Outline the reactions involved in ethanol metabolism
statement: A 48-year-old chronic alcoholic is brought to the emergency department after being found unresponsive. Laboratory tests reveal severe hypoglycemia. What is the most direct mechanism by which ethanol metabolism causes this metabolic complication?
options: Activation of the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex by excess acetyl-CoA.
Direct inhibition of glucose 6-phosphatase by ethanol.
Inhibition of the malate-aspartate shuttle by acetaldehyde.
Uncoupling of oxidative phosphorylation in the hepatic mitochondria.
Depletion of oxaloacetate as it is reduced to malate by excess NADH.
correctOption: Depletion of oxaloacetate as it is reduced to malate by excess NADH.
optionExplanations: While acetyl-CoA increases, the high NADH/NAD+ ratio actually inhibits the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex through the activation of PDH kinase.
Ethanol does not directly inhibit glucose 6-phosphatase; the hypoglycemia is due to a lack of substrate for the enzyme rather than enzyme inhibition.
The malate-aspartate shuttle is actually overwhelmed by the excessive cytosolic NADH rather than being inhibited by acetaldehyde.
The hypoglycemia is a result of impaired gluconeogenic flux in the cytosol and matrix, not primarily a result of mitochondrial uncoupling.

The high NADH generated by ethanol metabolism shifts the equilibrium of the malate dehydrogenase reaction toward malate, depleting oxaloacetate and thereby preventing its entry into the gluconeogenic pathway.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 116 (Book Page): The increase in NADH as ethanol is oxidized, will decrease the availability of OAA because the reversible oxidation of malate to OAA by malate dehydrogenase of the TCA cycle is driven in the reverse direction by the high availability of NADH.

category: Explain the significance of Cori cycle and glucosealanine cycle
coreConcept: Enzyme Directionality in the Cori Cycle
statement: In the liver, the enzyme Lactate Dehydrogenase (LDH) plays a critical role in the Cori cycle by catalyzing which specific reaction?
options: The oxidation of lactate to pyruvate while reducing NAD+ to NADH.
The phosphorylation of lactate using ATP to form phosphoenolpyruvate.
The carboxylation of lactate to form oxaloacetate in the mitochondria.
The transamination of lactate to form alanine and alpha-ketoglutarate.
The reduction of pyruvate to lactate to regenerate NAD+.
correctOption: The oxidation of lactate to pyruvate while reducing NAD+ to NADH.
optionExplanations: Correct. In the liver, the low NADH/NAD+ ratio and the influx of lactate from the blood drive the LDH reaction toward the oxidation of lactate to pyruvate, which then enters gluconeogenesis.
Incorrect. Lactate cannot be directly phosphorylated to PEP; it must first be converted to pyruvate and then go through the gluconeogenic bypass steps.
Incorrect. Lactate must be converted to pyruvate by LDH before it can be carboxylated to oxaloacetate by pyruvate carboxylase.
Incorrect. Lactate is not transaminated; amino acids like alanine undergo transamination.
Incorrect. This describes the direction of the reaction in the exercising muscle or in anaerobic conditions, not the liver's role in the Cori cycle.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 95 (Book Page): [The direction of the lactate dehydrogenase reaction depends on the relative intracellular concentrations of pyruvate and lactate, and on the ratio of NADH/NAD+ in the cell. For example, in liver and heart... these tissues oxidize lactate (obtained from the blood) to pyruvate.]

category: Enumerate clinically important inhibitors of electron transport chain and mention their site of action
coreConcept: Redox State Alteration by Site-Specific Blockage
statement: In a laboratory study of mitochondrial respiration, a researcher observes that the addition of a specific toxin results in all electron carriers before Complex III becoming fully reduced, while those after it remain oxidized. Which inhibitor was most likely added?
options: Cyanide
Antimycin A
2,4-Dinitrophenol
Atractyloside
Amobarbital (Amytal)
correctOption: Antimycin A
optionExplanations: Cyanide blocks Complex IV. This would cause all carriers in the entire chain (Complex I, II, III, and IV) to become fully reduced as they cannot pass electrons to oxygen.

Antimycin A inhibits Complex III. Electron flow is blocked at the cytochrome bc1 complex, causing all upstream components (NADH, FMN, CoQ) to stay reduced and downstream components (Cytochromes c, a, a3) to stay oxidized.
2,4-Dinitrophenol is an uncoupler that increases the rate of electron transport; it does not block the chain at a specific complex to create a reduced/oxidized gradient.
Atractyloside inhibits the ADP/ATP translocase, not a specific complex of the Electron Transport Chain directly, although it eventually stops respiration via respiratory control (tight coupling).
Amobarbital (Amytal) inhibits Complex I; this would leave carriers like Coenzyme Q and Cytochromes in an oxidized state, while only Complex I components would be reduced.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 76 (Book Page): These compounds prevent the passage of electrons by binding to a component of the chain, blocking the oxidation/reduction reaction. Therefore, all electron carriers before the block are fully reduced, whereas those located after the block are oxidized. [Figure 6.10 identifies Antimycin A at Complex III].

category: Define basal metabolic rate (BMR)
statement: In the categorization of energy expenditure, which of the following is a direct synonym for the Resting Metabolic Rate (RMR) in many physiological contexts?
options: Diet-induced thermogenesis
Specific dynamic action
Total daily energy expenditure
Basal metabolic rate
Physical activity level
correctOption: Basal metabolic rate
optionExplanations: Diet-induced thermogenesis is a synonym for the 'thermic effect of food,' the energy cost of digestion, not the RMR.
Specific dynamic action (SDA) is an older term for the thermic effect of food, representing the rise in metabolism after eating.
Total daily energy expenditure (TDEE) is the sum of RMR, the thermic effect of food, and physical activity; RMR is only one component of it.
Correct. Basal Metabolic Rate (BMR) is the older term used for what is now commonly called the Resting Metabolic Rate (RMR).
Physical activity level is a distinct category that describes energy used for movement, which is added to the RMR to calculate total expenditure.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 359 (Book Page): The energy expended by an individual in a resting, postabsorptive state is called the resting (formerly, basal) metabolic rate (RMR).

category: Elaborate key features of various transport systems for entry of glucose into cells
statement: How does the transport of glucose by the GLUT-2 isoform in hepatocytes differ from the transport mediated by other isoforms like GLUT-1 or GLUT-3?
options: GLUT-2 permits bidirectional transport based on blood glucose levels
GLUT-2 is insulin-dependent for its translocation to the plasma membrane
GLUT-2 is only found in cells lacking mitochondria like erythrocytes
GLUT-2 maintains a high-affinity (low Km) state for glucose
GLUT-2 utilizes energy to transport glucose against a concentration gradient
correctOption: GLUT-2 permits bidirectional transport based on blood glucose levels
optionExplanations: Unlike GLUT-1, 3, or 4 which primarily facilitate glucose uptake, GLUT-2 is uniquely bidirectional. It allows glucose to enter the liver for storage after a meal and to exit the liver during fasting when gluconeogenesis or glycogenolysis occurs.
GLUT-2 is Na+-independent and insulin-independent. Only GLUT-4 requires insulin for translocation to the plasma membrane.
GLUT-1 is the primary transporter in erythrocytes. GLUT-2 is found in the liver, kidney, and pancreatic beta cells, all of which contain mitochondria.
GLUT-2 is a low-affinity, high-capacity transporter with a high Km. This allows it to act as a sensor that only works efficiently when blood glucose is significantly elevated.
GLUT-2 is a facilitated diffusion transporter. It always moves glucose down a concentration gradient; it never uses energy to move glucose against a gradient (which is the role of SGLT).
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 97 (Book Page): GLUT-2, which is found in the liver and kidney, can either transport glucose into these cells when blood glucose levels are high, or transport glucose from these cells when blood glucose levels are low (for example, during fasting).

category: Delineate special nutritional requirements during pregnancy, lactation, growth, and old age
coreConcept: Nutritional and Metabolic Changes in Old Age
statement: A 70-year-old sedentary male presents with chronic constipation and a total daily caloric intake of 2,000 kcal. Nutritional analysis reveals he consumes 15 g of dietary fiber daily. Based on the Adequate Intake (AI) for his gender, what is the recommended fiber intake, and how does his current RMR likely compare to his younger years?
options: AI is 15 g; RMR decreases due to the thermic effect of food.
AI is 50 g; RMR is unaffected by age but influenced by fiber.
AI is 25 g; RMR increases with age due to decreased muscle mass.
AI is 38 g; RMR decreases with age because of reduced lean body mass.
AI is 30 g; RMR increases to compensate for lower bowel motility.
correctOption: AI is 38 g; RMR decreases with age because of reduced lean body mass.
optionExplanations: His current intake is 15 g, but the AI is 38 g. The thermic effect of food is a separate component from RMR.
50 g is above the established AI for fiber, and RMR definitely changes with age.
The AI of 25 g is for women, and RMR decreases, not increases, with age.
The AI for fiber in men is 38 g/day (he is deficient at 15 g). RMR decreases with age primarily due to the loss of lean muscle mass.
The AI for men is 38 g, and RMR does not increase to compensate for bowel motility; motility is assisted by fiber, not RMR.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 358 (Book Page): The recommended daily fiber intake (AI) is 25 g/day for women and 38 g/day for men... Page 351 (Book Page): [RMR] represents the energy required to carry out the normal body functions... [it is affected by] body composition.

category: Outline treatment strategies
statement: Alpha-glucosidase inhibitors, such as acarbose, are utilized as a treatment strategy for diabetes mellitus. What is the pharmacological basis for their effectiveness in clinical management?
options: They increase the secretion of glucagon from the pancreatic alpha cells to maintain homeostasis.
They promote the rapid conversion of glycogen to glucose in the post-absorptive state.
They slow the production of glucose from dietary starch to reduce post-prandial blood glucose rise.
They act as insulin sensitizers by activating the GLUT-4 transporters in skeletal muscle.
They inhibit the renal reabsorption of glucose at the sodium-dependent glucose cotransporter (SGLT).
correctOption: They slow the production of glucose from dietary starch to reduce post-prandial blood glucose rise.
optionExplanations: Acarbose is used to lower blood glucose, whereas glucagon increases blood glucose; inducing glucagon secretion would worsen the glycemic state of a diabetic patient.
Acarbose does not affect glycogenolysis; it specifically inhibits the brush border enzymes that break down oligosaccharides and disaccharides into monosaccharides.
By inhibiting alpha-glucosidase, these drugs delay the digestion of complex carbohydrates into glucose, resulting in a blunted and slower rise in blood glucose levels following a meal.
Insulin sensitizers like thiazolidinediones work via different mechanisms; acarbose works exclusively in the intestinal lumen to inhibit carbohydrate digestion.
SGLT inhibitors (gliflozins) are a separate class of diabetic medications that act in the kidney; acarbose does not have a primary effect on renal glucose transport.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 90 (Book Page): ( -Glucosidase inhibitors slow the production of glucose from dietary carbohydrates, thereby reducing the post-prandial rise in blood glucose and facilitating better blood glucose control in diabetics.

category: Explain the significance of Cori cycle and glucosealanine cycle
coreConcept: Energetic Efficiency of the Cori Cycle
statement: Which of the following best explains the net energetic 'cost' of the Cori cycle to the organism when evaluated from a whole-body perspective?
options: The cycle results in a net gain of 4 ATP, providing an extra energy source for the heart.
The cycle consumes 2 molecules of NADH in the muscle to produce 2 NADPH in the liver.
The liver produces 6 ATP during gluconeogenesis, resulting in a net whole-body gain.
The cycle is energy-neutral, as the 2 ATP produced in muscle are used in the liver.
The cycle results in a net loss of 4 high-energy phosphate bonds per turn.
correctOption: The cycle results in a net loss of 4 high-energy phosphate bonds per turn.
optionExplanations: Option B is incorrect because the cycle is an energy-consuming process for the body, not an energy-generating one.
Option E is incorrect because the cycle involves NADH/NAD+ redox reactions, not NADPH, and the liver uses NADH for gluconeogenesis.
Option D is incorrect because gluconeogenesis *consumes* energy; it does not produce ATP.
Option A is incorrect because the liver requires 6 high-energy phosphate bonds (4 ATP and 2 GTP) to produce glucose from lactate, which is more than the 2 ATP produced by the muscle.
Option C is correct. Muscle produces 2 ATP per glucose. Liver consumes 6 high-energy phosphates to regenerate that glucose. Net loss = 4 high-energy phosphates.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 113 (Book Page): The stoichiometry of gluconeogenesis from pyruvate couples the cleavage of six high-energy phosphate bonds... Page 96 (Book Page): Two molecules of ATP are generated for each molecule of glucose converted to two molecules of lactate.

category: Delineate special nutritional requirements during pregnancy, lactation, growth, and old age
coreConcept: Definition and Basis of Adequate Intake (AI) in Infants
statement: For a healthy 2-month-old infant who is exclusively breast-fed, the Dietary Reference Intake (DRI) for various nutrients is categorized as 'Adequate Intake' (AI). On what specific data is this AI based?
options: The highest average daily intake level that poses no risk of adverse health effects.
The estimated daily mean nutrient intake supplied by human milk for healthy, full-term infants.
Average daily nutrient intake level estimated to meet the needs of 50% of the population.
Clinical trials measuring the minimal requirement to prevent visible deficiency diseases.
Intake levels set at two standard deviations above the Estimated Average Requirement.
correctOption: The estimated daily mean nutrient intake supplied by human milk for healthy, full-term infants.
optionExplanations: This describes the Tolerable Upper Intake Level (UL), which is a safety limit rather than a recommended intake level.
As per the text, AI for infants is derived from the mean nutrient content of breast milk from healthy mothers, as it is considered the gold standard for that age.
This describes the Estimated Average Requirement (EAR), which is the foundation for the RDA but is not used when data is insufficient for AI.
AI is based on observed intakes by healthy groups, not on the 'minimal' requirement to prevent disease, which would be a lower threshold.
This describes the calculation for the Recommended Dietary Allowance (RDA), which requires a known EAR and standard deviation.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 358 (Book Page): For example, the AI for young infants, for whom human milk is the recommended sole source of food for the first 4–6 months, is based on the estimated daily mean nutrient intake supplied by human milk for healthy, full-term infants who are exclusively breast-fed.

category: Describe the effect of arsenic poisoning on carbohydrate metabolism and ATP production
statement: According to the biochemical properties of high-energy compounds, why does the complex formed between arsenate and glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate fail to produce ATP?
options: Arsenate irreversibly denatures the glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate dehydrogenase enzyme.
Arsenate acts as an allosteric inhibitor of phosphoglycerate kinase.
The complex spontaneously hydrolyzes to form 3-phosphoglycerate, skipping the high-energy phosphate transfer step.
The complex prevents the reduction of NAD+ to NADH, halting the pathway.
The complex is too stable to be processed by phosphoglycerate kinase.
correctOption: The complex spontaneously hydrolyzes to form 3-phosphoglycerate, skipping the high-energy phosphate transfer step.
optionExplanations: Arsenate competition is a form of reversible substrate analog inhibition rather than irreversible denaturation of the enzyme protein itself.
Arsenate's toxicity is due to substrate competition and subsequent intermediate instability, not direct allosteric inhibition of phosphoglycerate kinase.

The arsenate-intermediate (1-arseno-3-phosphoglycerate) is unstable in water. It hydrolyzes to 3-phosphoglycerate without the involvement of ADP, thus no ATP is generated via substrate-level phosphorylation.
The text notes that arsenate also prevents 'net NADH production', but the fundamental reason no ATP is produced is the spontaneous hydrolysis of the arsenic-substituted intermediate.
The complex is actually very unstable (not too stable), which is why it hydrolyzes spontaneously instead of being used as a substrate for the next enzyme.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 93 (Book Page): The poison does so by competing with inorganic phosphate as a substrate for glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate dehydrogenase, forming a complex that spontaneously hydrolyzes to form 3-phosphoglycerate

category: Enumerate clinically important inhibitors of electron transport chain and mention their site of action
coreConcept: Redox State Changes via ETC Blockade
statement: During an experiment involving isolated mitochondria, the addition of Antimycin A causes a distinct shift in the oxidation-reduction states of the electron carriers. Which of the following correctly describes the redox state of the components in this scenario?
options: Cytochrome c and Cytochrome a+a3 become fully reduced.
Complex IV is unable to bind molecular oxygen.
NADH and Coenzyme Q become fully oxidized.
All components of the chain remain in an intermediate steady state.
NADH and Coenzyme Q become fully reduced.
correctOption: NADH and Coenzyme Q become fully reduced.
optionExplanations: Cytochrome c and Cytochrome a+a3 are located after the site of Antimycin A inhibition (Complex III); since they cannot receive electrons, they lose those they have to oxygen and become fully oxidized.
Antimycin A does not affect the ability of Complex IV to bind oxygen; it merely prevents electrons from reaching Complex IV to facilitate the reduction of that oxygen.
Carriers before a block accumulate electrons because they cannot pass them forward; therefore, NADH and Coenzyme Q (before Complex III) become reduced, not oxidized.
The addition of a site-specific inhibitor disrupts the steady state, causing a polarization of redox states where one side of the block is fully reduced and the other is fully oxidized.
Because Antimycin A blocks Complex III, electrons accumulate in all carriers upstream, including Complex I (NADH) and the ubiquinone pool (CoQ), leaving them in a reduced state.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 76 (Book Page): [Therefore, all electron carriers before the block are fully reduced, whereas those located after the block are oxidized.]

category: Define energy balance
statement: Biochemical pathways often involve reactions with a large positive ΔG, such as ion transport against a gradient. How does the cell effectively drive these energetically unfavorable processes to maintain energy balance?
options: By ensuring the reaction proceeds until ΔG becomes positive.
By utilizing enzymes to lower the standard free energy change (ΔG°).
By increasing the concentration of the product to shift the equilibrium.
By decreasing the absolute temperature in degrees Kelvin.
By coupling the endergonic process with an exergonic reaction like ATP hydrolysis.
correctOption: By coupling the endergonic process with an exergonic reaction like ATP hydrolysis.
optionExplanations: Reactions proceed spontaneously only when ΔG is negative; they stop when ΔG reaches zero (equilibrium).
Enzymes lower activation energy (kinetics) but cannot change the standard free energy change (ΔG°) of a reaction.
Increasing the concentration of the product would make ΔG more positive, further hindering the reaction.
Decreasing temperature would generally decrease the rate of a reaction and is not a biological strategy for driving endergonic reactions.
Energy coupling allows the total ΔG of a sequence of reactions to be negative, making the entire process spontaneous.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 72 (Book Page): Reactions or processes that have a large positive ΔG... are made possible by coupling the endergonic movement of ions with a second, spontaneous process with a large negative ΔG, such as the exergonic hydrolysis of adenosine triphosphate (ATP).

category: Suggest a simple method for estimation of caloric requirements of sedentary adults, moderately active adults, and very active adults
statement: A 45-year-old male banker in Karachi, weighing 70 kg, is admitted for a non-emergent minor surgical procedure. He describes his lifestyle as purely sedentary, involving long hours of desk work and no exercise. To maintain his current weight during his recovery phase without overfeeding, what is his estimated daily caloric requirement based on weight-based approximations?
options: 2100 kcal/day
1800 kcal/day
2450 kcal/day
3200 kcal/day
2800 kcal/day
correctOption: 2100 kcal/day
optionExplanations: For a sedentary 70 kg adult, the calculation is 70 kg multiplied by 30 kcal/kg/day, which equals 2100 kcal/day to maintain energy balance.
1800 kcal/day is insufficient for a 70 kg male; this would be the approximate RMR for a 70 kg man but does not include the 30% addition for sedentary physical activity.
2450 kcal/day (70 kg x 35 kcal/kg) is the requirement for a moderately active adult, which contradicts the patient's description of a purely sedentary lifestyle.
3200 kcal/day represents a caloric surplus that would likely lead to metabolic complications and obesity in a patient with a sedentary baseline activity level.
2800 kcal/day (70 kg x 40 kcal/kg) is reserved for very active adults and would result in excessive weight gain in this sedentary patient.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 358 (Book Page): sedentary adults require about 30 kcal/kg/day to maintain body weight.

category: Elaborate the regulation and importance of gluconeogenesis
statement: In the hepatic regulation of glucose metabolism, the concentration of a specific allosteric effector determines whether the liver performs glycolysis or gluconeogenesis. When glucagon levels are high, the concentration of this effector drops, relieving the inhibition of which gluconeogenic enzyme?
options: Glucose 6-phosphatase
Pyruvate Carboxylase
Lactate Dehydrogenase
Fructose 1,6-bisphosphatase
Phosphoenolpyruvate Carboxykinase
correctOption: Fructose 1,6-bisphosphatase
optionExplanations: Glucose 6-phosphatase is regulated more by substrate availability and its location in the ER than by allosteric effectors like Fructose 2,6-bisphosphate.
Pyruvate Carboxylase is regulated primarily by Acetyl CoA levels, not by Fructose 2,6-bisphosphate.
Lactate Dehydrogenase is not a regulated enzyme of the gluconeogenic pathway; it operates near equilibrium.

Fructose 2,6-bisphosphate is a potent inhibitor of FBP-1. Glucagon leads to its destruction, thereby removing the 'brake' on gluconeogenesis and allowing Fructose 1,6-bisphosphate to be converted to Fructose 6-phosphate.
PEPCK is regulated mainly by gene transcription (induction by glucagon) rather than allosteric inhibition by Fructose 2,6-bisphosphate.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 113 (Book Page): Fructose 1,6-bisphosphatase, found in liver and kidney, is inhibited by fructose 2,6-bisphosphate... Glucagon lowers the level of fructose 2,6-bisphosphate, resulting in activation of fructose 1,6-bisphosphatase.

category: Outline treatment strategies
coreConcept: Management of acute G6PD hemolytic episodes
statement: A 24-year-old male is diagnosed with acute hemolytic anemia after receiving the antimalarial drug primaquine. Laboratories reveal Heinz bodies in the peripheral smear. What is the most immediate and critical treatment strategy for managing this patient's condition?
options: Initiation of a high-carbohydrate diet to stimulate the pentose phosphate pathway.
Performance of an emergency splenectomy to prevent the destruction of rigid erythrocytes.
Discontinuation of the precipitating oxidant drug and clinical monitoring.
Administration of large doses of oxidized glutathione (GSSG) to the patient.
Immediate blood transfusion regardless of current hemoglobin stability.
correctOption: Discontinuation of the precipitating oxidant drug and clinical monitoring.
optionExplanations: While G6PD is the rate-limiting enzyme of the HMP pathway, a high-carbohydrate diet cannot overcome a genetic deficiency of the enzyme to provide more NADPH in RBCs.
Splenectomy is a treatment for certain chronic hemolytic conditions like hereditary spherocytosis, but it is not indicated for the acute, self-limited hemolytic episodes of G6PD deficiency.

The primary management of G6PD-induced hemolysis is the withdrawal of the oxidant trigger (the 'AAA' drugs); once the drug is removed, reticulocytosis allows younger RBCs with higher enzyme activity to normalize hemoglobin levels.
Administering oxidized glutathione would be counterproductive and potentially toxic; the cell needs reduced glutathione (GSH) to detoxify peroxides, and this requires NADPH from G6PD.
Blood transfusion is reserved for severe, life-threatening anemia with hemodynamic instability; mild to moderate episodes in G6PD A- patients are often self-limiting once the trigger is removed.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 145 (Book Page): The anemia is self-limited because the older, vulnerable population of erythrocytes is replaced by younger RBCs with sufficient G6PD activity to withstand an assault.

category: Calculate the energy yield of TCA
statement: What is the total net yield of high-energy phosphate bonds (as ATP or GTP) generated from the complete mitochondrial oxidation of one molecule of Acetyl CoA via the Tricarboxylic Acid (TCA) cycle?
options: 24 ATP
10 ATP
12 ATP
15 ATP
38 ATP
correctOption: 12 ATP
optionExplanations: 24 ATP is the yield from two molecules of Acetyl CoA, which would represent the oxidation of one full molecule of glucose following glycolysis.
10 ATP is an incorrect calculation; it fails to account for either the substrate-level phosphorylation or the correct P:O ratio of one of the reduced coenzymes.

12 ATP is the correct yield per Acetyl CoA: 3 molecules of NADH are produced (yielding 9 ATP via the Electron Transport Chain), 1 molecule of FADH2 is produced (yielding 2 ATP), and 1 molecule of GTP is produced via substrate-level phosphorylation (equivalent to 1 ATP).

15 ATP represents the total yield from one molecule of Pyruvate, which includes the 3 ATP generated from the NADH produced by the Pyruvate Dehydrogenase complex prior to Acetyl CoA entering the cycle.

38 ATP is the traditional theoretical maximum yield for the complete aerobic oxidation of one molecule of glucose, accounting for glycolysis, the PDH complex, and the TCA cycle combined with various shuttle systems for cytosolic NADH.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 105 (Book Page): The total yield of ATP from the oxidation of one acetyl CoA is shown in Figure 9.7. [Figure 9.7 shows: 3 NADH = 9; FADH2 = 2; GDP + Pi = 1; Total = 12 ATP/acetyl CoA oxidized].

category: Elaborate the effect of oligomycin and uncouplers on ATP production
statement: In neonates, specialized brown adipose tissue produces heat to maintain body temperature through a process known as nonshivering thermogenesis. This is mediated by which of the following?
options: Activation of UCP1 (thermogenin) by fatty acids
Enhanced coupling of the electron transport chain to Complex V
Inhibition of the cytochrome oxidase complex
Inhibition of the glycerol 3-phosphate shuttle
Upregulation of ATP synthase activity in the matrix
correctOption: Activation of UCP1 (thermogenin) by fatty acids
optionExplanations: UCP1 (thermogenin) creates a proton leak in brown fat mitochondria. This leak is physiologically triggered by fatty acids in response to cold.
Nonshivering thermogenesis requires the 'uncoupling' of the ETC from Complex V, not enhanced coupling.
Inhibiting cytochrome oxidase would stop the ETC and prevent heat production from respiration.
The glycerol 3-phosphate shuttle is used to move reducing equivalents; its inhibition would not facilitate heat production.
Upregulating ATP synthase would produce more ATP, not the wasted heat required for thermogenesis.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 79 (Book Page): [UCP1, also called thermogenin, is responsible for the heat production in the brown adipocytes of mammals. UCP1 is activated by fatty acids.]

category: Explain the significance of Cori cycle and glucosealanine cycle
coreConcept: Enzymatic Blockage in the Cori Cycle
statement: A patient with a congenital deficiency of pyruvate carboxylase presents with hypoglycemia and hyperlacticacidemia. Which statement best explains why the Cori cycle is failing to maintain this patient's blood glucose levels?
options: Lactate is being directly converted to acetyl CoA, which cannot form glucose.
The kidneys are secreting all the lactate before it can reach the liver.
The muscle is unable to reduce pyruvate to lactate due to enzyme inhibition.
Lactate cannot be converted to pyruvate in the liver's cytosol.
The liver cannot convert pyruvate to oxaloacetate, a required step for gluconeogenesis.
correctOption: The liver cannot convert pyruvate to oxaloacetate, a required step for gluconeogenesis.
optionExplanations: Option D is incorrect because lactate must be converted to pyruvate first, and acetyl CoA cannot be converted back to glucose.
Option E is incorrect because the renal threshold is not the primary issue; the metabolic block in the liver prevents lactate utilization.
Option C is incorrect because muscle lactate production is generally normal; the problem lies in the liver's processing of that lactate.
Option A is incorrect because the conversion of lactate to pyruvate is catalyzed by lactate dehydrogenase, which is not deficient in this patient.

Option B is correct. The Cori cycle relies on the liver's ability to take lactate, turn it into pyruvate, and then use pyruvate carboxylase to turn pyruvate into oxaloacetate for gluconeogenesis. A deficiency here blocks the cycle.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 110 (Book Page): In gluconeogenesis, pyruvate is first carboxylated by pyruvate carboxylase to OAA... Page 118 (Book Page): Elevated lactate and pyruvate are also observed in pyruvate carboxylase deficiency.

category: Elaborate the glycerol 3-P shuttle and malate-aspartate shuttle for the transfer of reducing equivalents from cytosol into the mitochondria
statement: In the malate-aspartate shuttle, which specific molecule is exported from the mitochondrial matrix into the cytosol to be converted back into oxaloacetate?
options: Glutamate
Malate
Aspartate
alpha-Ketoglutarate
Pyruvate
correctOption: Aspartate
optionExplanations: Incorrect. Glutamate is imported into the matrix in exchange for aspartate or as part of the aminotransferase reaction.
Incorrect. Malate is imported into the matrix from the cytosol in this shuttle.
Correct. According to Figure 6.15B, aspartate is the molecule exported from the matrix to the cytosol, where it is then converted back to oxaloacetate via an aminotransferase.
Incorrect. While alpha-ketoglutarate is involved, the primary 'carrier' of the carbon skeleton back to the cytosol to regenerate the starting oxaloacetate is aspartate.
Incorrect. Pyruvate is not an intermediate in the malate-aspartate shuttle.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 79 (Book Page): [Figure 6.15B ... (alpha)-Ketoglutarate Aspartate ... Cytosol]

category: Enumerate clinically important inhibitors of electron transport chain and mention their site of action
statement: A laboratory researcher is testing various compounds to determine their effect on mitochondrial respiration. Which of the following substances acts specifically by inhibiting the transfer of electrons from the NADH dehydrogenase complex to coenzyme Q?
options: Antimycin A
Amytal
Oligomycin
Carbon monoxide
Sodium azide
correctOption: Amytal
optionExplanations: Antimycin A is a site-specific inhibitor that blocks the Electron Transport Chain at Complex III (Cytochrome bc1), preventing electron flow to Cytochrome c.
Amytal (a barbiturate) and Rotenone are classic inhibitors of Complex I (NADH dehydrogenase), preventing the transfer of electrons to ubiquinone (CoQ).
Oligomycin is an inhibitor of ATP synthase (Complex V) rather than a direct inhibitor of the electron transport complexes themselves, though it stops respiration via respiratory control.
Carbon monoxide binds to the heme iron of Complex IV, similar to cyanide, blocking the respiratory chain at its terminal step.
Sodium azide is an inhibitor of Complex IV (Cytochrome oxidase), specifically preventing the final reduction of oxygen to water.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 76 (Book Page): [Note: Figure illustrates normal direction of electron flow.] ... Amytal ... Rotenone [block Complex I].

category: Outline the reactions involved in ethanol metabolism
statement: Which specific metabolic environment or site is identified as a location for the reduction of pyruvate to ethanol by microorganisms?
options: Hepatic mitochondria
Skeletal muscle
Erythrocytes
Renal medulla
Intestinal flora
correctOption: Intestinal flora
optionExplanations: Hepatic mitochondria oxidize pyruvate to acetyl CoA or OAA; they do not synthesize ethanol from pyruvate.
Skeletal muscle reduces pyruvate to lactate during anaerobic exercise, not ethanol.
Erythrocytes lack mitochondria and perform anaerobic glycolysis to lactate only.
The renal medulla performs anaerobic glycolysis to lactate but does not possess the enzymes for ethanol synthesis.
Intestinal flora (bacteria) and yeast are the primary biological sites for the fermentation of pyruvate to ethanol.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 106 (Book Page): Reduction of pyruvate to ethanol (microorganisms) ... Occurs in yeast and some bacteria (including intestinal flora).

category: Enlist the hormones that play important roles in regulating carbohydrate metabolism
statement: A 24-year-old patient with Type 1 diabetes is brought to the emergency department after being found confused and diaphoretic. His blood glucose is 38 mg/dL. In a physiologically normal individual, which hormonal cascade would be the most immediate response to this glucose level to activate hepatic glycogen phosphorylase?
options: Epinephrine binding to alpha-adrenergic receptors to decrease intracellular calcium.
Glucagon binding to GPCRs, increasing cAMP, and activating protein kinase A to phosphorylate phosphorylase kinase.
Cortisol entering the nucleus to decrease the transcription of PEP-carboxykinase.
Insulin binding to tyrosine kinase receptors to activate protein phosphatase-1.
Thyroxine increasing the mitochondrial permeability to NADH to stimulate the TCA cycle.
correctOption: Glucagon binding to GPCRs, increasing cAMP, and activating protein kinase A to phosphorylate phosphorylase kinase.
optionExplanations: Epinephrine binding to alpha-1 adrenergic receptors in the liver actually increases intracellular calcium to activate phosphorylase kinase, not decreases it.

During hypoglycemia, glucagon is released. It binds to its GPCR, activates adenylyl cyclase, increases cAMP, and activates PKA. PKA then phosphorylates and activates phosphorylase kinase, which activates glycogen phosphorylase.
Cortisol increases (upregulates) the transcription of PEP-carboxykinase to promote gluconeogenesis, but this is a slower, long-term response compared to the cAMP cascade.
Insulin is secreted in response to high blood glucose (hyperglycemia) and leads to the dephosphorylation and inactivation of glycogen phosphorylase.
Thyroxine is not the acute regulator of the glycogenolytic cascade in response to immediate hypoglycemia.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 124 (Book Page): [The binding of hormones, such as glucagon or epinephrine, to plasma membrane G protein-coupled receptors (GPCR) signals the need for glycogen to be degraded... Binding of glucagon or epinephrine to their specific hepatocyte GPCR... results in the G protein-mediated activation of adenylyl cyclase... synthesis of cAMP, which activates cAMP-dependent protein kinase A (PKA).]

category: Enlist various types of glycogen storage diseases (GSDs)
statement: A neonate exhibits progressive liver cirrhosis and failure, leading to death in early childhood. Histological examination of the liver reveals an accumulation of abnormal glycogen with very long, unbranched outer chains. This clinical picture is most consistent with which GSD?
options: Type III (Cori disease)
Type VI (Hers disease)
Type V (McArdle syndrome)
Type II (Pompe disease)
Type IV (Andersen disease)
correctOption: Type IV (Andersen disease)
optionExplanations: Cori disease involves 'limit dextrins' (short branches) due to a debranching defect; Andersen involves long unbranched chains due to a branching defect.
Hers disease is a deficiency in liver phosphorylase; it is generally a mild condition with hepatomegaly and mild hypoglycemia, not progressive fatal cirrhosis with abnormal glycogen structure.
McArdle syndrome affects muscle only and does not cause liver failure or cirrhosis.
Pompe disease involves lysosomal accumulation and primarily presents with heart failure, not typically with early childhood cirrhosis due to abnormal glycogen structure.

Type IV GSD (Andersen disease) is caused by a deficiency in the branching enzyme. This results in glycogen with few branch points and long outer chains, which the body treats as a foreign substance, triggering an immune response that leads to liver cirrhosis.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 121 (Book Page): [Note: A GSD can also be caused by defects in branching enzyme, an enzyme of synthesis, resulting in Type IV: Andersen disease and causing death in early childhood.]

category: e
statement: The standard free energy change (ΔGo) of two consecutive reactions is additive. Given that the conversion of Glucose to Glucose 6-P has a ΔGo of -4,000 cal/mol and the conversion of Glucose 6-P to Fructose 6-P has a ΔGo of +400 cal/mol, what is the significance of the overall ΔGo for the combined pathway?
options: The overall ΔGo is -3,600 cal/mol, making the sequential process exergonic and energetically favorable.
The positive ΔGo of the second reaction acts as a rate-limiting barrier that prevents the first reaction from occurring.
The pathway is endergonic and cannot proceed without additional energy input.
The additivity of ΔGo only applies if the reactions share a common coenzyme like NAD+.
The overall ΔG must be zero because the reactions reach equilibrium instantaneously.
correctOption: The overall ΔGo is -3,600 cal/mol, making the sequential process exergonic and energetically favorable.
optionExplanations: Because the sum of the ΔGo values (-4000 + 400 = -3600) is negative, the entire sequence is thermodynamically spontaneous.
