Lipoic acid is part of the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex which produces acetyl-CoA, not the anaerobic ethanol synthesis pathway found in yeast.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 105 (Book Page): The decarboxylation of pyruvate by pyruvate decarboxylase occurs in yeast and certain other microorganisms... The enzyme requires thiamine pyrophosphate as a coenzyme... Figure 8.24: Pyruvate -> Acetaldehyde (via Pyruvate decarboxylase/TPP) -> Ethanol (via Alcohol dehydrogenase/NADH).

category: Enlist the hormones that play important roles in regulating carbohydrate metabolism
statement: Which specific pancreatic cells are responsible for the secretion of the hormone that triggers hepatic gluconeogenesis and glycogenolysis during the fasting state?
options: Alpha cells
F cells
Epsilon cells
Delta cells
Beta cells
correctOption: Alpha cells
optionExplanations: Alpha cells secrete glucagon, which is released during fasting to raise blood glucose levels via glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis.
F cells (or PP cells) secrete pancreatic polypeptide, which is involved in regulating pancreatic exocrine secretions and has no direct glycemic effect.
Epsilon cells produce ghrelin, which is involved in hunger signaling but is not the primary hormone of the pancreatic islets regulating glucose via the glucagon pathway.
Delta cells secrete somatostatin, which inhibits the release of both insulin and glucagon.
Beta cells secrete insulin, which is the primary anabolic hormone that lowers blood glucose and inhibits gluconeogenesis.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 114 (Book Page): [Glucagon... This hormone from the α cells of pancreatic islets... stimulates gluconeogenesis by three mechanisms.]

category: Enlist the components of complex I, II, III, and IV
coreConcept: Distribution of Fe–S Centers in the ETC
statement: Iron–sulfur (Fe–S) centers are essential for the transfer of electrons between prosthetic groups and mobile carriers. According to the structural organization of the respiratory chain, these centers are found in which complexes?
options: Complex I only
Complexes I, II, and III
Complex IV only
Complexes II, III, and IV
Complexes III and IV only
correctOption: Complexes I, II, and III
optionExplanations: While Complex I contains Fe–S centers, they are also documented components of Complexes II and III.
Iron–sulfur centers are critical components found in the first three complexes of the electron transport chain (I, II, and III).
Complex IV does not contain Fe–S centers; it utilizes heme iron and copper atoms for its electron transfer activities.
Fe–S centers are present in Complexes II and III, but they are absent in Complex IV, which instead contains cytochrome a and a3 components.
Complex III contains Fe–S centers (the Rieske center), but Complex IV does not; it relies on different metallic cofactors.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 75 (Book Page): [NADH dehydrogenase also contains iron atoms paired with sulfur atoms to make iron–sulfur centers (Figure 6.9). . . [Note: Complexes II and III also contain iron-sulfur centers.]]

category: Elaborate the reaction catalyzed by pyruvate dehydrogenase complex (PDH) along with regulation and significance
coreConcept: Structure and Coenzymes of the PDH Complex
statement: The pyruvate dehydrogenase complex (PDH) utilizes a multi-subunit structure to catalyze its reaction. Which specific subunit of this aggregate is responsible for the transfer of the acetyl group to Coenzyme A (CoA) using lipoic acid as a coenzyme?
options: Dihydrolipoyl dehydrogenase (E3)
Pyruvate dehydrogenase (E1)
PDH phosphatase
Dihydrolipoyl transacetylase (E2)
PDH kinase
correctOption: Dihydrolipoyl transacetylase (E2)
optionExplanations: Dihydrolipoyl dehydrogenase (E3) is involved in the regeneration of the oxidized form of lipoic acid and utilizes FAD and NAD+ as its primary electron carriers.
Pyruvate dehydrogenase (E1) is responsible for the initial decarboxylation of pyruvate and requires thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP) as a coenzyme, not the transfer to CoA.
PDH phosphatase is a regulatory enzyme that removes the inhibitory phosphate from the E1 subunit to activate the complex, rather than participating in substrate conversion.
Dihydrolipoyl transacetylase (E2) is the core subunit that catalyzes the transfer of the acetyl group from the dihydrolipoyl moiety to Coenzyme A, forming Acetyl CoA.
PDH kinase is a regulatory subunit that phosphorylates and inhibits the E1 subunit; it is not involved in the catalytic transfer of the acetyl group.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 102 (Book Page): The pyruvate dehydrogenase complex (PDH complex) is a multimolecular aggregate of three enzymes, pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDH or E1, also called a decarboxylase), dihydrolipoyl transacetylase (E2), and dihydrolipoyl dehydrogenase (E3). ... E2 requires lipoic acid and CoA.

category: Outline treatment strategies
coreConcept: Therapeutic Strategy for PDH Complex Deficiency
statement: A pediatric patient is diagnosed with congenital lactic acidosis due to an X-linked deficiency in the E1 component of the pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDH) complex. Genetic analysis identifies a mutation affecting the binding affinity for its coenzyme. What combined therapeutic approach is recommended for this specific subtype of PDH deficiency?
options: Administration of fluoride to inhibit glycolysis and prevent pyruvate formation.
High carbohydrate intake combined with anaerobic exercise training.
Total parenteral nutrition consisting exclusively of branched-chain amino acids.
Large doses of biotin and a low-protein diet to bypass the TCA cycle.
Dietary restriction of carbohydrates and supplementation with thiamine pyrophosphate.
correctOption: Dietary restriction of carbohydrates and supplementation with thiamine pyrophosphate.
optionExplanations: Fluoride is a toxin that inhibits enolase; using it therapeutically to stop glycolysis would be lethal as it would stop all energy production in non-oxidative tissues.
High carbohydrate intake would increase the pyruvate load, which cannot be converted to acetyl-CoA, leading to worsened lactic acidosis.
While some amino acids can provide acetyl-CoA directly, a diet consisting 'exclusively' of branched-chain amino acids would be nutritionally incomplete and dangerous.
Biotin is a coenzyme for carboxylases (like pyruvate carboxylase), not the PDH complex; it would not address the E1 deficiency of the dehydrogenase.

Reducing dietary carbohydrates limits the production of pyruvate, the substrate that cannot be metabolized. Supplementing with TPP is specifically effective if the mutation in the E1 subunit (decarboxylase) has reduced its affinity for this essential coenzyme.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 103 (Book Page): There is no proven treatment for pyruvate dehydrogenase deficiency: however, dietary restriction of carbohydrate and supplementation with TPP [thiamine pyrophosphate] may reduce symptoms in select patients.

category: Enlist the components of complex I, II, III, and IV
statement: In the stepwise transfer of electrons through the respiratory chain, which component is uniquely associated with the outer face of the inner mitochondrial membrane rather than being an integral protein complex?
options: NADH dehydrogenase
Cytochrome c
Succinate dehydrogenase
Cytochrome bc1
Cytochrome a + a3
correctOption: Cytochrome c
optionExplanations: NADH dehydrogenase is an integral protein complex (Complex I) spanning the membrane.
Cytochrome c is a small, mobile hemeprotein associated with the exterior (cytosolic side) of the inner mitochondrial membrane.
Succinate dehydrogenase is an integral protein complex (Complex II) of the inner membrane.
Cytochrome bc1 is the integral protein complex known as Complex III.
Cytochrome a + a3 is the integral protein complex known as Complex IV.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 76 (Book Page): [Note: Cytochrome c is associated with the outer face of the inner membrane and, like CoQ, is a mobile carrier of electrons.]

category: Diagnose G6PD (glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase) deficiency based on given data
statement: In the physiological loop involving G6PD, how does the erythrocyte maintain its antioxidant capacity when exposed to reactive oxygen species (ROS)?
options: Oxidized glutathione (GSSG) diffuses out of the cell to be reduced by the liver
NADH produced in glycolysis directly reduces glutathione peroxidase
Glutathione peroxidase uses ATP to synthesize new glutathione tripeptides
Superoxide dismutase converts hydrogen peroxide directly into reduced glutathione
G6PD produces NADPH, which is used by glutathione reductase to regenerate reduced glutathione
correctOption: G6PD produces NADPH, which is used by glutathione reductase to regenerate reduced glutathione
optionExplanations: Glutathione reduction is an intracellular process; the cell must regenerate GSH locally using NADPH-dependent glutathione reductase.
NADH is used in glycolysis; NADPH from the pentose phosphate pathway is the specific reductant for the glutathione system.
Glutathione peroxidase reduces H2O2 to water; it does not synthesize the glutathione tripeptide, which is a separate metabolic process.
Superoxide dismutase (SOD) converts superoxide to hydrogen peroxide; it does not interact with the glutathione pool directly.
G6PD is the primary source of NADPH. Glutathione reductase uses NADPH to reduce oxidized glutathione (GSSG) back to reduced glutathione (GSH), which then detoxifies ROS.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 140 (Book Page): The cell regenerates reduced glutathione in a reaction catalyzed by glutathione reductase, using NADPH as a source of reducing equivalents. Thus, NADPH indirectly provides electrons for the reduction of hydrogen peroxide

category: Identify the risk factors of malnutrition
coreConcept: Nutrient Ratios as Risk Factors for Marasmus
statement: A 9-month-old infant in a low-income household is fed predominantly with a very thin, watery cereal gruel because the mother's breast milk supply has ceased. The child appears emaciated with visible muscle wasting but no edema. What is the relative risk factor for this specific condition?
options: A high-fat diet that inhibits the absorption of essential water-soluble vitamins.
Consumption of proteins with a high PDCAAS value in insufficient quantities.
A relative deficiency of protein that is significantly greater than the caloric deficiency.
Excessive carbohydrate intake that maintains high visceral protein synthesis.
Chronic calorie deprivation that is relatively greater than the reduction in protein.
correctOption: Chronic calorie deprivation that is relatively greater than the reduction in protein.
optionExplanations: Thin cereal gruels are low in fat and protein; high-fat diets are not the risk factor here.
Native cereal gruels typically have a lower PDCAAS (quality) than animal-derived proteins.
This describes Kwashiorkor, which typically involves edema and occurs in older infants.
If carbohydrate intake were excessive relative to protein, the child would likely develop Kwashiorkor (edema) rather than the emaciation of Marasmus.
Marasmus is characterized by a pervasive lack of both calories and protein, with the caloric deficit being the predominant driver of the emaciated appearance.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 361 (Book Page): Marasmus occurs when calorie deprivation is relatively greater than the reduction in protein... usually occurs in children younger than 1 year of age when breast milk is supplemented with watery gruels of native cereals.

category: Discuss the metabolic fates of pyruvate
statement: Which enzyme catalyzes the irreversible oxidative decarboxylation of pyruvate to produce the major fuel for the tricarboxylic acid cycle?
options: Pyruvate dehydrogenase complex
Pyruvate carboxylase
Pyruvate decarboxylase
Lactate dehydrogenase
Alanine aminotransferase
correctOption: Pyruvate dehydrogenase complex
optionExplanations: The pyruvate dehydrogenase complex is a mitochondrial multienzyme aggregate that converts pyruvate to acetyl CoA, which serves as the primary substrate for the citric acid cycle and fatty acid synthesis.
Pyruvate carboxylase is a biotin-dependent enzyme that converts pyruvate into oxaloacetate, primarily for gluconeogenesis or replenishing TCA cycle intermediates, rather than producing acetyl CoA.
Pyruvate decarboxylase is found in yeast and certain microorganisms where it converts pyruvate to acetaldehyde and CO2, but this enzyme is not present in human metabolic pathways.
Lactate dehydrogenase catalyzes the reversible reduction of pyruvate to lactate in anaerobic conditions or in tissues lacking mitochondria, which does not produce the fuel for the TCA cycle.

Alanine aminotransferase is involved in the transamination of pyruvate to form the amino acid alanine, a process distinct from the oxidative decarboxylation required to enter the TCA cycle as acetyl CoA.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 105 (Book Page): Oxidative decarboxylation of pyruvate by pyruvate dehydrogenase complex is an important pathway in tissues with a high oxidative capacity, such as cardiac muscle... Pyruvate dehydrogenase irreversibly converts pyruvate, the end product of glycolysis, into acetyl CoA.

category: Diagnose G6PD (glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase) deficiency based on given data
coreConcept: Self-Limiting Nature of G6PD A- Hemolysis
statement: An 8-year-old male of African descent is brought to the emergency department with jaundice, dark urine, and fatigue. His symptoms began two days after he was treated with primaquine for malaria. Laboratory studies show anemia and the presence of Heinz bodies in the peripheral smear. Which finding is most likely in this patient during the recovery phase?
options: Persistent low G6PD activity in all circulating erythrocytes.
Absence of G6PD mRNA in the hepatic tissue samples.
Resolution of jaundice without an increase in serum unconjugated bilirubin.
Progressive decrease in hematocrit despite cessation of primaquine.
Increased reticulocytosis with higher G6PD activity than seen during the acute hemolytic phase.
correctOption: Increased reticulocytosis with higher G6PD activity than seen during the acute hemolytic phase.
optionExplanations: In G6PD A-, reticulocytes and young cells have relatively normal G6PD activity because the enzyme has not yet degraded.
G6PD deficiency is not typically a total lack of mRNA; missense mutations usually result in unstable proteins, and liver cells have alternative NADPH sources.
The resolution of jaundice occurs as the rate of hemolysis decreases, but the jaundice itself is a hallmark of increased unconjugated bilirubin during the acute phase of lysis.
The anemia is self-limiting; once the older, deficient cells are destroyed and the drug is stopped, the hematocrit begins to rise.

The recovery phase of G6PD A- involves the bone marrow releasing new reticulocytes. These young cells have higher G6PD activity than the older cells that were lysed, leading to a temporary normalization of enzyme activity levels on testing.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 145 (Book Page): The anemia is self-limited because the older, vulnerable population of erythrocytes is replaced by younger RBCs with sufficient G6PD activity to withstand an assault. ... In subjects with G6PD A– ... most of the enzyme activity present in the reticulocytes and younger erythrocytes.

category: Diagnose G6PD (glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase) deficiency based on given data
statement: Genetic data for a child with chronic nonspherocytic hemolytic anemia identifies a mutation in the G6PD gene. The child exhibits constant hemolysis even in the absence of oxidative stress. Which classification of G6PD variant is most likely associated with this clinical data?
options: Class IV
Class III
Class II
Class I
Class V
correctOption: Class I
optionExplanations: Class IV represents normal enzyme activity (>60%) with no clinical symptoms.
Class III variants (e.g., G6PD A-) are moderate with 10-60% activity and only cause hemolysis during acute oxidant stress.
Class II variants (e.g., Mediterranean) are severe and episodic, occurring with triggers, but typically not as chronic non-oxidant anemia like Class I.
Class I variants are the most severe, with less than 10% residual enzyme activity and chronic anemia regardless of oxidant exposure.
Class V (rarely discussed) refers to increased enzyme activity, which would not cause anemia.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 145 (Book Page): Class I mutations (rare) are the most severe and are associated with chronic nonspherocytic anemia, which occurs even in the absence of oxidative stress.

category: Delineate special nutritional requirements during pregnancy, lactation, growth, and old age
statement: In the context of public health nutrition, a committee is setting the Estimated Average Requirement (EAR) for a nutrient. Which of the following best describes the proportion of the population whose requirements are met by the EAR?
options: 100% of the population.
97% to 98% of the population.
2% to 3% of the population.
95% of the population.
50% of the population.
correctOption: 50% of the population.
optionExplanations: No DRI standard is typically set to meet 100% of the population's needs, as individual requirements vary too significantly at the extremes of the distribution curve.
97% to 98% is the population percentage whose requirements are met by the Recommended Dietary Allowance (RDA), which is set 2 standard deviations above the EAR.
2% to 3% represents the risk of inadequacy at the level of the RDA, not the EAR. Intakes below the EAR have a 50% or higher probability of being inadequate.
95% is a statistical confidence interval but does not correspond to a specific DRI standard like EAR or RDA.
The EAR is the median requirement; by definition, it meets the needs of exactly 50% (one half) of the healthy individuals in a specific group.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 349 (Book Page): Estimated Average Requirement (EAR): The EAR is the average daily nutrient intake level estimated to meet the requirement of one half of the healthy individuals in a particular life stage and gender group.

category: Define basal metabolic rate (BMR)
statement: The Resting Metabolic Rate (RMR) is sensitive to the proportion of daily energy expenditure. In a typical sedentary individual, which range accurately reflects the percentage of total daily calories consumed by the RMR?
options: Exactly 100%
optionExplanations: The reference text explicitly states that 50–70% of daily energy expenditure in sedentary people is due to RMR.
TEE always includes RMR plus the thermic effect of food and physical activity; RMR alone cannot be 100% of the expenditure if the person is alive and eating.
This range is associated with the thermic effect of food, not the RMR.
Physical activity typically accounts for 30–50% above the RMR in sedentary individuals, making RMR the larger portion.
While RMR is the largest component, it rarely reaches 95% because the thermic effect of food (10%) is constant.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 359 (Book Page): [From 50–70% of the daily energy expenditure in sedentary individuals is attributable to the RMR (Figure 27.6).]

category: Elaborate the effect of various physiological and pathological factors on BMR
statement: Which of the following terms specifically describes the energy expended by an individual to carry out normal body functions like respiration and blood flow while in a resting, postabsorptive state?
options: Activity thermogenesis
Adequate Intake (AI)
Resting metabolic rate (RMR)
Estimated Energy Requirement (EER)
Thermic effect of food
correctOption: Resting metabolic rate (RMR)
optionExplanations: Activity thermogenesis refers to energy expended during physical exercise, which is distinct from the basal functions covered by RMR.
Adequate Intake (AI) is a dietary reference standard used when an EAR or RDA cannot be determined; it is not a measure of metabolic expenditure.
Resting metabolic rate (RMR) is the standard term for energy used at rest to maintain essential physiological systems like ion transport and cellular integrity.
The Estimated Energy Requirement (EER) is the average dietary energy intake predicted to maintain an energy balance in a healthy adult based on several variables, not just resting functions.
The thermic effect of food refers to the heat production by the body during the digestion and absorption of nutrients, which occurs above the resting level.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 359 (Book Page): The energy expended by an individual in a resting, postabsorptive state is called the resting (formerly, basal) metabolic rate (RMR). It represents the energy required to carry out the normal body functions, such as respiration, blood flow, ion transport, and maintenance of cellular integrity.

category: Explain the significance of Cori cycle and glucosealanine cycle
coreConcept: Nitrogen disposal in the Glucose-Alanine cycle
statement: What is the primary metabolic fate of the nitrogen transported to the liver during the glucose-alanine cycle?
options: Conversion into uric acid via the purine degradation pathway.
Incorporation into the urea cycle for urinary excretion.
Conversion into essential amino acids for muscle repair.
Transport back to the muscle as glutamine.
Oxidation in the mitochondria to produce ammonium nitrate.
correctOption: Incorporation into the urea cycle for urinary excretion.
optionExplanations: Uric acid is the end product of purine degradation (e.g., adenosine, guanosine), not the primary end product for general amino acid nitrogen from protein catabolism.

When alanine reaches the liver, it undergoes transamination, transferring its amino group to α-ketoglutarate to form glutamate. Glutamate then releases ammonia (or transfers nitrogen to aspartate), which enters the urea cycle to be excreted as urea.
Essential amino acids cannot be synthesized by the human body from alanine; they must be obtained from the diet.
While glutamine is another nitrogen carrier, the specific return path of the 'glucose-alanine cycle' is the transport of glucose back to the muscle, not glutamine.
Nitrogen is not oxidized to ammonium nitrate in human metabolism; it is processed into urea or excreted as ammonium ions in the urine.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 74 (Book Page): The synthesis of glucose, urea, and heme occur partially in the matrix of mitochondria. Page 109 (Book Page): This oxidation provides energy for the production of the majority of ATP... The cycle occurs totally in the mitochondria and is, therefore, in close proximity to the reactions of electron transport.

category: Elaborate key features of various transport systems for entry of glucose into cells
statement: The pancreatic beta cells function as glucose sensors to determine the threshold for insulin secretion. Which feature of the GLUT-2 transporter facilitates this sensing role during periods of hyperglycemia?
options: High Km (low affinity), ensuring glucose entry is proportional to blood glucose levels.
Physical association with the mitochondria to directly transport glucose-6-phosphate.
Low Km (high affinity), ensuring the transporter is always saturated with glucose.
Covalent modification by insulin to increase its transport speed.
Requirement of ATP to move glucose into the cell against a gradient.
correctOption: High Km (low affinity), ensuring glucose entry is proportional to blood glucose levels.
optionExplanations: GLUT-2 has a high Km (low affinity), meaning it does not reach its maximum rate until glucose levels are high. This allows the rate of glucose entry into the beta cell to reflect blood glucose levels.
GLUT transporters only move free glucose across the plasma membrane; they do not associate with mitochondria or transport phosphorylated sugars like glucose-6-phosphate.
A low Km would mean the transporter is saturated even at low glucose levels, making it unable to sense increases in blood sugar after a meal.
GLUT-2 is insulin-independent; insulin does not modify its structure or translocation to increase speed.
GLUT-2 uses facilitated diffusion (passive), not active transport requiring ATP.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 90 (Book Page): In β cells, glucokinase functions as the glucose sensor, determining the threshold for insulin secretion... GLUT-2 insures that blood glucose equilibrates rapidly across the membrane of the hepatocyte. [Note: GLUT-2 is also found in pancreatic β cells.]

category: Elaborate the regulation and importance of gluconeogenesis
statement: A researcher is comparing the gluconeogenic capacity of the liver and skeletal muscle. He observes that while both can store glycogen, only the liver can contribute to blood glucose maintenance. This physiological contrast is due to the absence of which enzyme in skeletal muscle?
options: Pyruvate carboxylase
Phosphoglucomutase
Glucose 6-phosphatase
Fructose 1,6-bisphosphatase
Phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase
correctOption: Glucose 6-phosphatase
optionExplanations: Muscle does contain pyruvate carboxylase, but it uses it mainly to replenish TCA cycle intermediates (anaplerotic role) rather than for gluconeogenesis.
Phosphoglucomutase is present in muscle to interconvert G1P (from glycogen) to G6P for glycolysis.
Glucose 6-phosphatase is required to remove the phosphate from G6P to allow free glucose to exit the cell via GLUT transporters. Muscle lacks this enzyme, trapping glucose for its own use.
Fructose 1,6-bisphosphatase is the rate-limiting enzyme of gluconeogenesis; while predominantly in liver/kidney, its absence is not the primary reason muscle cannot release glucose into the blood.
PEPCK is present in muscle but is used for other metabolic tasks; the final release of glucose is strictly dependent on Glucose 6-phosphatase.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 113 (Book Page): Muscle lacks glucose 6-phosphatase, and therefore muscle glycogen can not be used to maintain blood glucose levels.

category: Explain how ethanol consumption causes hypoglycemia and fatty liver
statement: The development of a 'fatty liver' in chronic alcoholism is partly attributed to the redirected metabolism of dihydroxyacetone phosphate (DHAP). Which metabolic shift, driven by a high NADH/NAD+ ratio, provides the necessary backbone for triacylglycerol accumulation?
options: Reduction of DHAP to glycerol 3-phosphate
Isomerization of DHAP to glucose 6-phosphate
Dephosphorylation of DHAP to free glycerol
Conversion of DHAP to fructose 1,6-bisphosphate
Oxidation of DHAP to glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate
correctOption: Reduction of DHAP to glycerol 3-phosphate
optionExplanations: The high NADH produced by ethanol metabolism favors the reduction of DHAP to glycerol 3-phosphate via glycerol phosphate dehydrogenase. Glycerol 3-phosphate serves as the backbone for the synthesis of triacylglycerols, which accumulate in the liver causing steatosis.
DHAP cannot be directly isomerized to glucose 6-phosphate; it must first pass through several steps of gluconeogenesis, which is inhibited by ethanol.
There is no direct dephosphorylation of DHAP to glycerol; glycerol is produced through the glycerophosphate pathway which requires DHAP reduction as an initial step in this context.
Conversion of DHAP to fructose 1,6-bisphosphate is a step in gluconeogenesis that is actually blocked because the preceding steps are inhibited by precursor depletion.
Oxidation of DHAP occurs in glycolysis, but the high NADH/NAD+ ratio favors reductive reactions, not oxidative ones.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 79 (Book Page): In the glycerophosphate shuttle... two electrons are transferred from NADH to dihydroxyacetone phosphate by cytosolic glycerophosphate dehydrogenase. The glycerol 3-phosphate produced is oxidized...

category: Enlist symptoms and signs
coreConcept: Clinical and Biochemical Signs of Pompe Disease
statement: A pediatrician evaluates two infants for suspected Glycogen Storage Diseases (GSD). The first infant presents with massive cardiomegaly and heart failure, while the second presents with severe fasting hypoglycemia and renomegaly. Which finding specifically identifies the pathology in the first infant as Pompe disease?
options: A marked rise in blood lactate during strenuous muscle activity
Severe hyperuricemia and hyperlipidemia on laboratory testing
Accumulation of abnormal glycogen vacuoles within lysosomes
Presence of limit dextrins in the cytosol of hepatocytes
Inability to release free glucose into the blood due to phosphatase deficiency
correctOption: Accumulation of abnormal glycogen vacuoles within lysosomes
optionExplanations: The absence of a rise in blood lactate is a feature of McArdle syndrome (Type V), not Pompe disease.
Hyperuricemia and hyperlipidemia are characteristic signs of Von Gierke disease (Type Ia) due to metabolic shunting when glucose 6-phosphate cannot be converted to glucose.
Pompe disease is a lysosomal storage disease caused by a deficiency of alpha(1->4)-glucosidase, leading to glycogen accumulation in lysosomes, which classically manifests as massive cardiomegaly.
Limit dextrins accumulate in Cori disease (Type III) due to debranching enzyme deficiency, which is not primarily associated with heart failure.
This describes Von Gierke disease (Type Ia), which explains the hypoglycemia in the second infant but not the cardiomegaly in the first.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 122 (Book Page): Type II: Pompe disease... Excessive glycogen concentrations found in abnormal vacuoles in the lysosomes... Massive cardiomegaly... Infantile form: early death typically from heart failure.

category: Delineate special nutritional requirements during pregnancy, lactation, growth, and old age
coreConcept: Establishing Nutrient AI for Growth in Infancy
statement: The Adequate Intake (AI) for carbohydrates and other nutrients in young infants (0–6 months) is determined differently than the Recommended Dietary Allowance (RDA) for adults. Which of the following is the primary basis for establishing these requirements in early growth?
options: Observation of nutrient levels in the urine of healthy term infants
Calculated metabolic rate based on the infant's total surface area
A fixed percentage of the total calories provided by supplemental cereals
The Estimated Average Requirement (EAR) plus two standard deviations
The estimated daily mean nutrient intake supplied by human milk
correctOption: The estimated daily mean nutrient intake supplied by human milk
optionExplanations: Urinary levels are used to assess excretion, but they do not provide a direct measure of the dietary intake required to support the rapid growth observed in healthy infants.
While surface area is used in some pediatric calculations, the AI specifically relies on the natural gold standard of infant nutrition, human milk, rather than thermodynamic modeling.
Supplemental cereals are not the basis for AI in early infancy (0-6 months); current guidelines emphasize human milk as the sole source of nutrition during this period.
The RDA is calculated from the EAR plus two standard deviations, but for infants, the lack of sufficient experimental data necessitates the use of the AI instead.
The AI for infants is derived from the nutrient profile of breast milk from healthy, exclusively breast-fed mothers, as this naturally supports optimal growth and development.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 358 (Book Page): For example, the AI for young infants, for whom human milk is the recommended sole source of food for the first 4–6 months, is based on the estimated daily mean nutrient intake supplied by human milk for healthy, full-term infants who are exclusively breast-fed.

category: Explain the significance of Cori cycle and glucosealanine cycle
coreConcept: Enzymatic Mechanism of the Glucose-Alanine Cycle
statement: In the skeletal muscle during the glucose-alanine cycle, what is the essential enzymatic transformation required to prepare the carbon skeleton for export to the liver?
options: Transamination of pyruvate with glutamate to form alanine and alpha-ketoglutarate.
Oxidative decarboxylation of pyruvate to acetyl CoA by the PDH complex.
Phosphorylation of pyruvate to phosphoenolpyruvate by pyruvate kinase.
Carboxylation of pyruvate to oxaloacetate by pyruvate carboxylase.
Reduction of pyruvate to lactate by lactate dehydrogenase using NADH.
correctOption: Transamination of pyruvate with glutamate to form alanine and alpha-ketoglutarate.
optionExplanations: In the glucose-alanine cycle, muscle-derived pyruvate undergoes transamination where it accepts an amino group from glutamate (derived from other amino acids), forming alanine for export to the liver.
The PDH complex converts pyruvate to acetyl CoA for oxidation in the TCA cycle; this is a 'loss' of carbons for gluconeogenesis and is not part of the alanine export cycle.
The conversion of pyruvate to PEP is irreversible in glycolysis and cannot be achieved by pyruvate kinase; this is the 'roadblock' overcome by the liver during gluconeogenesis.
Muscle uses pyruvate carboxylase only to replenish TCA intermediates, not for the synthesis of glucose or the export of alanine.
The reduction of pyruvate to lactate is the characteristic step of the Cori cycle, not the glucose-alanine cycle.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 109 (Book Page): Fructose, glycerol, lactate, and the alpha-keto acids obtained from the transamination of glucogenic amino acids are the most important gluconeogenic precursors.

category: Describe the reactions, regulation, and biomedical importance of uronic acid pathway and sorbitol pathway
statement: When comparing the two sequential reactions of the polyol pathway, which of the following accurately contrasts the coenzyme requirements for the production of fructose from glucose?
options: The first reaction requires FAD and the second reaction requires NAD+.
The first reaction requires TPP and the second reaction requires Lipoic acid.
The first reaction requires ATP and the second reaction requires NADPH.
Both reactions require NADPH as a reducing agent.
The first reaction requires NADPH and the second reaction requires NAD+.
correctOption: The first reaction requires NADPH and the second reaction requires NAD+.
optionExplanations: FAD is not a primary cofactor for the polyol pathway; it is used in the electron transport chain and TCA cycle.
Thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP) and lipoic acid are cofactors for decarboxylation reactions, such as the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex, not the polyol pathway.
The polyol pathway does not directly consume ATP; it is an alternate pathway to glycolysis.
Only the first reaction (reduction of glucose) requires NADPH; the second is an oxidation reaction.
The reduction of glucose to sorbitol (aldose reductase) uses NADPH. The subsequent oxidation of sorbitol to fructose (sorbitol dehydrogenase) uses NAD+.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 140 (Book Page): In cells of the liver, ovaries, and seminal vesicles, there is a second enzyme, sorbitol dehydrogenase, which can oxidize the sorbitol to produce fructose (see Figure 12.4).

category: Explain how ethanol consumption causes hypoglycemia and fatty liver
statement: In the liver of an individual consuming ethanol, the accumulation of Acetyl CoA occurs alongside a high NADH/NAD+ ratio. Why does this lead to 'fatty liver' (steatosis) rather than increased TCA cycle activity?
options: Ethanol prevents the transport of fatty acids into the mitochondria.
OAA is overly abundant, causing Citrate to inhibit the TCA cycle.
High NADH inhibits the TCA cycle, and Acetyl CoA is diverted to fatty acid synthesis.
Ethanol is converted directly into triacylglycerols in the cytosol.
Acetyl CoA is an allosteric inhibitor of the fatty acid synthase complex.
correctOption: High NADH inhibits the TCA cycle, and Acetyl CoA is diverted to fatty acid synthesis.
optionExplanations: While ethanol may affect various pathways, the primary driver for fatty liver is the increased availability of Acetyl CoA and NADH favoring lipogenesis.
OAA is actually depleted in the presence of high NADH, not abundant.

Ethanol metabolism produces Acetyl CoA and high NADH. High NADH inhibits several TCA cycle enzymes. Since OAA is also depleted (converted to malate), Acetyl CoA cannot enter the TCA cycle and is instead used as a building block for fatty acid synthesis, leading to steatosis.
Ethanol is metabolized to acetaldehyde and then to Acetyl CoA; it is the Acetyl CoA that is then synthesized into fatty acids and then triacylglycerols.
Acetyl CoA is the substrate and precursor for fatty acid synthesis, not an inhibitor.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 103 (Book Page): Acetyl CoA accumulates and leads to activation of pyruvate carboxylase... [Note: Acetyl CoA inhibits pyruvate dehydrogenase (by activating PDH kinase, see Page 103 (Book Page)). Thus, this single compound can divert pyruvate toward gluconeogenesis and away from the TCA cycle.] ... Page 97 (Book Page): Acetyl CoA [is] the building block for fatty acid synthesis.

category: Infer the consequences of deficiency and excess of these hormones
coreConcept: Metabolic Consequences of Insulin Deficiency (Type 1 Diabetes)
statement: A 10-year-old girl is brought to the clinic with polyuria, polydipsia, and significant weight loss. Laboratory findings reveal a blood glucose of 450 mg/dL and the presence of ketone bodies in the urine. Which of the following hormonal consequences best explains the accelerated gluconeogenesis and muscle wasting observed in this patient?
options: Absolute insulin deficiency allowing unopposed glucagon action.
Increased insulin levels promoting the synthesis of glucokinase.
Excess insulin causing increased uptake of amino acids into muscle.
Epinephrine deficiency preventing the mobilization of fatty acids.
Glucagon deficiency leading to inhibited hepatic glucose output.
correctOption: Absolute insulin deficiency allowing unopposed glucagon action.
optionExplanations: Correct. In Type 1 Diabetes, the lack of insulin means glucagon acts unopposed, leading to massive gluconeogenesis from muscle-derived amino acids and weight loss.
Insulin levels are absent or severely low in this scenario; therefore, the induction of glucokinase is impaired, contributing to hyperglycemia.
Insulin is an anabolic hormone; its presence promotes protein synthesis and amino acid uptake, which is the opposite of muscle wasting.
Epinephrine deficiency is not the primary driver here; rather, the lack of insulin prevents inhibition of hormone-sensitive lipase, increasing fatty acid mobilization.
Glucagon deficiency would result in hypoglycemia, not the hyperglycemia and ketoacidosis seen in this patient.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 122 (Book Page): Decreased levels of insulin favor mobilization of amino acids from muscle protein, and provide the carbon skeletons for gluconeogenesis... elevated levels of glucagon and low levels of insulin, such as occur during fasting... increase gluconeogenesis.

category: Enlist the components of complex I, II, III, and IV
statement: A researcher is isolating protein complexes from the inner mitochondrial membrane. They identify a complex that contains FAD as a prosthetic group and is capable of accepting electrons from succinate. Which structural components are characteristic of this specific assembly?
options: FMN and heme groups
Heme a and heme a3 with copper
FAD and copper centers
FAD and iron-sulfur centers
FMN and iron-sulfur centers
correctOption: FAD and iron-sulfur centers
optionExplanations: FMN is the characteristic flavin of Complex I, not Complex II. Heme groups are components of cytochromes found in Complexes III and IV.
Heme a, heme a3, and copper are the hallmark components of Complex IV, the final cytochrome in the respiratory chain, and are not found in the succinate-metabolizing Complex II.
While Complex II contains FAD, it does not contain copper centers; copper is restricted to the terminal cytochrome oxidase (Complex IV).

Complex II (succinate dehydrogenase) is uniquely identified among the complexes by its tightly bound FAD (flavin adenine dinucleotide) which accepts electrons from succinate, and its iron-sulfur centers which facilitate the transfer of those electrons to coenzyme Q.
This description refers to Complex I (NADH dehydrogenase), which utilizes FMN to accept electrons from NADH, whereas Complex II utilizes FAD.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 75 (Book Page): CoQ is a mobile carrier and can accept hydrogen atoms both from FMNH2, produced on NADH dehydrogenase (Complex I), and from FADH2, produced on succinate dehydrogenase (Complex II)... Note: Complexes II and III also contain iron-sulfur centers.

category: Define energy balance
statement: During the process of digestion and absorption of macronutrients, the body's heat production increases significantly above resting levels. Which physiological term best describes this mechanism?
options: Basal metabolic rate
Diet-induced thermogenesis
Resting metabolic rate
Physical activity expenditure
Energy density of food
correctOption: Diet-induced thermogenesis
optionExplanations: Basal metabolic rate (BMR) refers to the minimum calories needed for life-sustaining functions at rest, excluding the thermic effect of food.
The thermic effect of food, or diet-induced thermogenesis, is the specific increase in metabolic rate (heat production) that occurs as a direct result of processing nutrients.

Resting metabolic rate (RMR) represents energy expended in a postabsorptive state for normal body functions like respiration and blood flow, but is distinct from the active heat production during digestion.
Physical activity expenditure is the energy used for muscular work and varies based on the duration and intensity of exercise, not digestion.
Energy density refers to the amount of calories per gram of a specific macronutrient (e.g., 9 kcal/g for fat), which is a characteristic of the food itself, not a metabolic process.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 359 (Book Page): The production of heat by the body increases as much as 30% above the resting level during the digestion and absorption of food. This effect is called the thermic effect of food or diet-induced thermogenesis.

category: Enlist the components of complex I, II, III, and IV
statement: The respiratory chain involves several metal-containing proteins. Which specific structural component found in Complex IV allows it to facilitate the final, four-electron reduction of molecular oxygen to water?
options: Isoprenoid hydrophobic tail
Copper atoms
Heme group of Cytochrome b
Iron-sulfur (Fe4S4) clusters
Flavin mononucleotide (FMN)
correctOption: Copper atoms
optionExplanations: The isoprenoid tail is a structural feature of Coenzyme Q (Ubiquinone), not a protein complex component.
Copper atoms in the cytochrome a + a3 complex (Complex IV) are essential for the catalytic reduction of O2 to H2O.
Cytochrome b is part of Complex III, not Complex IV, and does not react with oxygen.
While Fe-S clusters are in I, II, and III, they are not the primary mechanism for the oxygen reduction site in Complex IV.
FMN is the prosthetic group for Complex I, not Complex IV.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 76 (Book Page): [Cytochrome oxidase contains copper atoms that are required for this complex reaction to occur.]

category: Suggest dietary advice for patients suffering from diabetes mellitus, hypertension, obesity, renal disease, lactose intolerance, gluten enteropathy, hypercholesterolemia, and hemorrhoids
coreConcept: Physiologic Benefits of Omega-3 Fatty Acids
statement: A patient is advised to increase consumption of fatty fish like salmon to reduce the risk of cardiovascular mortality. What is the primary physiological benefit of the ω-3 fatty acids found in fish oil compared to ω-6 fatty acids?
options: They suppress cardiac arrhythmias and reduce serum triacylglycerols.
They are more effective at lowering LDL cholesterol than ω-6 fatty acids.
They increase the rate of the HMG-CoA reductase reaction.
They inhibit the absorption of fat-soluble vitamins.
They are the only precursors for the synthesis of arachidonic acid.
correctOption: They suppress cardiac arrhythmias and reduce serum triacylglycerols.
optionExplanations: The unique benefits of fish-derived Omega-3s (EPA/DHA) are their anti-arrhythmic and triacylglycerol-lowering effects, which provide cardioprotection independent of LDL levels.
Omega-3 fatty acids actually have little effect on LDL or HDL cholesterol levels; Omega-6 fatty acids are more potent at lowering LDL.
Increasing the HMG-CoA reductase reaction would increase cholesterol synthesis, which is the opposite of the desired effect in cardiovascular health.
Omega-3 fatty acids do not inhibit the absorption of vitamins; they are lipids that actually facilitate the absorption of fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K).
Arachidonic acid is an Omega-6 fatty acid synthesized from linoleic acid, not from Omega-3 fatty acids.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 355 (Book Page): Dietary ω-3 polyunsaturated fats suppress cardiac arrhythmias, reduce serum triacylglycerols, decrease the tendency for thrombosis, lower blood pressure, and substantially reduce risk of cardiovascular mortality.

category: Clearly differentiate between substrate level phosphorylation and oxidative phosphorylation
statement: Which of the following describes a key metabolic loop where the product of a substrate-level phosphorylation reaction regulates the most important control point of oxidative phosphorylation?
options: ATP produced by pyruvate kinase allosterically inhibits phosphofructokinase-1.
Citrate inhibits phosphofructokinase-1 when the TCA cycle is saturated.
Pyruvate activates the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex in the matrix.
Glucose 6-phosphate inhibits hexokinase to prevent phosphate sequestration.
ADP levels rise to stimulate the rate of oxidative phosphorylation via respiratory control.
correctOption: ADP levels rise to stimulate the rate of oxidative phosphorylation via respiratory control.
optionExplanations: This is a regulatory loop within glycolysis, not a control point of oxidative phosphorylation, which is primarily regulated by the availability of ADP and the proton gradient.

Citrate is an intermediate of the TCA cycle, not a product of substrate-level phosphorylation, and its inhibition of PFK-1 coordinates glycolysis with mitochondrial activity but is not the primary regulator of OXPHOS.
Pyruvate is a substrate, not a product of substrate-level phosphorylation (it is the end product of the PK reaction), and its activation of PDH kinase is a separate regulatory mechanism.
This is a simple feedback inhibition in glycolysis to conserve ATP and phosphate; it does not directly regulate the mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation machinery.

Oxidative phosphorylation is governed by 'respiratory control,' where the rate of electron transport and ATP synthesis is tightly coupled to the availability of ADP. When ADP is high (signaling low ATP), OXPHOS increases.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 78 (Book Page): a. Oligomycin... This dependency of cellular respiration on the ability to phosphorylate ADP to ATP is known as respiratory control... [Note: Respiratory control also results from decreased availability of ADP or Pi.]

category: Enlist symptoms and signs
coreConcept: Classic Galactosemia vs. Galactokinase Deficiency Signs
statement: A newborn infant begins to vomit and develops jaundice shortly after the first few feedings of breast milk. Physical examination reveals bilateral lens opacities (cataracts). Urinalysis is positive for reducing sugars. Which enzymic deficiency is most likely to produce this constellation of clinical signs?
options: Galactokinase.
UDP-hexose 4-epimerase.
Galactose 1-phosphate uridyltransferase (GALT).
Aldose reductase.
Fructokinase.
correctOption: Galactose 1-phosphate uridyltransferase (GALT).
optionExplanations: Galactokinase deficiency also causes cataracts due to galactitol accumulation, but it does not typically cause the severe jaundice, vomiting, or liver damage seen in GALT deficiency.
While epimerase deficiency is possible, it is much rarer than GALT deficiency and 'Classic Galactosemia' is the standard diagnosis for this pediatric presentation.
Classic Galactosemia (GALT deficiency) presents with vomiting, jaundice, liver damage, and cataracts. The accumulation of galactose 1-phosphate is toxic to the liver and kidneys.
Aldose reductase is the enzyme that converts galactose to galactitol (causing cataracts); its deficiency would actually prevent cataracts in these patients, not cause the disease.
Fructokinase deficiency is a benign condition (Essential Fructosuria) and would not be triggered by breast milk (which contains lactose/galactose, not fructose).
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 133 (Book Page) / 531: Classic Galactosemia... Galactose 1-phosphate uridyltransferase (GALT) deficiency. ... Causes galactosemia and galactosuria, vomiting, diarrhea, and jaundice. Accumulation of galactose 1-phosphate and galactitol in nerve, lens, liver, and kidney tissue causes liver damage, severe mental retardation, and cataracts.

category: Explain how ethanol consumption causes hypoglycemia and fatty liver
statement: The 'fatty liver' observed in alcoholics is partly due to the increased synthesis of triacylglycerols. Which glycolytic intermediate is diverted toward lipid synthesis as a result of the high NADH/NAD+ ratio produced by ethanol metabolism?
options: Dihydroxyacetone phosphate
Phosphoenolpyruvate
3-Phosphoglycerate
Fructose 6-phosphate
2-Phosphoglycerate
correctOption: Dihydroxyacetone phosphate
optionExplanations: In the presence of high NADH, dihydroxyacetone phosphate (DHAP) is reduced to glycerol 3-phosphate by glycerol 3-phosphate dehydrogenase. Glycerol 3-phosphate then serves as the substrate for triacylglycerol synthesis.
Phosphoenolpyruvate is a precursor for pyruvate or OAA but is not the direct backbone for triacylglycerol synthesis.
3-Phosphoglycerate is a glycolytic intermediate but is not the primary branch point for the glycerol backbone of lipids.
Fructose 6-phosphate is further up the glycolytic pathway and is not directly converted to the glycerol backbone.
2-Phosphoglycerate is an intermediate near the end of glycolysis and is not involved in the fatty liver mechanism.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 93 (Book Page): DHAP must be isomerized to glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate for further metabolism... [Note: high NADH drives DHAP to glycerol 3-phosphate].

category: Describe the TCA cycle along with regulation & significance
statement: Which enzyme within the tricarboxylic acid cycle is considered the most important control point and catalyzes the primary rate-limiting oxidative decarboxylation?
options: Succinate thiokinase
Aconitase
Alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase
Fumarase
Isocitrate dehydrogenase
correctOption: Isocitrate dehydrogenase
optionExplanations: Succinate thiokinase catalyzes a reversible reaction (substrate-level phosphorylation) and is not a rate-limiting control point for the cycle.
Aconitase is an isomerase that is near equilibrium in the cell; it is not a control point or a rate-limiting step.
While alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase is a regulated, irreversible step, it is typically considered secondary to isocitrate dehydrogenase in terms of overall cycle pacing.
Fumarase catalyzes a freely reversible hydration of fumarate to malate and does not participate in the regulation or rate-limiting control of the cycle.

Isocitrate dehydrogenase is the primary rate-limiting enzyme. It is allosterically activated by ADP and Ca2+ and strongly inhibited by ATP and NADH, allowing it to sense the energy status of the cell.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 104 (Book Page): Isocitrate dehydrogenase catalyzes the irreversible oxidative decarboxylation of isocitrate... This is one of the rate-limiting steps of the TCA cycle.

category: Calculate the energy yield of TCA
statement: Within the structure of a mitochondrion, where are the majority of the enzymes responsible for the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle localized?
options: Mitochondrial matrix
Inner mitochondrial membrane
Outer mitochondrial membrane
Cytosolic side of the outer membrane
Intermembrane space
correctOption: Mitochondrial matrix
optionExplanations: The mitochondrial matrix is the gel-like interior that contains the soluble enzymes for the TCA cycle, fatty acid oxidation, and the PDH complex.
The inner mitochondrial membrane houses the electron transport chain (Complexes I-IV) and ATP synthase (Complex V), but only succinate dehydrogenase of the TCA cycle.
The outer mitochondrial membrane is highly permeable and contains pores; it does not house the metabolic enzymes for the TCA cycle.
The cytosolic side of the outer membrane is the site of various other metabolic reactions, such as the initial steps of fatty acid activation, but not the TCA cycle.
The intermembrane space has a milieu similar to the cytosol; it contains cytochrome c during electron transport but not the TCA enzymes.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 74 (Book Page): Matrix of the mitochondrion: ... These molecules include the enzymes responsible for the oxidation of pyruvate, amino acids, fatty acids (by (beta)-oxidation), and those of the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle.

category: Calculate the energy yield of TCA
statement: A neonate is diagnosed with Fumarase deficiency, an autosomal recessive disorder. If the TCA cycle proceeds normally from acetyl CoA until it reaches the block at fumarate, what is the net ATP yield produced per molecule of acetyl CoA?
options: 11 ATP
7 ATP
3 ATP
6 ATP
9 ATP
correctOption: 9 ATP
optionExplanations: Eleven ATP would be the yield if the cycle reached malate but could not complete the final oxidation to oxaloacetate.
Seven ATP represents the two NADH (6) plus the GTP (1), but omits the FADH2 produced at the succinate to fumarate step.
Three ATP is the yield of only the first NADH produced by isocitrate dehydrogenase.
Six ATP represents the energy from the first two NADH molecules (at isocitrate and alpha-ketoglutarate steps).

Correct. From acetyl CoA to fumarate, the cycle produces: 1 NADH (3 ATP) at isocitrate DH, 1 NADH (3 ATP) at alpha-KG DH, 1 GTP (1 ATP) at succinate thiokinase, and 1 FADH2 (2 ATP) at succinate DH. Total = 3 + 3 + 1 + 2 = 9 ATP.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 114 (Book Page): Figure 9.8: Acetyl CoA -> Citrate -> Isocitrate -> (alpha)-Ketoglutarate -> Succinyl CoA -> Succinate -> Fumarate. (Calculation of NADH, NADH, GTP, FADH2).

category: Suggest a simple method for estimation of caloric requirements of sedentary adults, moderately active adults, and very active adults
statement: A 75-kg male patient is hospitalized for an elective procedure. In his pre-admission history, he describes his lifestyle as 'very active' due to his work in a logging camp. Post-surgery, while confined to a hospital bed during recovery (sedentary state), what change in his daily caloric intake is necessary to maintain his current body weight, assuming his weight remains stable at 75 kg?
options: Increase intake by 375 kcal/day to support wound healing.
Maintain intake at 3,000 kcal/day as metabolic rate is fixed.
Decrease intake by 750 kcal/day to match his new sedentary state.
Decrease intake by 375 kcal/day to transition to a moderate activity level.
Limit intake to 1,500 kcal/day to prevent post-surgical obesity.
correctOption: Decrease intake by 750 kcal/day to match his new sedentary state.
optionExplanations: While healing requires energy, his overall activity has plummeted; increasing intake based on a sedentary state would cause weight gain.
The resting metabolic rate is only part of the total expenditure; physical activity provides the greatest variation, so intake must be adjusted.
As a very active adult, he required 75 kg * 40 kcal/kg = 3,000 kcal. In his sedentary hospital state, he requires 75 kg * 30 kcal/kg = 2,250 kcal. The necessary decrease is 750 kcal.
A decrease of 375 kcal (75 * 5) only moves him from very active (40) to moderately active (35), but he is now sedentary (30).
1,500 kcal/day represents 20 kcal/kg, which is below the maintenance level for a sedentary adult (30 kcal/kg).
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 358 (Book Page): sedentary adults require about 30 kcal/kg/day... very active adults require 40 kcal/kg/day.

category: Enlist the components of complex I, II, III, and IV
statement: Complex I and Complex II are distinct entry points into the electron transport chain. However, they both utilize which of the following shared structural components to facilitate the movement of electrons toward Coenzyme Q?
options: Cytochrome c
Iron-sulfur (Fe-S) centers
Flavin mononucleotide (FMN)
Copper atoms
Heme a + a3
correctOption: Iron-sulfur (Fe-S) centers
optionExplanations: Cytochrome c is a mobile carrier that operates only between Complexes III and IV; it is not a structural component of Complex I or II.
Iron-sulfur centers are common to Complexes I, II, and III, acting as the internal wires that relay electrons through the protein complexes.
FMN is specific to Complex I and is not found in Complex II or Complex III.
Copper atoms are unique to Complex IV and are not structural components of the electron entry complexes (I and II).
Heme a + a3 is specific to the terminal complex (Complex IV) and is not involved in the initial electron entry steps.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 75 (Book Page): [NADH dehydrogenase also contains iron atoms paired with sulfur atoms to make iron–sulfur centers (Figure 6.9). ... Note: Complexes II and III also contain iron-sulfur centers.]

category: Delineate special nutritional requirements during pregnancy, lactation, growth, and old age
statement: An 82-year-old man living alone presents with extreme muscle wasting, anemia, and weakness. He has lost 15% of his body weight over the last 4 months. He does not have edema. What is the most likely nutritional diagnosis based on the clinical presentation of calorie-predominant deprivation?
options: Marasmus
Essential Fructosuria
Kwashiorkor
Scurvy
Hereditary Fructose Intolerance
correctOption: Marasmus
optionExplanations: Marasmus represents a chronic deficiency of total calories. The body uses its own muscle and fat stores for energy, leading to emaciation (muscle wasting) without the edema seen in protein-specific deficiency.
Essential Fructosuria is a benign, asymptomatic genetic deficiency of fructokinase and has no relationship to muscle wasting or calorie deprivation.
Kwashiorkor is characterized by protein deficiency with relatively preserved calories, resulting in edema and decreased plasma proteins, which are absent here.
Scurvy is a vitamin C deficiency resulting in collagen defects and bleeding gums; while it can occur in the elderly, it does not explain the generalized emaciation described.
Hereditary Fructose Intolerance is a genetic defect in aldolase B that presents in infancy upon weaning; it is not a diagnosis for a weight-losing 82-year-old.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 369 (Book Page): [Marasmus occurs when calorie deprivation is relatively greater than the reduction in protein... typical symptoms include arrested growth, extreme muscle wasting (emaciation), weakness, and anemia. Victims of marasmus do not show the edema...]

category: Delineate the reactions involved in synthesis of glucose from various gluconeogenic substrates
statement: A researcher is studying the utilization of glycerol as a gluconeogenic substrate. They observe that while the liver efficiently converts glycerol to dihydroxyacetone phosphate, adipocytes do not. What is the biochemical basis for this observation?
options: Adipocytes lack the glycerol phosphate dehydrogenase required to oxidize glycerol 3-phosphate.
Adipocytes preferentially shunt all available glycerol into the pentose phosphate pathway.
Adipocytes cannot transport glycerol across the cell membrane against a concentration gradient.
Adipocytes lack the mitochondrial transporters required to move glycerol into the matrix.
Adipocytes essentially lack glycerol kinase, preventing the initial phosphorylation of glycerol.
correctOption: Adipocytes essentially lack glycerol kinase, preventing the initial phosphorylation of glycerol.
optionExplanations: Glycerol phosphate dehydrogenase is present; the blockade occurs at the very first step of glycerol utilization.
Glycerol must be phosphorylated to glycerol-3-phosphate before it can be converted to DHAP; it does not enter the pentose phosphate pathway directly.
Glycerol transport is not the limiting factor; the inability to trap glycerol by phosphorylation is the issue.
Glycerol metabolism occurs in the cytosol (phosphorylation) and mitochondria (oxidation), but the primary deficiency is the cytosolic kinase.

Glycerol kinase is required to convert glycerol to glycerol 3-phosphate. Because adipocytes lack this enzyme, they cannot reuse the glycerol released during lipolysis for gluconeogenesis or triacylglycerol resynthesis.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 109 (Book Page): [Glycerol is phosphorylated by glycerol kinase to glycerol phosphate... [Note: Adipocytes cannot phosphorylate glycerol because they essentially lack glycerol kinase.]]

category: Describe the TCA cycle along with regulation & significance
coreConcept: ATP Yield of the TCA Cycle
statement: What is the total yield of adenosine triphosphate (ATP) produced from the complete mitochondrial oxidation of one molecule of acetyl CoA through the TCA cycle and oxidative phosphorylation?
options: 9 ATP
3 ATP
38 ATP
15 ATP
12 ATP
correctOption: 12 ATP
optionExplanations: 9 ATP is the total yield from the three NADH molecules produced in the cycle, but it neglects the contributions of FADH2 and GTP.
3 ATP is the yield from the oxidation of a single NADH molecule in the electron transport chain, not the entire acetyl CoA molecule.
38 ATP (or 36) is the theoretical yield for the complete oxidation of one molecule of glucose, not a single acetyl CoA.
15 ATP is the total yield from one molecule of pyruvate, as it includes the additional NADH produced during the pyruvate dehydrogenase step.
One acetyl CoA generates 3 NADH (9 ATP), 1 FADH2 (2 ATP), and 1 GTP (1 ATP), totaling 12 ATP via oxidative and substrate-level phosphorylation.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 105 (Book Page): The total yield of ATP from the oxidation of one acetyl CoA is shown in Figure 9.7. ... 3 NADH -> 9; FADH2 -> 2; GTP -> 1; Total 12 ATP/acetyl CoA oxidized.

category: Elaborate key features of various transport systems for entry of glucose into cells
statement: In the liver, the regulation of glucose entry and retention is managed by a specific interaction where glucokinase is sequestered in the nucleus by a regulatory protein (GKRP). This sequestration is triggered by:
options: Accumulation of glucose 6-phosphate
Elevated intracellular levels of glucose
High concentrations of fructose 6-phosphate
Increased binding of insulin to its receptor
The presence of fructose 1-phosphate
correctOption: High concentrations of fructose 6-phosphate
optionExplanations: Glucokinase is not directly inhibited by its product, glucose 6-phosphate, unlike hexokinase; it is indirectly regulated via F6P and GKRP.
Increased glucose levels actually trigger the release of glucokinase from the nucleus into the cytosol to promote phosphorylation.
Fructose 6-phosphate, which is in equilibrium with glucose 6-phosphate, signals that further glucose trapping is unnecessary and triggers nuclear sequestration by GKRP.
Insulin promotes the synthesis of glucokinase (long-term) but the acute nuclear translocation is regulated by metabolite levels like F6P and glucose.
Fructose 1-phosphate actually inhibits the formation of the glucokinase-GKRP complex, thereby promoting glucokinase activity.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 91 (Book Page): In the presence of fructose 6-phosphate, glucokinase is translocated into the nucleus and binds tightly to the regulatory protein, thus rendering the enzyme inactive.

category: Delineate special nutritional requirements during pregnancy, lactation, growth, and old age
statement: An elite athlete's diet is being reviewed to ensure it meets the Acceptable Macronutrient Distribution Ranges (AMDR). According to standard nutritional guidelines for healthy adults, what is the established range for protein intake as a percentage of total calories?
options: Over 70%
optionExplanations: The AMDR for protein in adults is set at 10–35% of total caloric intake to ensure adequate essential amino acid supply while reducing chronic disease risk.
5–10% is the specific AMDR for omega-6 polyunsaturated fatty acids, not total protein.
20–35% is the AMDR for total dietary fat in adults.
Intakes over 70% for protein are well beyond the AMDR and can lead to excessive urinary nitrogen and calcium loss.
45–65% is the AMDR for total carbohydrates in adults.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 352 (Book Page): The AMDR for adults is 45–65% of their total calories from carbohydrates, 20–35% from fat, and 10–35% from protein (Figure 27.7).

category: Define energy balance
statement: A researcher is studying the components of energy expenditure. Which physiological process is primarily responsible for the 50–70% of daily energy use in a sedentary individual?
options: The synthesis of ketone bodies and gluconeogenesis during the post-prandial phase.
The metabolic cost associated with the digestion and absorption of macronutrients.
The energy required for ion transport and maintenance of cellular integrity at rest.
The adaptive thermogenesis triggered by cold exposure in brown adipose tissue.
The mechanical work performed during muscular contraction in light physical activity.
correctOption: The energy required for ion transport and maintenance of cellular integrity at rest.
optionExplanations: While these are metabolic processes, they do not constitute the bulk of the 50-70% of energy spent on basic survival functions at rest.
This is the thermic effect of food (TEF), which accounts for only 5-10% of total energy expenditure.
The Resting Metabolic Rate (RMR) accounts for 50-70% of expenditure and covers fundamental processes like ion pumping (Na+/K+ ATPase) and maintaining cell structure.
Nonshivering thermogenesis via UCP1 is a minor contributor to total energy balance in adults compared to RMR.
In sedentary individuals, physical activity accounts for only about 30% of expenditure, making it secondary to RMR.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 359 (Book Page): It represents the energy required to carry out the normal body functions, such as respiration, blood flow, ion transport, and maintenance of cellular integrity. In an adult, the RMR is about 1,800 kcal for men (70 kg) and 1,300 kcal for women (50 kg). From 50–70% of the daily energy expenditure in sedentary individuals is attributable to the RMR.

category: Explain hemolytic anemia in subjects suffering from G6PD deficiency
coreConcept: Oxidant Drug Triggers in G6PD Deficiency
statement: Which of the following 'AAA' drugs is correctly matched with its specific contraindication in G6PD deficiency as per the oxidant stress mnemonic?
options: Quinine - Antimalarial
Penicillin - Antibiotic
Acetaminophen - Antipyretic
Sulfamethoxazole - Antibiotic
Aspirin (low dose) - Antipyretic
correctOption: Sulfamethoxazole - Antibiotic
optionExplanations: The text notes that primaquine is an antimalarial trigger, but quinine is not.
Penicillin is not typically associated with the oxidant stress that triggers G6PD-related hemolytic anemia.
The text explicitly states that acetaminophen is an antipyretic but is NOT among the oxidant drugs that typically trigger G6PD hemolysis.
Sulfamethoxazole is a sulfa-based antibiotic and is a classic example of the 'Antibiotic' category in the AAA mnemonic that precipitates hemolysis.

While high doses of aspirin might be problematic, the text specifies acetanilid as the classic antipyretic trigger, noting acetaminophen is not a trigger; it does not list low-dose aspirin as the primary example.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 145 (Book Page): Commonly used drugs that produce hemolytic anemia in patients with G6PD deficiency are best remembered from the mnemonic AAA—Antibiotics (for example, sulfamethoxazole and chloramphenicol), Antimalarials (for example, primaquine but not quinine), and Antipyretics (for example, acetanilid but not acetaminophen).

category: chemiosmotic hypothesis)
statement: A 24-year-old female is brought to the emergency department after ingesting a large quantity of aspirin. She presents with a temperature of 103°F, tachypnea, and profuse sweating. Laboratory analysis reveals a significant decrease in the ATP/ADP ratio in her muscle cells despite a high rate of oxygen consumption. Which of the following best explains the cellular mechanism for her elevated body temperature?
options: Blockage of the F1 domain of ATP synthase prevents the dissipation of the mitochondrial pH gradient.
Increased permeability of the inner mitochondrial membrane to protons allows energy to be released as heat.
Inhibition of the electron transport chain at Complex IV leads to the accumulation of reactive oxygen species.
A defect in the glycerophosphate shuttle prevents the transport of reducing equivalents into the matrix.
Overstimulation of the cytochrome P450 monooxygenase system in the liver increases metabolic heat.
correctOption: Increased permeability of the inner mitochondrial membrane to protons allows energy to be released as heat.
optionExplanations: Blocking the F1 domain (like Oligomycin) would stop electron transport and decrease oxygen consumption; this patient has high oxygen consumption.

High doses of salicylates act as uncouplers, increasing the proton permeability of the inner mitochondrial membrane. The respiratory chain runs rapidly to try to build the gradient, but the energy is lost as heat instead of ATP.
Inhibition at Complex IV would stop oxygen consumption and electron flow, which is the opposite of what occurs in uncoupling.
Shuttle defects would slow down the supply of electrons to the ETC, potentially slowing metabolism, but would not explain the rapid oxygen use and heat production seen in uncoupling.
While P450 systems use NADPH and oxygen, the massive heat production in salicylate poisoning is primarily due to the global uncoupling of mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 79 (Book Page): [In high doses, aspirin and other salicylates uncouple oxidative phosphorylation. This explains the fever that accompanies toxic overdoses of these drugs.]

category: Compare the energy content of macro nutrients and alcohol
statement: During the digestion and absorption of a meal, the body's heat production increases significantly. What is the typical percentage of total daily energy expenditure attributed to this 'thermic effect of food'?
optionExplanations: This is too low; 1-2% is roughly the percentage of weight that liver glycogen contributes to muscle weight, not a thermic energy value.
This range (20-35%) is the AMDR for fat intake, not the thermic effect of food.
Correct. The thermic effect of food (diet-induced thermogenesis) accounts for approximately 5-10% of the daily energy budget.
No single energy-requiring process (other than perhaps extreme physical activity in elite athletes) consumes 100% of daily calories.
This range (50-70%) is the portion of energy expenditure attributed to the resting metabolic rate (RMR) in sedentary individuals.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 359 (Book Page): Over a 24–hour period, the thermic response to food intake may amount to 5–10% of the total energy expenditure.

category: Describe the TCA cycle along with regulation & significance
statement: A 1-month-old male infant is brought to the pediatric clinic with signs of severe neurodegeneration, muscle spasticity, and developmental delay. Laboratory results confirm a congenital lactic acidosis. An X-linked dominant mutation in the E1 component of a specific complex is suspected. If this enzyme is deficient, which of the following is the most likely metabolic consequence?
options: Reduced availability of thiamine pyrophosphate
Overproduction of oxaloacetate from pyruvate
Impaired conversion of citrate to isocitrate
Inability to oxidize succinate to fumarate
Failure to convert pyruvate to acetyl CoA
correctOption: Failure to convert pyruvate to acetyl CoA
optionExplanations: While E1 requires TPP, the clinical case describes a genetic enzyme deficiency (structural mutation) rather than a simple nutritional vitamin deficiency like Beriberi.
Oxaloacetate is produced from pyruvate by pyruvate carboxylase; in PDH deficiency, pyruvate is shunted to lactate, not preferentially to oxaloacetate.
Impaired citrate-to-isocitrate conversion would suggest aconitase deficiency, which is not the standard cause of X-linked congenital lactic acidosis.
Failure to oxidize succinate would implicate succinate dehydrogenase (Complex II), leading to different mitochondrial pathologies.
Deficiency in the E1 (decarboxylase) component of the PDH complex prevents the entry of glycolytic pyruvate into the TCA cycle as acetyl CoA, forcing its reduction to lactate and causing acidosis.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 103 (Book Page): A deficiency in the E1 component of the PDH complex... results in an inability to convert pyruvate to acetyl CoA, causing pyruvate to be shunted to lactic acid via lactate dehydrogenase. This causes particular problems for the brain.

category: Elaborate key features of various transport systems for entry of glucose into cells
statement: Glucose transporters (GLUT proteins) share a common structural feature essential for their function within the phospholipid bilayer. How many transmembrane helices are typically found in these proteins?
options: Ten helices
Fourteen helices
Two helices
Twelve helices
Seven helices
correctOption: Twelve helices
optionExplanations: Ten helices is incorrect; the established structural model for the GLUT family requires more spanning regions.
Fourteen helices is higher than the identified count of 12 transmembrane segments in the GLUT protein family.
Two helices would be insufficient to form the complex tertiary structure of a glucose transporter pore.
The standard structural model for GLUT isoforms involves 12 alpha-helices spanning the cell membrane.
Seven transmembrane helices are a classic feature of G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs), not the GLUT family.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 97 (Book Page): [Note: GLUT proteins contain 12 transmembrane helices.]

category: Define body mass index (BMI)
coreConcept: Thermic Effect of Food and Total Energy Expenditure
statement: When assessing a patient with a Body Mass Index (BMI) in the 'obese' range, the physician must consider the 'thermic effect of food'. How does this metabolic component interact with a high BMI and total energy expenditure?
options: It is only present in individuals with a BMI below 25, as obese individuals have a 'blunted' response.
A high BMI causes the thermic effect of food to become negative, leading to more fat storage.
It accounts for about 5-10% of total energy expenditure, representing the energy used for digestion and absorption.
It represents 50-70% of total energy expenditure, thus dominating the BMI's role in weight maintenance.
The thermic effect of food increases proportionately with BMI, making weight loss easier for the obese.
correctOption: It accounts for about 5-10% of total energy expenditure, representing the energy used for digestion and absorption.
optionExplanations: The thermic effect of food occurs in all individuals following nutrient ingestion; it is not absent in obese individuals.
The thermic effect of food is always an energy-expending process (heat production); it cannot be 'negative' in the context of physiological thermodynamics.
The thermic effect of food is the energy cost of processing nutrients; at 5-10% of TEE, it is a constant factor in the energy balance equation regardless of BMI.
The Resting Metabolic Rate (RMR), not the thermic effect of food, represents 50-70% of the daily energy expenditure in sedentary individuals.
The thermic effect of food is related to the caloric content of the meal and the efficiency of digestion, not necessarily a direct positive correlation with BMI.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 351 (Book Page): [Thermic effect of food: Over a 24–hour period, the thermic response to food intake may amount to 5–10% of the total energy expenditure.]

category: Define energy balance
statement: During a biochemical experiment, a system moves from an organized state to one of increased disorder. Which thermodynamic parameter describes this change, and what is its role in predicting spontaneity?
options: Enthalpy (∆H); it measures the change in randomness of the reactants.
Entropy (∆S); a high ∆S always ensures that a reaction will be spontaneous.
Entropy (∆S); it measures randomness but does not predict spontaneity in isolation.
Free Energy (G); it measures randomness and predicts the speed of the reaction.
Enthalpy (∆H); it is the sole predictor of whether a reaction is favorable.
correctOption: Entropy (∆S); it measures randomness but does not predict spontaneity in isolation.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. Enthalpy measures heat change, not randomness.
Incorrect. Spontaneity also depends on the change in enthalpy (∆H). If ∆H is very large and positive, it could outweigh a high ∆S.
Correct. Entropy is the measure of randomness or disorder (∆S). While it is a component of the free energy equation, it cannot predict spontaneity on its own without enthalpy and temperature.
Incorrect. Free energy (G) predicts spontaneity, but it is not a measure of randomness itself (that is S), nor does it predict kinetics (speed).
