citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 91 (Book Page): Elevated levels of citrate, an intermediate in the TCA cycle (see Page 101 (Book Page)), also inhibit PFK-1. [Note: Citrate inhibition favors the use of glucose for glycogen synthesis, see Page 117 (Book Page).]

category: Enlist the components of complex I, II, III, and IV
statement: In the electron transport chain, iron-sulfur (Fe-S) centers are essential for the transfer of hydrogen atoms or electrons between carriers. According to the structural organization of the chain, which complexes contain these Fe-S centers as part of their protein framework?
options: Complexes II, III, and IV
All five complexes (I through V)
Complexes I, II, and III
Only Complex I and Complex III
Only Complex I and Complex II
correctOption: Complexes I, II, and III
optionExplanations: Complex IV contains cytochromes a and a3 and copper atoms, but is not described as containing iron-sulfur centers in the referenced text.
Complex V (ATP synthase) is not involved in the redox transfer of electrons and does not contain iron-sulfur centers.
Iron-sulfur centers are prosthetic groups integrated into the protein structures of Complexes I, II, and III to facilitate electron flow.
Complex II is omitted; it contains Fe-S centers necessary for transferring electrons from FADH2 to Coenzyme Q.
While Complexes I and II contain Fe-S centers, Complex III also possesses them, making this choice incomplete.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 75 (Book Page): [NADH dehydrogenase also contains iron atoms paired with sulfur atoms to make iron–sulfur centers (Figure 6.9). . . [Note: Complexes II and III also contain iron-sulfur centers.]]

category: Calculate the energy yield of TCA
statement: Assuming the standard free energy required for the phosphorylation of ADP to ATP is +7.3 kcal/mol, calculate the total caloric energy captured in the form of ATP from the complete mitochondrial oxidation of one molecule of Acetyl CoA.
options: 109.5 kcal/mol
52.58 kcal/mol
21.9 kcal/mol
73.0 kcal/mol
87.6 kcal/mol
correctOption: 87.6 kcal/mol
optionExplanations: 109.5 kcal/mol (15 x 7.3) is the energy captured from one molecule of Pyruvate, not Acetyl CoA.
52.58 kcal/mol is the total free energy released by the transport of a pair of electrons from NADH to oxygen, but not all of this is captured as ATP.
21.9 kcal/mol (3 x 7.3) is the energy captured from a single molecule of NADH.
73.0 kcal/mol (10 x 7.3) is an incorrect total yield calculation.
The total ATP yield for one Acetyl CoA is 12 ATP. Multiplying 12 ATP by the energy captured per ATP (7.3 kcal/mol) gives a total of 87.6 kcal/mol of energy conserved.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 77 (Book Page): The standard free energy for the phosphorylation of ADP to ATP is +7.3 kcal/mol. ... [Page 105 (Book Page)] The total yield of ATP from the oxidation of one acetyl CoA is... 12 ATP.

category: Compare key features of aerobic and anaerobic glycolysis
statement: Which mechanistic step describes the reoxidation of NADH in anaerobic glycolysis as compared to the aerobic pathway?
options: NADH is reoxidized by the glycerol 3-phosphate shuttle yielding 2 ATP molecules.
NADH is reoxidized via the malate-aspartate shuttle in the inner mitochondrial membrane.
NADH is oxidized by glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate dehydrogenase to produce 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate.
NADH is oxidized by the electron transport chain to produce 3 ATP per molecule.
NADH is oxidized to NAD+ during the reduction of pyruvate to lactate by lactate dehydrogenase.
correctOption: NADH is oxidized to NAD+ during the reduction of pyruvate to lactate by lactate dehydrogenase.
optionExplanations: The glycerol 3-phosphate shuttle is an aerobic mechanism for reoxidizing cytosolic NADH by transferring electrons to mitochondrial FAD.
The malate-aspartate shuttle is a mechanism used in aerobic metabolism to transport reducing equivalents into the mitochondria.
Glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate dehydrogenase reduces NAD+ to NADH; it does not reoxidize NADH.
This describes the aerobic process where NADH enters the respiratory chain, which is impossible in anaerobic conditions due to lack of oxygen.
In anaerobic glycolysis, the NADH formed during the oxidation of glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate must be reoxidized to NAD+ by reducing pyruvate to lactate to allow glycolysis to continue.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 88 (Book Page): Alternatively, pyruvate is reduced to lactate as NADH is oxidized to NAD+. This conversion of glucose to lactate is called anaerobic glycolysis because it can occur without the participation of oxygen.

category: Enlist inherited and acquired causes of lactic acidosis and give biochemical explanation for lactic acidosis in each condition
statement: Which of the following describes the primary biochemical fate of pyruvate in human mature erythrocytes, and why does this lead to the baseline production of lactate?
options: Carboxylation to oxaloacetate to replenish the tricarboxylic acid cycle.
Reduction to lactate to regenerate NAD+ for continued glycolysis.
Oxidative decarboxylation to acetyl CoA due to high mitochondrial density.
Decarboxylation to acetaldehyde as a precursor for ethanol synthesis.
Transamination to alanine to transport nitrogen to the liver.
correctOption: Reduction to lactate to regenerate NAD+ for continued glycolysis.
optionExplanations: Carboxylation to oxaloacetate requires mitochondria and the enzyme pyruvate carboxylase, neither of which are functional in mature red blood cells.

Because red blood cells lack mitochondria, they cannot reoxidize NADH via the electron transport chain. They must reduce pyruvate to lactate using lactate dehydrogenase to regenerate the NAD+ required for the glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate dehydrogenase step of glycolysis.
Mature erythrocytes lack mitochondria and therefore cannot perform oxidative decarboxylation of pyruvate via the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex.
Decarboxylation of pyruvate to acetaldehyde and subsequently ethanol occurs in yeast and some microorganisms, but the enzyme pyruvate decarboxylase is not present in humans.
Transamination to alanine occurs primarily in skeletal muscle via the glucose-alanine cycle, not as the primary fate in erythrocytes.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 95 (Book Page): Lactate, formed by the action of lactate dehydrogenase, is the final product of anaerobic glycolysis in eukaryotic cells... The formation of lactate is the major fate for pyruvate in... red blood cells, because these... lack mitochondria.

category: Outline the reactions involved in ethanol metabolism
statement: While ethanol is primarily oxidized by alcohol dehydrogenase in the liver, microorganisms utilize a different metabolic sequence to produce ethanol. In these organisms, which reaction immediately follows the decarboxylation of pyruvate?
options: Oxidation of acetaldehyde to acetate using NAD+.
Reduction of pyruvate directly to ethanol in a single step.
Condensation of acetaldehyde with Acetyl CoA.
Phosphorylation of acetaldehyde to form phosphoethanolamine.
Reduction of acetaldehyde to ethanol using NADH.
correctOption: Reduction of acetaldehyde to ethanol using NADH.
optionExplanations: This is the reverse of the pathway. In microorganisms producing ethanol, acetaldehyde is reduced, not oxidized.
The conversion is a two-step process: first decarboxylation to acetaldehyde, then reduction to ethanol, as shown in the metabolic fate summary..
There is no such condensation step in the outlined reactions of ethanol synthesis in the provided text.
The text does not mention any phosphorylation of acetaldehyde in the context of ethanol metabolism.

In the microbial pathway, pyruvate is first decarboxylated to acetaldehyde. Subsequently, acetaldehyde is reduced to ethanol by the enzyme alcohol dehydrogenase. This step is crucial for the regeneration of NAD+ from NADH, allowing glycolysis to continue in anaerobic conditions.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 106 (Book Page): reduced by microorganisms to ethanol by pyruvate decarboxylase... (Figure 8.24) Pyruvate -> Acetaldehyde -> Ethanol (NADH + H+ -> NAD+).

category: Elaborate the role of genetic, environmental, and behavioral factors in determining body weight
coreConcept: Environmental and Behavioral Triggers of Marasmus vs Kwashiorkor
statement: A 10-month-old infant in a famine-stricken region presents with extreme muscle wasting, anemia, and weakness, but lacks edema or fatty liver changes. What behavioral or environmental trigger most distinguishes this condition from Kwashiorkor?
options: A positive nitrogen balance caused by the ingestion of native cereal gruels.
The weaning of the child after one year of age onto a predominantly carbohydrate diet.
Inadequate intake of total calories starting within the first year of life.
A diet consisting predominantly of high-quality animal proteins after weaning.
The over-consumption of fiber leading to interference with nitrogen balance.
correctOption: Inadequate intake of total calories starting within the first year of life.
optionExplanations: Both conditions involve a negative nitrogen balance. Gruels are deficient in calories/protein, not promoters of nitrogen balance.
This describes Kwashiorkor, which typically occurs after weaning at about one year of age when the diet is high in carbs but low in protein.
Correct. Marasmus is characterized by total calorie deprivation starting <1 year of age, often due to inadequate breast milk supplementation, and lacks the edema seen in protein-specific deprivation.
Animal proteins would prevent PEM; both marasmus and kwashiorkor involve deprivation.
Fiber does not cause the extreme wasting seen in marasmus; it is a lack of energy (calories) that drives the pathology.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 361 (Book Page): Marasmus... usually occurs in children younger than 1 year of age when breast milk is supplemented with watery gruels of native cereals that are usually deficient in protein and calories.

category: Delineate special nutritional requirements during pregnancy, lactation, growth, and old age
coreConcept: Metabolic Impact of Trans Fatty Acids
statement: A dietary researcher is comparing the metabolic effects of different lipids. They observe that a specific type of fatty acid, produced during the partial hydrogenation of vegetable oils, behaves more like saturated fats by elevating serum LDL cholesterol and increasing the risk of coronary heart disease. Which of the following describes these fatty acids?
options: Short-chain fatty acids produced by the fermentation of soluble fiber.
Monounsaturated fatty acids with a cis-configured double bond.
ω-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids found in cold-water fish.
Trans fatty acids found in commercial baked goods and margarines.
Essential fatty acids like linoleic acid and α-linolenic acid.
correctOption: Trans fatty acids found in commercial baked goods and margarines.
optionExplanations: Short-chain fatty acids (like butyrate) are beneficial for colonic health and do not share the pathogenic properties of trans-unsaturated or saturated fatty acids.
Cis-monounsaturated fatty acids (like oleic acid in olive oil) are associated with lowering LDL and maintaining/raising HDL, reducing CHD risk.
ω-3 fatty acids are generally cardioprotective and reduce triacylglycerols, which is the opposite of the effect described.
Trans fats are artificial isomers that increase LDL and decrease HDL, significantly raising the risk of coronary heart disease, more so than most natural fats.
Essential fatty acids (ω-6 and ω-3) are required for health and generally help improve lipid profiles compared to saturated or trans fats.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 355 (Book Page)-364: Trans fatty acids... behave more like saturated fatty acids in the body, that is, they elevate serum LDL (but not HDL), and they increase the risk of CHD... Trans fatty acids are formed during the hydrogenation of liquid vegetable oils.

category: Illustrate the reactions of glycogenesis, glycogenolysis along with their regulation and significance
statement: During the process of glycogenolysis, glycogen phosphorylase stops its sequential cleavage of glycosidic bonds when it reaches a specific structure. How many glucosyl units remain on the chain before the branch point at this 'limit dextrin' stage?
options: One
Four
Two
Eight to ten
Three
correctOption: Four
optionExplanations: One residue remains only after the 4:4 transferase activity of the debranching enzyme has moved the other three residues.
Glycogen phosphorylase is sterically hindered by branch points and ceases activity when precisely four glucosyl residues remain on a branch. This structure is termed a 'limit dextrin'.
Two residues is not a recognized milestone in the glycogenolysis cleavage pathway.
Eight to ten is the average distance between branch points, but not the distance at which the enzyme stops.
Three residues are moved by the transferase activity, but the phosphorylase itself stops when four remain.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 120 (Book Page): Glycogen phosphorylase sequentially cleaves the α (1 → 4) glycosidic bonds... until four glucosyl units remain on each chain before a branch point. The resulting structure is called a limit dextrin, and phosphorylase cannot degrade it any further.

category: Outline treatment strategies
statement: A patient with Sucrase-Isomaltase complex deficiency suffers from abdominal cramps and flatulence after eating desserts. What is the current established pharmacological and dietary management for this genetic disorder?
options: Total parenteral nutrition to bypass the intestinal mucosal lining.
High-fructose diet to bypass the need for sucrose cleavage.
Oral administration of glucose-6-phosphatase before meals.
Dietary restriction of sucrose and enzyme replacement therapy.
Administration of alpha-amylase inhibitors to prevent dextrin formation.
correctOption: Dietary restriction of sucrose and enzyme replacement therapy.
optionExplanations: Total parenteral nutrition is an extreme measure reserved for severe intestinal failure; Sucrase-isomaltase deficiency is manageable with dietary control.
A high-fructose diet might avoid sucrose, but fructose itself is not the missing enzyme's substrate; the focus is on removing the complex sugar that cannot be broken down.
Glucose-6-phosphatase is a hepatic/renal enzyme involved in gluconeogenesis, not a digestive enzyme for dietary disaccharides.
Restricting sucrose reduces the osmotic load in the colon, while enzyme replacement (like sacrosidase) helps hydrolyze sucrose into glucose and fructose for absorption.
Amylase inhibitors would affect starch digestion (alpha-1,4 bonds) but would not help with the specific inability to cleave sucrose or isomaltose.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 88 (Book Page): Treatment includes the dietary restriction of sucrose, and enzyme replacement therapy.

category: Compare the energy content of macro nutrients and alcohol
statement: Two children in a famine-stricken area present with different forms of protein-energy malnutrition. Child A is 9 months old, severely emaciated with muscle wasting but no edema. Child B is 2 years old, recently weaned onto a starch-heavy diet, and presents with a swollen abdomen and depigmented hair. How do their energy deficits contrast?
options: Child A has relatively greater calorie deprivation; Child B has relatively greater protein deprivation.
Child A has a primary protein deficit; Child B has a primary carbohydrate deficit.
Both children have identical calorie-to-protein deficit ratios.
Child A’s condition is caused by high fat intake; Child B’s by alcohol toxicity.
Child A is suffering from kwashiorkor; Child B is suffering from marasmus.
correctOption: Child A has relatively greater calorie deprivation; Child B has relatively greater protein deprivation.
optionExplanations: Correct. Child A has marasmus (total calorie deficit), while Child B has kwashiorkor (protein-specific deficit despite starch/calorie intake).
Child A (Marasmus) lacks total calories; Child B (Kwashiorkor) lacks protein despite having some carbohydrate calories.
The ratios are the key differentiator: marasmus is a balanced starvation, while kwashiorkor is a protein-deficient state.
Both conditions are forms of malnutrition, not toxicity or high fat intake; kwashiorkor often follows weaning onto a low-protein, high-carbohydrate starch diet (like watery gruel).
This is reversed. Child A (emaciated, no edema) is marasmus; Child B (swollen abdomen, edema) is kwashiorkor.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 361 (Book Page): Kwashiorkor occurs when protein deprivation is relatively greater than the reduction in total calories... Marasmus occurs when calorie deprivation is relatively greater than the reduction in protein.

category: Define basal metabolic rate (BMR)
statement: A 20-year-old sedentary female patient (height 165 cm, weight 50 kg) is participating in a nutrition study. Based on standard physiological approximations for her profile, what is her estimated resting metabolic rate (RMR), and how does it compare to her likely total daily energy expenditure?
options: Her RMR is approximately 2,000 kcal, which is the standard daily requirement listed on food labels.
Her RMR is approximately 1,300 kcal, and it accounts for roughly 60% of her daily energy expenditure.
Her RMR is approximately 1,800 kcal, and it accounts for 100% of her daily expenditure.
Her RMR is approximately 1,300 kcal, and her total expenditure is likely around 2,140 kcal.
Her RMR is approximately 500 kcal, with the remainder of her 1,300 kcal limit coming from activity.
correctOption: Her RMR is approximately 1,300 kcal, and it accounts for roughly 60% of her daily energy expenditure.
optionExplanations: Option D is incorrect; 2,000 kcal is a general daily average requirement used for food labeling, not the resting metabolic rate for a 50 kg female.
Option C is correct as per the specific data for a 50 kg woman provided in Figure 27.6, where the RMR is 1,300 kcal, representing 60% of her total estimated expenditure of 2,140 kcal.
Option A is incorrect because 1,800 kcal is the average RMR for a 70 kg man, not a 50 kg woman, and RMR never accounts for 100% of daily expenditure due to food processing.
Option B is incorrect; while 1,300 kcal is her RMR, adding 60% of RMR for a sedentary lifestyle (as per text: 30-50% more) would yield approximately 1,700-1,950 kcal, not 2,140.
Option E is incorrect because 1,300 kcal is her RMR (the baseline), not her total caloric limit, and 500 kcal is far below the essential maintenance energy for a 50 kg adult.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 359 (Book Page): In an adult, the RMR is about 1,800 kcal for men (70 kg) and 1,300 kcal for women (50 kg). ... Figure 27.6: Resting metabolic rate 1300 kcal = 60%.

category: Enlist the components of complex I, II, III, and IV
coreConcept: Proton pumping sites in the ETC
statement: In the process of oxidative phosphorylation, the flow of electrons through the respiratory chain is coupled to the 'pumping' of protons. Which complex is distinct because it contains electron-carrying components but does not function as a proton pump?
options: Succinate dehydrogenase
ATP synthase
Cytochrome bc1
NADH dehydrogenase
Cytochrome c oxidase
correctOption: Succinate dehydrogenase
optionExplanations: Correct. Although Complex II contains FAD and Fe-S centers and transfers electrons to CoQ, it does not have the necessary mechanism to pump protons across the membrane.
Complex V (ATP synthase) is not a proton pump; it allows protons to flow back into the matrix to drive ATP synthesis.
Complex III (Cytochrome bc1) is a major site of proton pumping into the intermembrane space.
Complex I (NADH dehydrogenase) is one of the three major proton pumps in the electron transport chain.
Complex IV (Cytochrome c oxidase) pumps protons and represents the final pumping site before electrons reach oxygen.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 77 (Book Page): Electron transport is coupled to the phosphorylation of ADP by the transport (‘pumping’) of protons (H + ) across the inner mitochondrial membrane... at Complexes I, III, and IV. Page 78 (Book Page), Figure 6.13: [Note: Protons are not pumped at Complex II.]

category: Enlist the components of complex I, II, III, and IV
statement: A 12-year-old boy presents with progressive muscle weakness and exercise-induced fatigue. A muscle biopsy reveals abnormal mitochondrial proliferation, and a histochemical stain for Succinate Dehydrogenase shows intensified activity in specific fibers. Which component of the electron transport chain is being directly assessed by this stain?
options: Complex V
Complex I
Complex II
Complex IV
Complex III
correctOption: Complex II
optionExplanations: Complex V is ATP synthase. It is not involved in the oxidation of succinate and therefore would not be detected by a succinate dehydrogenase histochemical stain.
Complex I is NADH dehydrogenase. While it is found in mitochondria, the standard diagnostic stain mentioned in the clinical context specifically targets succinate dehydrogenase (Complex II).

Succinate dehydrogenase is the official name of Complex II. In mitochondrial myopathies, the proliferation of mitochondria can be visualized using a stain for this enzyme, as it is a key marker for mitochondrial density.
Complex IV is cytochrome c oxidase. It is often stained for in mitochondrial studies, but the succinate dehydrogenase stain specifically identifies Complex II activity.
Complex III is Cytochrome bc1. It is not the target of the succinate dehydrogenase stain, although it functions immediately downstream from Complex II.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 80 (Book Page): Muscle fibers from a patient with a mitochondrial myopathy show abnormal mitochondrial proliferation when stained for succinate dehydrogenase, an enzyme of Complex II.

category: Explain how ethanol consumption causes hypoglycemia and fatty liver
statement: A researcher observes that during ethanol metabolism, the increase in the NADH/NAD+ ratio inhibits the conversion of lactate to pyruvate. This metabolic block is significant because it prevents the entry of lactate into which specific metabolic pathway?
options: Glycogenesis
Pentose Phosphate Pathway
Gluconeogenesis
Glycolysis
Fatty Acid Synthesis
correctOption: Gluconeogenesis
optionExplanations: Glycogenesis is the synthesis of glycogen from glucose 6-phosphate; it is not the pathway prevented by the inability to convert lactate to pyruvate.
The Pentose Phosphate Pathway is involved in NADPH and ribose production and is not the primary pathway blocked by the lactate/pyruvate redox shift.
Lactate is a major precursor for gluconeogenesis. By driving the reaction toward lactate, ethanol metabolism prevents the formation of pyruvate, which is necessary for the synthesis of new glucose.
Glycolysis is the breakdown of glucose to pyruvate; while ethanol affects its intermediates, the specific block of lactate to pyruvate prevents glucose synthesis, not breakdown.
While ethanol metabolism provides precursors for fatty acid synthesis (like glycerol 3-P), the block of lactate conversion specifically impairs the gluconeogenic pathway.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 116 (Book Page): ...the reversible reduction of pyruvate to lactate by lactate dehydrogenase of glycolysis is driven in the forward direction by NADH. Thus, two important gluconeogenic substrates, OAA and pyruvate, are decreased... result in a decrease in gluconeogenesis.

category: Define energy balance
statement: In the process of energy balance, the body can release energy as heat instead of capturing it as ATP. This process, known as nonshivering thermogenesis, is primarily mediated by which mechanism in brown adipocytes?
options: Reduction of the electrical gradient by opening of sodium channels
A 'proton leak' created by uncoupling protein-1 (thermogenin)
Increased conversion of ATP to cAMP by adenylyl cyclase
Activation of the F1 domain of ATP synthase by fatty acids
Increased efficiency of the electron transport chain complexes
correctOption: A 'proton leak' created by uncoupling protein-1 (thermogenin)
optionExplanations: While a gradient is reduced, it is the proton (H+) gradient across the inner mitochondrial membrane, not a sodium gradient.
UCP1 (thermogenin) allows protons to flow down their electrochemical gradient into the matrix without passing through ATP synthase, releasing the potential energy as heat.
The cAMP-PKA pathway may trigger the activation of lipolysis to provide fatty acids, but it is not the direct mediator of the heat production itself.
Fatty acids activate UCP1, but UCP1 functions by bypassing the ATP synthase (Complex V), not by activating its F1 domain.
UCP1 actually decreases the efficiency of the overall process of oxidative phosphorylation by uncoupling electron transport from ATP synthesis.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 79 (Book Page): UCP1, also called thermogenin, is responsible for the heat production in the brown adipocytes of mammals... these carrier proteins create a “proton leak,” that is, they allow protons to re-enter the mitochondrial matrix without energy being captured as ATP.

category: Categorize individuals into underweight, normal, overweight, obese, and morbidly obese based on theirs BMI values
statement: A 10-year-old child presents with extreme muscle wasting, an 'old man' facial appearance, and a weight-for-height that results in a BMI of 12.5 kg/m". The child is alert but has a very low subcutaneous fat level. Based on this BMI and clinical presentation, what is the most likely diagnosis and its biochemical hallmark?
options: Morbid obesity; the child has Prader-Willi syndrome.
Marasmus; characterized by severe BMI deficit and a primary deficiency of total calories.
Obese Class I; characterized by high insulin levels and fatty liver.
Kwashiorkor; characterized by a BMI in the 'Overweight' range due to massive abdominal edema.
Normal weight; the child is simply going through a growth spurt.
correctOption: Marasmus; characterized by severe BMI deficit and a primary deficiency of total calories.
optionExplanations: Morbid obesity requires a BMI ≥ 40.0. The clinical description of muscle wasting contradicts obesity.

Marasmus is the 'wasting' form of PEM due to total calorie deprivation. A BMI of 12.5 is extremely underweight, reflecting the exhaustion of both adipose and muscle energy stores (glycogen, then fat, then protein).
A BMI of 12.5 is the extreme opposite of the Obese range (≥ 30.0).
Kwashiorkor is protein deficiency with some calorie intake; it often presents with edema that might falsely elevate BMI or keep it near normal despite tissue wasting.
A BMI of 12.5 is dangerously low and pathologically underweight (normal is 18.5-24.9).
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 341 (Book Page): [BMI] Underweight: < 18.5. Page 361 (Book Page): [Marasmus] arrested growth, extreme muscle wasting.

category: Infer the consequences of deficiency and excess of these hormones
statement: A runner is nearing the end of a marathon. Epinephrine levels are peak. In the liver, epinephrine binds to alpha-1 adrenergic receptors, triggering a physiological loop that differs from its action on beta-receptors. What is the primary second messenger in this specific alpha-1 pathway?
options: Calcium-calmodulin complex
Fructose 2,6-bisphosphate
Cyclic AMP
Pyruvate dehydrogenase phosphatase
3',5'-guanosine monophosphate
correctOption: Calcium-calmodulin complex
optionExplanations: Alpha-1 adrenergic signaling in the liver uses the IP3/DAG pathway to release intracellular calcium, which binds calmodulin to activate phosphorylase kinase.
Fructose 2,6-bisphosphate is a metabolic regulator of glycolysis/gluconeogenesis, not a second messenger for the alpha-1 adrenergic receptor.
cAMP is the second messenger for epinephrine binding to beta-adrenergic receptors, not alpha-1 receptors.
Pyruvate dehydrogenase phosphatase is an enzyme that activates the PDH complex in response to calcium, but it is not the second messenger itself.
cGMP is the second messenger associated with nitric oxide and vascular relaxation, not hepatic adrenergic signaling.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 126 (Book Page): Binding of epinephrine to hepatocyte alpha-1-adrenergic G protein-coupled receptors activates a phospholipid-dependent cascade... that results in movement of Ca2+ from the ER into the cytoplasm. A Ca2+-calmodulin complex forms and activates hepatic phosphorylase kinase b.

category: Outline treatment strategies
coreConcept: Management and Prevention of G6PD Crisis
statement: A 19-year-old male of Mediterranean descent presents with acute jaundice, dark urine, and fatigue after being treated with sulfamethoxazole for a urinary tract infection. Laboratory results show a significant drop in hemoglobin and the presence of Heinz bodies. In addition to treating the underlying infection, what is the most critical preventative strategy to manage this patient's condition long-term?
options: Switching to a ketogenic diet to provide alternative fuels for erythrocytes.
Chronic administration of corticosteroids to suppress the immune response.
Weekly prophylactic blood transfusions to maintain a hematocrit above 40%.
Daily supplementation with high-dose Vitamin K and iron.
Avoidance of oxidant triggers including specific antibiotics, antimalarials, and fava beans.
correctOption: Avoidance of oxidant triggers including specific antibiotics, antimalarials, and fava beans.
optionExplanations: Erythrocytes lack mitochondria and cannot utilize ketone bodies; they are entirely dependent on the pentose phosphate pathway for NADPH, making diet-induced ketosis useless.
The hemolysis in G6PD deficiency is not immune-mediated but is a biochemical failure of the glutathione system; thus, corticosteroids are not indicated for management.
Transfusions are only indicated for acute, severe life-threatening anemia; chronic prophylaxis is unnecessary as the marrow typically compensates between episodes of oxidative stress.
Vitamin K and iron do not address the oxidative stress mechanism of G6PD deficiency and do not prevent the hemolysis caused by NADPH depletion.

The cornerstone of G6PD management is the strict avoidance of oxidant stressors (drugs like sulfa, antimalarials like primaquine, and fava beans) that overwhelm the cell's limited antioxidant capacity.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 145 (Book Page): Commonly used drugs that produce hemolytic anemia in patients with G6PD deficiency are best remembered from the mnemonic AAA—Antibiotics (for example, sulfamethoxazole...)... Antimalarials... and Antipyretics.

category: Enlist various types of glycogen storage diseases (GSDs)
coreConcept: Convergent Pathway Failure in GSD Type Ia
statement: A metabolic study of a GSD patient reveals that while the glycogen structure is normal, the total amount is significantly increased. Furthermore, the patient exhibits severe fasting hypoglycemia because the liver cannot generate free glucose from either glycogenolysis or gluconeogenesis. What is the most likely physiological explanation for this combined failure?
options: Inability to dephosphorylate glucose 6-phosphate, the terminal step for both glucose-producing pathways.
Deficiency in the lysosomal α(1→4)-glucosidase preventing glycogen recycling.
Deficiency in the GLUT-2 transporter preventing the exit of glucose from the hepatocyte.
Lack of the 4:4 transferase activity of the debranching enzyme complex.
Mutation in the hepatic glycogen phosphorylase preventing the initiation of phosphorolysis.
correctOption: Inability to dephosphorylate glucose 6-phosphate, the terminal step for both glucose-producing pathways.
optionExplanations: Glucose 6-phosphatase is the common final enzyme for both gluconeogenesis and glycogenolysis. Its deficiency prevents the liver from releasing free glucose into the blood regardless of the source of the glucose 6-phosphate.

Lysosomal α(1→4)-glucosidase deficiency causes Pompe disease, which primarily affects cardiac and muscle tissue and does not typically present with severe fasting hypoglycemia as cytoplasmic pathways remain intact.

GLUT-2 is a glucose transporter; while its deficiency (Fanconi-Bickel syndrome) affects glucose transport, the question focuses on the biochemical failure to produce free glucose from intracellular phosphorylated precursors via specific GSD-linked enzyme defects.
Deficiency of the 4:4 transferase activity (Cori disease) results in abnormal glycogen structure (limit dextrins), whereas this case specifies a normal glycogen structure.
Hepatic glycogen phosphorylase deficiency (Hers disease) only affects glycogenolysis; gluconeogenesis remains functional, so fasting hypoglycemia is generally mild compared to Von Gierke disease.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 122 (Book Page): Type Ia glycogen storage disease... is characterized by severe fasting hypoglycemia, because free glucose is unable to be produced from either gluconeogenesis or glycogenolysis.

category: Elaborate the effect of various physiological and pathological factors on BMR
statement: A nutritionist is estimating the daily caloric requirement for a moderately active adult weighing 70 kg. Based on the standard approximations for physical activity, what is the estimated total energy requirement?
options: 2,450 kcal/day
2,800 kcal/day
3,500 kcal/day
2,100 kcal/day
3,000 kcal/day
correctOption: 2,450 kcal/day
optionExplanations: For a moderately active adult, the calculation is 70 kg multiplied by 35 kcal/kg/day, resulting in 2,450 kcal/day.
2,800 kcal/day is based on 40 kcal/kg/day, which is the requirement for very active individuals.
3,500 kcal/day is excessively high for a 70 kg adult unless they are engaged in extreme athletic training beyond 'very active' status.
2,100 kcal/day is based on 30 kcal/kg/day, which is the requirement for sedentary adults.
3,000 kcal/day is a general rounding that does not follow the specific multiplier for moderate activity provided in the text.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 358 (Book Page): ...moderately active adults require 35 kcal/kg/day; and very active adults require 40 kcal/kg/day.

category: Explain hemolytic anemia in subjects with pyruvate kinase deficiency based on your biochemical knowledge
statement: Based on the feed-forward regulation loop mentioned in biochemical pathways, how does the activity of phosphofructokinase-1 (PFK-1) influence pyruvate kinase in the liver, and by extension, the metabolic flux in erythrocytes?
options: PFK-1 increases the production of NADH, which acts as a co-repressor for the pyruvate kinase gene.
PFK-1 consumes ATP, thereby reducing the inhibition of pyruvate kinase by high energy levels.
PFK-1 activates protein kinase A, which phosphorylates and inactivates pyruvate kinase.
PFK-1 inhibits pyruvate kinase via the accumulation of citrate.
PFK-1 produces fructose 1,6-bisphosphate, which allosterically activates pyruvate kinase.
correctOption: PFK-1 produces fructose 1,6-bisphosphate, which allosterically activates pyruvate kinase.
optionExplanations: NADH is a product of the glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate dehydrogenase reaction, not PFK-1, and it is not a gene repressor for PK in this context.
PFK-1 does consume ATP, but its regulatory link to PK is via the metabolite fructose 1,6-bisphosphate, not directly via ATP levels.
Protein kinase A is activated by cAMP (triggered by glucagon), which then inactivates liver pyruvate kinase; PFK-1 is not the trigger for this covalent modification.
Citrate inhibits PFK-1, it does not act as an inhibitor for pyruvate kinase in this feed-forward mechanism.

The product of the PFK-1 reaction, Fructose 1,6-bisphosphate, acts as a feed-forward allosteric activator of pyruvate kinase, ensuring that the final step of glycolysis keeps pace with the rate-limiting step.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 102 (Book Page): [In liver, pyruvate kinase is activated by fructose 1,6-bisphosphate, the product of the phosphofructokinase reaction. This feed-forward (instead of the more usual feedback) regulation has the effect of linking the two kinase activities: increased phosphofructokinase activity results in elevated levels of fructose 1,6-bisphosphate, which activates pyruvate kinase.]

category: Explain the significance of Cori cycle and glucosealanine cycle
coreConcept: Nitrogen Disposal in the Glucose-Alanine Cycle
statement: During the glucose-alanine cycle, what is the fate of the amino group once alanine reaches the hepatocyte?
options: It remains attached to the pyruvate skeleton to form serine in the cytosol.
It is transferred to alpha-ketoglutarate to form glutamate, ultimately providing nitrogen for urea synthesis.
It is transferred to oxaloacetate to form aspartate, which then enters the TCA cycle.
It is released as free ammonia into the bloodstream for renal excretion.
It is utilized to synthesize essential amino acids within the hepatic mitochondria.
correctOption: It is transferred to alpha-ketoglutarate to form glutamate, ultimately providing nitrogen for urea synthesis.
optionExplanations: Alanine is stripped of its amino group to become pyruvate; it does not become serine in this cycle.
In the liver, alanine transaminates with alpha-ketoglutarate to reform pyruvate (the carbon skeleton for gluconeogenesis) and glutamate (the carrier for nitrogen destined for the urea cycle).
While aspartate is involved in the urea cycle, the immediate transamination of alanine typically involves glutamate/alpha-ketoglutarate.
Ammonia is toxic and is not released as a free gas into the blood; it is processed into urea within the liver.
Essential amino acids cannot be synthesized by the body; they must be obtained from the diet.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 92 (Book Page)/101: Alanine... [is an intermediate of] protein metabolism. [Catabolism] transform[s] a wide variety of molecules into a few common end products... CO2, H2O, and NH3.

category: Define energy balance
coreConcept: Thermic Effect of Food (TEF) vs. RMR
statement: When comparing the three major processes of human energy expenditure, how does the thermic effect of food differ from the resting metabolic rate (RMR)?
options: It represents the energy required for blood flow and cellular integrity.
It is measured in the postabsorptive state twelve hours after a meal.
It constitutes the greatest variation in energy expenditure among individuals.
It increases heat production as much as 30% above the resting level during digestion.
It remains constant regardless of nutrient ingestion.
correctOption: It increases heat production as much as 30% above the resting level during digestion.
optionExplanations: Respiration, blood flow, and the maintenance of cellular integrity are the primary functions accounted for by the Resting Metabolic Rate (RMR), not the thermic effect of food.
RMR is measured in the postabsorptive state; the thermic effect of food is the metabolic rise that occurs specifically after the state of fasting is broken by food intake.
Physical activity, not the thermic effect of food, provides the greatest variation in energy expenditure, ranging from 30% to over 100% of the RMR.
The thermic effect of food is a transient increase in metabolic rate (up to 30% above RMR) specifically associated with the processing of macronutrients.
The thermic effect of food is inherently variable and specifically triggered by the ingestion, digestion, and absorption of nutrients, unlike the relatively stable RMR.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 359 (Book Page): The production of heat by the body increases as much as 30% above the resting level during the digestion and absorption of food. This effect is called the thermic effect of food or diet-induced thermogenesis. Over a 24–hour period, the thermic response to food intake may amount to 5–10% of the total energy expenditure.

category: Define gluconeogenesis and enumerate gluconeogenic substrates (precursors)
statement: Which of the following statements most accurately defines the process of gluconeogenesis in human physiology?
options: The mobilization of glucose 1-phosphate from hepatic glycogen stores during a fast.
The conversion of dietary starch into glucose within the intestinal lumen.
The cytosolic degradation of glucose to pyruvate to generate adenosine triphosphate.
The conversion of acetyl coenzyme A into glucose via a direct reversal of the pyruvate dehydrogenase reaction.
The synthesis of glucose from non-carbohydrate precursors such as lactate and glycerol.
correctOption: The synthesis of glucose from non-carbohydrate precursors such as lactate and glycerol.
optionExplanations: This refers to glycogenolysis, the breakdown of glycogen, which is distinct from the de novo synthesis of glucose (gluconeogenesis).
Intestinal digestion of starch is a catabolic process involving glycoside hydrolases, not the anabolic synthesis of glucose from non-carbohydrate sources.
This describes glycolysis, which is the degradative pathway for glucose, essentially the opposite of gluconeogenesis.

Acetyl CoA cannot be used for net glucose synthesis because the pyruvate dehydrogenase reaction is irreversible and there is no pathway to convert acetyl CoA to pyruvate or oxaloacetate for gluconeogenesis.
Gluconeogenesis is specifically defined as the metabolic pathway that results in the generation of glucose from certain non-carbohydrate carbon substrates.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 109 (Book Page): Instead, glucose is synthesized by a special pathway, gluconeogenesis, that requires both mitochondrial and cytosolic enzymes. ... Gluconeogenic precursors are molecules that can be used to produce a net synthesis of glucose.

category: Suggest dietary advice for patients suffering from diabetes mellitus, hypertension, obesity, renal disease, lactose intolerance, gluten enteropathy, hypercholesterolemia, and hemorrhoids
statement: In a patient with hypercholesterolemia, the physician recommends replacing dietary saturated fats with monounsaturated fatty acids (MUFAs). Which of the following best describes the metabolic effect of this substitution on the plasma lipoprotein profile?
options: Increases plasma triacylglycerols and decreases total cholesterol.
Lowers HDL cholesterol significantly but has no effect on LDL.
Lowers LDL cholesterol while maintaining or increasing HDL cholesterol.
Increases both LDL and HDL cholesterol levels while decreasing VLDL.
Has no effect on LDL but selectively lowers the VLDL fraction.
correctOption: Lowers LDL cholesterol while maintaining or increasing HDL cholesterol.
optionExplanations: Substitution of MUFAs for saturated fats generally results in a decrease in total cholesterol rather than an increase in triacylglycerols, provided the total caloric intake remains balanced.
This describes an undesirable outcome; typically, it is the polyunsaturated omega-6 fatty acids that, when consumed in excess, might lower HDL alongside LDL, whereas MUFAs are protective of HDL.

Monounsaturated fats, such as those found in olive oil, are uniquely beneficial compared to polyunsaturated fats (which may lower both LDL and HDL) because they effectively reduce the pro-atherogenic LDL while preserving or boosting anti-atherogenic HDL.

This is incorrect because saturated fats, not MUFAs, are associated with increased LDL; MUFAs are specifically utilized to lower LDL without the adverse effect of decreasing the protective HDL fraction.
MUFAs have a well-documented effect on lowering LDL cholesterol by upregulating LDL receptor activity or decreasing the production of LDL precursors, making this option physiologically inaccurate.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 353 (Book Page): When substituted for saturated fatty acids in the diet, monounsaturated fats lower both total plasma cholesterol and LDL cholesterol, but maintain or increase HDL cholesterol.

category: Calculate the energy yield of TCA
statement: A research scientist calculates the efficiency of energy capture in the TCA cycle. If one turn of the cycle starting with Acetyl CoA produces 12 ATP equivalents, and the standard free energy for the phosphorylation of ADP to ATP is +7.3 kcal/mol, how much total energy is captured as high-energy phosphate bonds per Acetyl CoA oxidized?
options: 14.6 kcal/mol
21.9 kcal/mol
52.58 kcal/mol
87.6 kcal/mol
109.5 kcal/mol
correctOption: 87.6 kcal/mol
optionExplanations: 14.6 kcal/mol is the energy from only 2 ATP (such as that captured from FADH2), which is an incomplete representation of the TCA cycle's total energetic output.
21.9 kcal/mol represents the energy captured from just one molecule of NADH (3 ATP x 7.3 kcal). It does not account for the other coenzymes or GTP produced in the TCA cycle.
52.58 kcal/mol is the total free energy released by the transfer of one pair of electrons from NADH to oxygen, not the energy captured as ATP.
Correct. One turn of the TCA cycle produces 12 ATP equivalents. Multiplied by the energy required to synthesize one ATP (7.3 kcal/mol), the total energy captured is 12 x 7.3 = 87.6 kcal/mol.
109.5 kcal/mol represents the energy from 15 ATP (15 x 7.3). This is the energy captured from the oxidation of Pyruvate to CO2, not Acetyl CoA to CO2.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 105 (Book Page): The total yield of ATP from the oxidation of one acetyl CoA is... 12 ATP/acetyl CoA oxidized. [Page 77 (Book Page): The standard free energy for the phosphorylation of ADP to ATP is +7.3 kcal/mol.]

category: Categorize individuals into underweight, normal, overweight, obese, and morbidly obese based on theirs BMI values
statement: In the context of metabolic syndrome and adipose tissue dysfunction, what is the primary pathophysiological shift observed when an individual's BMI transitions from the 'Normal' range into the 'Obese' category (BMI ≥ 30 kg/m²)?
options: Shift from glucose to fatty acid oxidation in the brain to preserve energy
Enhanced secretion of adiponectin to counteract insulin resistance
Increased sensitivity of skeletal muscle to insulin to manage glucose load
Decrease in leptin production due to adipocyte exhaustion
Hypertrophy of adipocytes leading to pro-inflammatory cytokine release
correctOption: Hypertrophy of adipocytes leading to pro-inflammatory cytokine release
optionExplanations: The brain primarily utilizes glucose and only uses ketone bodies during prolonged starvation; it does not shift to fatty acid oxidation as a response to obesity.
Adiponectin levels typically decrease as BMI increases into the obese range, contributing to the development of insulin resistance and systemic inflammation.
Obesity is strongly associated with insulin resistance in skeletal muscle, not increased sensitivity, due to the inhibitory effects of free fatty acids and inflammatory markers.
Leptin production actually increases in proportion to adipose tissue mass in obesity; however, 'leptin resistance' develops, where the brain fails to respond to the satiety signals.

As BMI reaches the obese threshold (≥30), adipocytes undergo significant hypertrophy. Large adipocytes become dysfunctional, releasing pro-inflammatory cytokines like TNF-alpha and IL-6, which drive systemic insulin resistance.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 357 (Book Page): Dietary fats most strongly influence the incidence of coronary heart disease (CHD); evidence linking dietary fat and the risk for cancer or obesity is much weaker.

category: Suggest dietary advice for patients suffering from diabetes mellitus, hypertension, obesity, renal disease, lactose intolerance, gluten enteropathy, hypercholesterolemia, and hemorrhoids
statement: A 35-year-old female experiences bloating and osmotic diarrhea after consuming dairy products. If this condition is an acquired enzyme deficiency rather than a genetic one, which of the following is the most likely cause?
options: Inhibition of fructokinase by high-fructose corn syrup.
Excessive intake of gluten leading to villous atrophy.
Autoimmune destruction of the pancreatic acinar cells.
Loss of brush border enzymes due to severe diarrhea.
Inherited mutation in the DNA sequence of chromosome 2.
correctOption: Loss of brush border enzymes due to severe diarrhea.
optionExplanations: Fructokinase is a hepatic enzyme; its inhibition would affect fructose metabolism but would not cause the intestinal symptoms of lactose malabsorption.

While gluten enteropathy causes villous atrophy and can lead to secondary lactose intolerance, the most common 'acquired' and 'temporary' cause mentioned is the rapid loss during severe diarrheal illness.
Pancreatic acinar cell destruction would affect amylase and lipase secretion (luminal digestion), not the brush border disaccharidases specifically associated with lactose metabolism.

Acquired lactase deficiency occurs when the intestinal mucosa is damaged (e.g., by infection or inflammation), leading to the sloughing of the microvilli where disaccharidases like lactase are located.
This describes primary (congenital) lactose intolerance, which is the age-dependent loss of lactase activity due to genetic expression changes, not an acquired temporary loss.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 88 (Book Page): Alterations in disaccharide degradation can also be caused by a variety of intestinal diseases... For example, brush border enzymes are rapidly lost in normal individuals with severe diarrhea, causing a temporary, acquired enzyme deficiency.

category: Describe the glycolytic pathway along with its regulation and significance
statement: Which reaction represents the primary 'committed' and rate-limiting step of the glycolytic pathway?
options: Dehydration of 2-phosphoglycerate to phosphoenolpyruvate
Isomerization of glucose 6-phosphate to fructose 6-phosphate
Phosphorylation of fructose 6-phosphate to fructose 1,6-bisphosphate
Cleavage of fructose 1,6-bisphosphate to dihydroxyacetone phosphate
Phosphorylation of glucose to glucose 6-phosphate
correctOption: Phosphorylation of fructose 6-phosphate to fructose 1,6-bisphosphate
optionExplanations: The dehydration step catalyzed by enolase is a reversible reaction that occurs late in the pathway and is not the rate-limiting control point.
The isomerization step is a reversible reaction that is not rate-limiting or regulated; it serves to prepare the sugar for the next phosphorylation.
The PFK-1 reaction is the committed step because once fructose 1,6-bisphosphate is formed, the molecule is destined for cleavage and completion of the glycolytic pathway.
The cleavage of the hexose into trioses by aldolase is a reversible reaction and is not the primary regulated control point of the pathway.
While irreversible, the phosphorylation of glucose is not the committed step because G6P can enter other pathways like the pentose phosphate pathway or glycogen synthesis.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 91 (Book Page): The irreversible phosphorylation reaction catalyzed by phosphofructokinase-1 (PFK-1) is the most important control point and the rate-limiting and committed step of glycolysis.

category: Define gluconeogenesis and enumerate gluconeogenic substrates (precursors)
statement: Which of the following compounds is considered a strictly ketogenic substrate and therefore cannot be used as a precursor for the net synthesis of glucose in humans?
options: Oxaloacetate
Leucine
Glycerol
Alpha-ketoglutarate
Lactate
correctOption: Leucine
optionExplanations: Oxaloacetate is a direct precursor to phosphoenolpyruvate (PEP) in the gluconeogenic pathway, catalyzed by PEP-carboxykinase.
Leucine is one of the two strictly ketogenic amino acids; its catabolism yields only acetyl CoA or acetoacetate, which cannot be used for net glucose synthesis.
Glycerol is a glucogenic precursor derived from the breakdown of triacylglycerols and enters the gluconeogenic pathway as dihydroxyacetone phosphate.
Alpha-ketoglutarate is an intermediate of the TCA cycle that can be converted to oxaloacetate and then into the gluconeogenic pathway; it is glucogenic.
Lactate is a major gluconeogenic substrate, particularly via the Cori cycle, where it is converted back to pyruvate and then glucose in the liver.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 110 (Book Page): Acetyl coenzyme A (CoA) and compounds that give rise only to acetyl CoA (for example, acetoacetate and amino acids such as lysine and leucine) cannot give rise to a net synthesis of glucose. ... These compounds give rise instead to ketone bodies ... and are therefore termed ketogenic.

category: Describe the transport of pyruvate from cytosol to mitochondria
statement: Classification of the mitochondrial inner membrane's transport capacity is essential for understanding cellular metabolism. Which of the following correctly classifies the inner membrane's relationship with pyruvate?
options: Permeable to pyruvate but impermeable to ADP
Impermeable to pyruvate, requiring specialized carriers
Selective for pyruvate diffusion but impermeable to small ions
Freely permeable to pyruvate due to a lack of protein
Highly porous, allowing all glycolytic intermediates to pass
correctOption: Impermeable to pyruvate, requiring specialized carriers
optionExplanations: The inner membrane is impermeable to both pyruvate and ADP (which requires its own adenine nucleotide carrier).
The inner membrane is a specialized barrier that necessitates the presence of specific transport proteins to move metabolites like pyruvate into the matrix.
Pyruvate cannot diffuse through the membrane; transport is strictly protein-mediated.
The inner membrane is unusually rich in protein (50%), not lacking it, and is strictly impermeable to pyruvate.
The outer membrane is porous; the inner membrane is highly selective and impermeable to prevent loss of mitochondrial gradients.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 74 (Book Page): Although the outer membrane contains special pores... the inner mitochondrial membrane is a specialized structure that is impermeable to most small ions... and small molecules such as ATP, ADP, pyruvate, and other metabolites.

category: Identify various causes of malnutrition
statement: Regarding the Dietary Reference Intakes (DRI), which standard is defined as the average daily nutrient intake level estimated to meet the requirement of one half of the healthy individuals in a particular life stage and gender group?
options: Recommended Dietary Allowance (RDA)
Adequate Intake (AI)
Estimated Average Requirement (EAR)
Tolerable Upper Intake Level (UL)
Acceptable Macronutrient Distribution Range (AMDR)
correctOption: Estimated Average Requirement (EAR)
optionExplanations: The RDA is set to meet the needs of nearly all (97-98%) individuals, not just half.
The AI is an estimate used when an EAR or RDA cannot be determined; it is based on observed intakes of healthy groups.
The EAR is the median requirement for a population group and serves as the basis for calculating the RDA.
The UL is the highest level of daily intake that is likely to pose no risk of adverse health effects, intended to prevent toxicity.
The AMDR provides ranges of intake for macronutrients (carbs, fats, proteins) expressed as a percentage of total energy.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 349 (Book Page): Estimated Average Requirement (EAR): The EAR is the average daily nutrient intake level estimated to meet the requirement of one half of the healthy individuals in a particular life stage and gender group.

category: Elaborate key features of various transport systems for entry of glucose into cells
statement: GLUT-2 is a specialized glucose transporter with unique physiological roles in the liver and kidney. What is a key feature of its function in these tissues?
options: It only transports glucose into the cell during periods of starvation
It is the primary glucose sensor in neurons of the hypothalamus
It can transport glucose either into or out of cells depending on blood sugar levels
It has an extremely low Km, making it saturated at fasting glucose levels
Its expression on the cell surface is primarily regulated by insulin
correctOption: It can transport glucose either into or out of cells depending on blood sugar levels
optionExplanations: GLUT-2 functions during both high blood sugar (uptake for storage/glycolysis) and low blood sugar (release from gluconeogenesis/glycogenolysis).
While hexokinase serves as a sensor in the hypothalamus, the primary GLUT-2 sensor function is in the pancreatic beta cells and liver.
Unlike other GLUTs, GLUT-2 is a high-capacity, low-affinity transporter that allows for rapid equilibration of glucose across the cell membrane in both directions.
GLUT-2 has a high Km (low affinity), which means its rate of transport is proportional to the glucose concentration over a wide range, allowing it to sense hyperglycemia.
GLUT-2 is insulin-independent; only GLUT-4 is insulin-dependent for its recruitment to the plasma membrane.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 89 (Book Page): In contrast, GLUT-2, which is found in the liver and kidney, can either transport glucose into these cells when blood glucose levels are high, or transport glucose from these cells when blood glucose levels are low.

category: Diagrammatically illustrate the organization of electron transport chain (ETC) depicting the flow of electrons
statement: During the initial step of electron flow from NADH to the respiratory chain, which sequence of prosthetic groups correctly describes the passage of electrons within Complex I?
options: NADH → Coenzyme Q → Cytochrome bc1 → Cytochrome c
NADH → FAD → Cytochrome b → Coenzyme Q
NADH → FMN → Iron-Sulfur centers → Coenzyme Q
NADH → Copper centers → Cytochrome c → Oxygen
NADH → Iron-Sulfur centers → FAD → Cytochrome a
correctOption: NADH → FMN → Iron-Sulfur centers → Coenzyme Q
optionExplanations: While this represents a general flow through the ETC, it misses the internal prosthetic groups (FMN, Fe-S) of Complex I and incorrectly suggests NADH gives electrons directly to CoQ.
FAD is used in Complex II (succinate dehydrogenase) and other flavoproteins, not Complex I, and Cytochrome b is part of Complex III.

In Complex I (NADH dehydrogenase), electrons from NADH are first transferred to FMN, then passed through a series of Iron-Sulfur (Fe-S) centers, and finally delivered to the mobile carrier Coenzyme Q.
Copper centers are characteristic of Complex IV (Cytochrome oxidase), which is the final step of the ETC, not the entry point for NADH.
The sequence is incorrect as electrons move from the flavin (FMN) to Fe-S centers, not the other way around, and FAD/Cyto a are not part of Complex I.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 75 (Book Page): Complex I has a tightly bound molecule of flavin mononucleotide (FMN...)... NADH dehydrogenase also contains iron atoms paired with sulfur atoms to make iron–sulfur centers. These are necessary for the transfer of the hydrogen atoms to the next member of the chain, coenzyme Q (ubiquinone).

category: Discuss the importance of HMP shunt
statement: A researcher is studying the metabolic resilience of mature human erythrocytes. Which mechanism best explains how the importance of the hexose monophosphate shunt is demonstrated in maintaining red blood cell integrity under oxidative stress?
options: By providing NADPH to glutathione reductase to regenerate reduced glutathione for the detoxification of reactive oxygen species.
By producing ATP via substrate-level phosphorylation to maintain the Na+/K+ ATPase pump.
By facilitating the conversion of glucose to sorbitol to prevent osmotic swelling of the erythrocyte membrane.
By generating NADH to serve as a coenzyme for methemoglobin reductase to keep iron in the ferrous state.
By synthesizing ribose 5-phosphate for de novo nucleotide synthesis to repair damaged ribosomal RNA.
correctOption: By providing NADPH to glutathione reductase to regenerate reduced glutathione for the detoxification of reactive oxygen species.
optionExplanations: NADPH is the essential electron donor for glutathione reductase; reduced glutathione (G-SH) is mandatory for glutathione peroxidase to neutralize hydrogen peroxide, protecting the cell from oxidative hemolysis.
The HMP shunt does not produce ATP; the Na+/K+ pump in erythrocytes is maintained by ATP derived from anaerobic glycolysis.
Glucose conversion to sorbitol (polyol pathway) is generally detrimental in hyperglycemia (causing osmotic stress) and is not a protective mechanism of the HMP shunt.
While methemoglobin reductase uses NADH, the specific importance of the HMP shunt is the production of NADPH for the glutathione system, not NADH.
Mature erythrocytes lack a nucleus and ribosomes and do not perform de novo nucleotide or protein synthesis; ribose synthesis is not their primary use for the HMP shunt.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 144 (Book Page): [Erythrocytes] are totally dependent on the pentose phosphate pathway for their supply of NADPH because, unlike other cell types, erythrocytes do not have an alternate source for this essential coenzyme... [which] provide[s] electrons for the reduction of hydrogen peroxide.

category: Describe the TCA cycle along with regulation & significance
statement: Fluoroacetate is a potent toxin used as a rodenticide. After entering the cell, it is converted to fluorocitrate, which halts the TCA cycle. Which enzyme is directly inhibited by the formation of fluorocitrate?
options: Citrate synthase
Isocitrate dehydrogenase
Fumarase
Aconitase
Succinate thiokinase
correctOption: Aconitase
optionExplanations: Citrate synthase is the enzyme that mistakenly uses fluoroacetyl CoA as a substrate to create fluorocitrate, but it is not the target of inhibition.
Isocitrate dehydrogenase follows aconitase in the cycle; it is not directly inhibited by fluorocitrate but ceases to function due to lack of substrate (isocitrate).
Fumarase catalyzes the hydration of fumarate to malate and is independent of the citrate-aconitase step inhibited by fluorocitrate.
Aconitase is the specific target of fluorocitrate. Inhibition of aconitase prevents the isomerization of citrate to isocitrate, causing the TCA cycle to stop.
Succinate thiokinase catalyzes the cleavage of succinyl CoA to succinate; it is located downstream and is not affected by fluorocitrate.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 104 (Book Page): [Note: Aconitase is inhibited by fluoroacetate... Fluoroacetate is converted to fluoroacetyl CoA, which condenses with oxaloacetate to form fluorocitrate—a potent inhibitor of aconitase—resulting in citrate accumulation.]

category: Enlist the components of complex I, II, III, and IV
statement: The final complex of the electron transport chain, cytochrome c oxidase, requires which of the following mineral cofactors to facilitate the four-electron reduction of molecular oxygen to water?
options: Copper
Zinc
Magnesium
Selenium
Manganese
correctOption: Copper
optionExplanations: Copper atoms ($Cu_A$ and $Cu_B$) are essential structural components of Complex IV, working alongside hemes a and a3 to transfer electrons to oxygen.
Zinc is found in many transcription factors and enzymes (like carbonic anhydrase) but is not a component of the electron transport chain.
Magnesium is a common cofactor for kinases and ATP-utilizing enzymes but is not a component of the cytochrome c oxidase complex.
Selenium is a component of glutathione peroxidase, an antioxidant enzyme, but is not involved in the protein complexes of the ETC.
Manganese is a cofactor for enzymes like superoxide dismutase in the mitochondria but not for the ETC complexes.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 76 (Book Page): [Cytochrome a + a 3 : This cytochrome complex ... is also called cytochrome oxidase. ...Cytochrome oxidase contains copper atoms that are required for this complex reaction to occur.]

category: Explain how the free energy generated by the transport of electrons by ETC is used to produce ATP from ADP + Pi (i
statement: A 24-year-old female presents to the emergency department with a temperature of 41°C (105.8°F), profuse sweating, and rapid breathing after consuming a 'fat burner' containing 2,4-dinitrophenol (DNP). Which of the following best describes the molecular mechanism responsible for her hyperthermia?
options: Dissipation of the proton gradient without capturing energy as ATP
Competitive inhibition of the ATP/ADP transporter
Irreversible inhibition of the Cytochrome a + a3 complex
Prevention of NADH formation by inhibiting the TCA cycle
Binding to the F0 domain to close the proton channel
correctOption: Dissipation of the proton gradient without capturing energy as ATP
optionExplanations: DNP is a lipophilic proton carrier that allows protons to leak across the inner mitochondrial membrane back into the matrix, bypassing ATP synthase. This collapses the electrochemical gradient, releasing the energy of electron transport as heat.
DNP does not primarily target the ATP/ADP transporter; it affects the inner membrane's permeability to protons.
Cyanide and carbon monoxide inhibit Cytochrome a + a3 (Complex IV), which would stop oxygen consumption, unlike DNP which increases it.
DNP actually increases the rate of the TCA cycle and electron transport as the body attempts to maintain a gradient that is constantly leaking.
Oligomycin binds to the F0 domain to close the channel; DNP makes the entire membrane permeable to protons, bypassing the channel.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 71 (Book Page): This uncoupler [2,4-dinitrophenol] causes electron transport to proceed at a rapid rate without establishing a proton gradient... energy is released as heat rather than being used to synthesize ATP.

category: Elaborate the effect of oligomycin and uncouplers on ATP production
statement: A researcher is comparing two chemical agents that affect mitochondrial function. Agent X inhibits both electron transport and phosphorylation, while Agent Y allows electron transport to proceed rapidly but prevents ATP synthesis. Which of the following is the most likely identification of these two agents?
options: Agent X is oligomycin; Agent Y is 2,4-dinitrophenol
Agent X is thermogenin; Agent Y is amytal
Agent X is aspirin; Agent Y is oligomycin
Agent X is rotenone; Agent Y is oligomycin
Agent X is 2,4-dinitrophenol; Agent Y is cyanide
correctOption: Agent X is oligomycin; Agent Y is 2,4-dinitrophenol
optionExplanations: Oligomycin inhibits ATP synthase, which stops the ETC due to respiratory control (Agent X). 2,4-dinitrophenol is an uncoupler that increases the permeability of the membrane, dissipating the gradient and allowing the ETC to run at maximum speed without making ATP (Agent Y).
Thermogenin is a natural uncoupler, and amytal is a site-specific inhibitor of Complex I.
Aspirin in high doses is an uncoupler (Agent Y behavior), and oligomycin stops the ETC (Agent X behavior).
Rotenone is a site-specific inhibitor (Complex I), but Agent Y must be an uncoupler, which oligomycin is not.
DNP is an uncoupler (speeds up ETC), and cyanide is a site-specific inhibitor of Complex IV (stops ETC).
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 79 (Book Page): This uncoupler causes electron transport to proceed at a rapid rate without establishing a proton gradient... energy is released as heat rather than being used to synthesize ATP.

category: Delineate special nutritional requirements during pregnancy, lactation, growth, and old age
statement: In planning a diet for an elderly patient with reduced appetite, a dietitian emphasizes the 'protein-sparing' effect of carbohydrates. What is the physiological basis for this recommendation?
options: A high-carbohydrate diet increases the PDCAAS score of dietary gelatin.
Adequate carbohydrate intake prevents the deamination of amino acids for gluconeogenesis.
Carbohydrates increase the biological value of plant proteins via complementation.
Carbohydrates are required to catalyze the synthesis of non-essential amino acids.
Carbohydrates prevent the fecal loss of nitrogen by slowing gastric emptying.
correctOption: Adequate carbohydrate intake prevents the deamination of amino acids for gluconeogenesis.
optionExplanations: The PDCAAS score is a property of the protein itself and its digestibility; it is not altered by the presence of carbohydrates.

When carbohydrate intake is sufficient (at least 130 g/day), the body does not need to use amino acids as a carbon source for gluconeogenesis to supply the brain with glucose, thus 'sparing' protein for tissue repair.
Complementation refers to mixing different plant proteins to provide a complete amino acid profile, not the interaction between carbohydrates and proteins.
Carbohydrates provide carbon skeletons, but the sparing effect specifically refers to the prevention of using amino acids for energy/glucose.
While fiber (a carbohydrate) affects gastric emptying, the 'protein-sparing' effect is a metabolic/gluconeogenic mechanism, not an absorptive one.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 369 (Book Page): carbohydrate is considered to be “protein-sparing,” because it allows amino acids to be used for repair and maintenance of tissue protein rather than for gluconeogenesis.

category: Outline treatment strategies
statement: A pediatric patient with Type Ia Glycogen Storage Disease (Von Gierke disease) suffers from severe fasting hypoglycemia. What is the metabolic rationale for the recommended treatment of nocturnal gastric infusions of glucose?
options: It provides a continuous exogenous source of glucose to maintain blood levels because the liver cannot dephosphorylate glucose 6-phosphate.
It stimulates protein phosphatase-1 to activate glycogen phosphorylase a.
It bypasses the need for the branching enzyme, amylo-(1->4)->(1->6)-transglucosidase.
It induces the synthesis of glucose 6-phosphate translocase in the endoplasmic reticulum.
It prevents the accumulation of glycogen in the lysosomal vacuoles.
correctOption: It provides a continuous exogenous source of glucose to maintain blood levels because the liver cannot dephosphorylate glucose 6-phosphate.
optionExplanations: Correct. Because the patient lacks glucose 6-phosphatase, the liver cannot release free glucose from glycogenolysis or gluconeogenesis. Frequent or continuous glucose prevents the brain-damaging hypoglycemia of fasting.
Incorrect. Protein phosphatase-1 *inactivates* glycogen phosphorylase by converting the 'a' form to the 'b' form.
Incorrect. Von Gierke disease involves glucose 6-phosphatase, not the branching enzyme (which is Andersen disease).
Incorrect. Type Ia is a deficiency of the phosphatase itself; Type Ib is the deficiency of the translocase. Infusing glucose does not induce these proteins.
Incorrect. Lysosomal glycogen accumulation is specific to Type II (Pompe disease).
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 122 (Book Page): Treatment: Nocturnal gastric infusions of glucose or regular administration of uncooked cornstarch... Affects liver and kidney. Fasting hypoglycemia–severe.

category: Differentiate between Kwashiorkor and Marasmus based on the given data
statement: In the context of Protein Energy Malnutrition (PEM), how does the 'protein-sparing effect' of carbohydrates influence the metabolic state of Kwashiorkor compared to Marasmus?
options: High carbohydrate intake in Kwashiorkor prevents the mobilization of muscle protein for gluconeogenesis.
Carbohydrates prevent the need for any amino acids in the diet.
Lack of carbohydrates in Kwashiorkor leads to massive emaciation without edema.
Carbohydrates in Marasmus are converted to visceral proteins.
Carbohydrates increase the excretion of nitrogen in the urine.
correctOption: High carbohydrate intake in Kwashiorkor prevents the mobilization of muscle protein for gluconeogenesis.
optionExplanations: In Kwashiorkor, carbohydrate intake is often sufficient to 'spare' protein from gluconeogenesis, but the overall lack of dietary amino acids still prevents synthesis of essential visceral proteins.
Amino acids are always essential for repair; carbohydrates only spare them from being burned for energy.
Kwashiorkor is defined by the presence of edema; the 'skin and bones' emaciation is the hallmark of Marasmus where calories (carbs) are absent.
In Marasmus, carbohydrates are severely deficient, so there is no protein-sparing effect, leading to massive breakdown of body protein for energy.
Carbohydrates decrease nitrogen excretion because they reduce the catabolism of proteins for energy production.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 361 (Book Page): carbohydrate is considered to be “protein-sparing,” because it allows amino acids to be used for repair and maintenance of tissue protein rather than for gluconeogenesis. ... [Kwashiorkor] diet consists predominantly of carbohydrates.

category: Elaborate key features of various transport systems for entry of glucose into cells
statement: An infant presents with severe osmotic diarrhea and dehydration shortly after birth. Lab tests reveal that while the child cannot absorb glucose or galactose, fructose absorption is completely normal. A mutation in the gene for which transport system is the most likely cause?
options: Sodium-independent facilitated diffusion
GLUT-1
GLUT-2
GLUT-5
SGLT-1
correctOption: SGLT-1
optionExplanations: The patient specifically fails to absorb sugars that require sodium-dependent transport (glucose/galactose), while the sodium-independent one (fructose) works fine.
GLUT-1 is for basal uptake in the brain and RBCs; a deficiency here would present with neurological issues, not intestinal malabsorption.
GLUT-2 is the basolateral exit for all three sugars; if it were deficient (Fanconi-Bickel syndrome), fructose absorption would also be impaired at the exit step.
GLUT-5 is the fructose transporter; the patient absorbs fructose normally, so GLUT-5 is functioning correctly.
SGLT-1 is responsible for the apical uptake of both glucose and galactose in the intestine. Its absence causes these sugars to remain in the lumen, causing osmotic diarrhea.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 89 (Book Page): This type of transport [SGLT] occurs in the epithelial cells of the intestine (see Page 79 (Book Page)), renal tubules, and choroid plexus. ... galactose and glucose are transported into the mucosal cells by an active, energy-requiring process ... SGLT-1.

category: Delineate special nutritional requirements during pregnancy, lactation, growth, and old age
statement: When defining the Dietary Reference Intakes (DRI), specific standards are adjusted for women during pregnancy and lactation. This adjustment is an example of the DRI incorporating which of the following variables?
options: Tolerable Upper Intake Levels based on body surface area
Physiological states that alter nutrient requirements
Adequate Intakes based on sedentary lifestyle habits
Standard deviations of nutrient absorption in elderly patients
Estimated Average Requirements for chronic disease prevention only
correctOption: Physiological states that alter nutrient requirements
optionExplanations: ULs are based on safety limits to avoid toxicity, not specifically on body surface area adjustments for pregnancy.
Correct. The DRI framework specifically accounts for life stages like pregnancy and lactation because these states significantly increase the demand for various macro- and micronutrients.
AIs for pregnancy are based on meeting the needs of that specific physiological state, not on sedentary habits which would actually decrease energy needs.
While age is a factor, the question specifically asks about pregnancy and lactation, which are distinct physiological states unrelated to elderly absorption statistics.
EARs are used to estimate group requirements and serve as the basis for RDAs, covering both health maintenance and deficiency prevention, not just chronic disease.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 358 (Book Page): The DRI consist of four dietary reference standards... designated for specific age groups, physiologic states, and gender... influenced by special factors, such as pregnancy and lactation in women.

category: Elaborate the glycerol 3-P shuttle and malate-aspartate shuttle for the transfer of reducing equivalents from cytosol into the mitochondria
statement: When comparing the bioenergetic yield of cytosolic NADH, why does the glycerol 3-phosphate shuttle result in a lower ATP yield than the malate-aspartate shuttle?
options: The glycerol 3-phosphate shuttle is only found in tissues with low metabolic rates.
The malate-aspartate shuttle utilizes a proton gradient to drive malate entry into the matrix.
The glycerol 3-phosphate shuttle consumes one ATP during the phosphorylation of dihydroxyacetone phosphate.
The reducing equivalents in the glycerol 3-phosphate shuttle bypass Complex I of the electron transport chain.
NADH produced in the matrix by the malate-aspartate shuttle has a lower reduction potential than FADH2.
correctOption: The reducing equivalents in the glycerol 3-phosphate shuttle bypass Complex I of the electron transport chain.
optionExplanations: Both shuttles are active in various tissues; for example, glycerol 3-P is prominent in the brain and muscle.
Malate entry is an exchange, but the ATP difference is purely due to the mitochondrial electron acceptor (NAD+ vs FAD).
No ATP is consumed in the shuttle itself; the difference is in the entry point of the electron transport chain.
The glycerol 3-phosphate shuttle transfers electrons to FAD (forming FADH2) which enters at CoQ, bypassing the proton-pumping Complex I, thus yielding fewer ATP.
NADH actually has a higher (more negative) reduction potential than FADH2, which is why it enters earlier in the chain.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 79 (Book Page): The glycerophosphate shuttle, therefore, results in the synthesis of two ATPs for each cytosolic NADH oxidized. This contrasts with the malate-aspartate shuttle... which produces NADH (rather than FADH2) in the mitochondrial matrix and, therefore, yields three ATPs.

category: Define and classify nutrients into macro and micronutrients
