category: Enlist the components of balanced diet and elaborate the importance of each component
statement: In the Dietary Reference Intakes (DRI), which criteria represents the highest average daily nutrient intake level that is likely to pose no risk of adverse health effects to almost all individuals?
options: Acceptable Macronutrient Distribution Range (AMDR).
Tolerable Upper Intake Level (UL).
Estimated Average Requirement (EAR).
Adequate Intake (AI).
Recommended Dietary Allowance (RDA).
correctOption: Tolerable Upper Intake Level (UL).
optionExplanations: AMDR refers to the percentage of total calories from macronutrients (fats, proteins, carbs), not a specific nutrient intake ceiling.
The UL is specifically designed to warn against excessive intake from fortified foods and supplements that could cause toxicity.
The EAR meets the requirement of only 50% of the population, not the safety threshold.
The AI is a recommended intake used when an RDA cannot be determined; it is not a safety limit.
The RDA is the intake target to meet the needs of 97-98% of people, not the safety ceiling.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 358 (Book Page): The UL is the highest average daily nutrient intake level that is likely to pose no risk of adverse health effects to almost all individuals in the general population.

category: Suggest dietary advice for patients suffering from diabetes mellitus, hypertension, obesity, renal disease, lactose intolerance, gluten enteropathy, hypercholesterolemia, and hemorrhoids
statement: A 45-year-old male is advised to increase his daily fiber intake to manage chronic hemorrhoids. According to nutritional guidelines for adults, what is the specific Adequate Intake (AI) of total fiber recommended for a male of this age to improve bowel motility and reduce luminal pressure?
options: 15 grams per day
25 grams per day
50 grams per day
130 grams per day
38 grams per day
correctOption: 38 grams per day
optionExplanations: 15 grams per day represents the average fiber intake in many Western diets, which is considered inadequate for preventing conditions like constipation or hemorrhoids.
25 grams per day is the recommended Adequate Intake (AI) for adult women, not men.
50 grams per day exceeds the standard AI and is often used as a therapeutic target for reversing specific pathologies like severe diverticulosis, but it is not the standard AI.
130 grams per day is the RDA for total carbohydrates for adults based on brain glucose requirements, not the recommendation for dietary fiber.
38 grams per day is the specific AI for adult men. Fiber reduces hemorrhoidal symptoms by drawing fluid into the intestinal lumen, increasing motility, and softening stools.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 358 (Book Page): The recommended daily fiber intake (AI) is 25 g/day for women and 38 g/day for men. However, most American diets are far lower in fiber—approximately 15 g/day.

category: Describe the TCA cycle along with regulation & significance
statement: A researcher observes that in anaplerotic reactions, pyruvate can be carboxylated to replenish oxaloacetate (OAA) for the TCA cycle. Which allosteric activator is required for this reaction to occur in the liver?
options: Acetyl CoA
Malate
Citrate
Glutamate
NADH
correctOption: Acetyl CoA
optionExplanations: Acetyl CoA is the obligate activator for pyruvate carboxylase; it signals the need for more OAA to either condense with acetyl CoA or enter gluconeogenesis.
Malate is an intermediate that can be oxidized to OAA, but it is not the regulatory signal that activates pyruvate carboxylase.
Citrate inhibits glycolysis and citrate synthase but does not activate pyruvate carboxylase.
Glutamate can be converted to alpha-ketoglutarate as an anaplerotic source, but it does not regulate the pyruvate carboxylase enzyme.
NADH inhibits various dehydrogenases in the TCA cycle but does not serve as an activator for the anaplerotic carboxylation of pyruvate.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 97 (Book Page): Carboxylation of pyruvate to oxaloacetate (OAA) by pyruvate carboxylase is a biotin-dependent reaction... Activated by acetyl CoA.

category: Define energy balance
statement: A public health researcher is assessing the nutritional adequacy of a community. When comparing the Estimated Average Requirement (EAR) and the Recommended Dietary Allowance (RDA) for a specific nutrient, what is the fundamental diagnostic difference between these two standards?
options: The EAR is used as the foundation to set the RDA, which covers nearly all healthy individuals.
The EAR is set at 2 standard deviations above the RDA.
The RDA meets the requirements of 50% of the population, whereas the EAR meets 98%.
The RDA is a minimal requirement, while the EAR provides a margin of safety.
The EAR is designated only when scientific evidence is insufficient to calculate an Adequate Intake.
correctOption: The EAR is used as the foundation to set the RDA, which covers nearly all healthy individuals.
optionExplanations: Correct; the EAR is the statistical median used to calculate the RDA, which is then set higher to ensure coverage for almost everyone in the group.
This is mathematically reversed; the RDA is actually set at 2 standard deviations above the EAR.
The EAR meets the requirements of 50% (half) of the population, while the RDA is designed to meet the requirements of 97-98%.
Neither is a minimal requirement; the EAR is an average and the RDA specifically provides the margin of safety for the population.
Adequate Intake (AI) is used when the EAR/RDA cannot be determined, not the other way around.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 357 (Book Page): The EAR is the average daily nutrient intake level estimated to meet the requirement of one half of the healthy individuals... The EAR serves as the foundation for setting the RDA. If the standard deviation (SD) of the EAR is available... the RDA is set at 2 SDs above the EAR, that is, RDA = EAR + 2SD.

category: Describe the effect of arsenic poisoning on carbohydrate metabolism and ATP production
statement: Which specific functional group in the structure of reduced lipoic acid is the target for the formation of a stable, toxic complex with trivalent arsenic?
options: Carboxyl group
Phosphate group
Hydroxyl group
Amino group
Thiol (–SH) group
correctOption: Thiol (–SH) group
optionExplanations: The carboxyl group of lipoic acid is used to attach the coenzyme to the lysine residue of the enzyme (forming lipoamide), not for arsenic binding.
Phosphate groups are the target of pentavalent arsenate competition in glycolysis, but trivalent arsenite targets thiol groups.
Hydroxyl groups are not the primary target for the stable, covalent-like bonding seen with trivalent arsenic in this metabolic context.
Lipoic acid does not contain an amino group that serves as a target for arsenic toxicity in carbohydrate metabolism.
Arsenite reacts with reduced lipoic acid's two sulfhydryl (thiol) groups to form a stable six-membered ring, which prevents the coenzyme from functioning in the transfer of acyl groups.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 103 (Book Page): Arsenite (the trivalent form of arsenic) forms a stable complex with the thiol (–SH) groups of lipoic acid, making that compound unavailable to serve as a coenzyme.

category: Categorize individuals into underweight, normal, overweight, obese, and morbidly obese based on theirs BMI values
statement: A 45-year-old female is 1.60 meters tall and weighs 72 kilograms. After calculating her Body Mass Index (BMI), a physician must categorize her status to determine her risk for coronary heart disease (CHD). What is her correct BMI classification?
options: Obese (Class I)
Normal weight
Underweight
Overweight
Obese (Class II)
correctOption: Overweight
optionExplanations: Obese Class I begins at a BMI of 30.0 kg/m². This patient's BMI of 28.1 does not yet reach the threshold for clinical obesity.
Normal weight requires a BMI below 25.0 kg/m². In this case, the BMI is approximately 28.1 (72 / 1.6²), which exceeds the normal threshold.
Underweight categorization would require a BMI below 18.5 kg/m², which is significantly lower than this patient's calculated value of 28.1.
The BMI is calculated as Weight(kg) / Height(m)². Here, 72 / (1.6 * 1.6) = 28.125 kg/m². The range for 'Overweight' is 25.0 to 29.9 kg/m², placing her in this category.
Obese Class II begins at a BMI of 35.0 kg/m², which is much higher than the calculated 28.1 for this individual.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 360 (Book Page): Although caloric intake in the United States has shown a modest increase since 1971, the incidence of obesity has dramatically increased (see Page 341 (Book Page)).

category: Delineate special nutritional requirements during pregnancy, lactation, growth, and old age
statement: A 28-year-old woman in her second trimester of pregnancy requires specific nutritional adjustments to support fetal development. Regarding protein metabolism in this physiological state, which nitrogen balance status is typically observed?
options: Positive nitrogen balance
Negative nitrogen balance
Equilibrium
Obligatory nitrogen loss
Zero nitrogen balance
correctOption: Positive nitrogen balance
optionExplanations: Positive nitrogen balance is the hallmark of anabolic states like pregnancy, where nitrogen intake exceeds excretion to facilitate the accretion of new maternal and fetal protein structures.
Negative nitrogen balance occurs when nitrogen loss exceeds intake, such as during trauma, starvation, or burns, which would be detrimental to fetal health and maternal tissue maintenance.
Nitrogen equilibrium is characteristic of healthy, non-growing adults where nitrogen intake equals excretion; however, pregnancy requires a net gain in nitrogen for fetal tissue synthesis.
Obligatory nitrogen loss refers to the baseline nitrogen excreted even when intake is zero; it does not describe the overall metabolic balance in a pregnant individual.
Zero nitrogen balance is another term for equilibrium and does not reflect the net protein synthesis and tissue growth essential for a healthy pregnancy.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 360 (Book Page): Positive nitrogen balance... occurs when nitrogen intake exceeds nitrogen excretion. It is observed during situations in which tissue growth occurs, for example, in childhood, pregnancy, or during recovery from an emaciating illness.

category: Calculate the number of ATP produced during aerobic and anaerobic glycolysis
statement: In a patient with a hereditary deficiency of Glucose 6-phosphate Translocase (Type Ib Glycogen Storage Disease), the liver is unable to maintain blood glucose during fasting. When this patient's hepatocytes attempt to produce glucose from pyruvate via gluconeogenesis, what is the total number of high-energy phosphate bonds (ATP/GTP) required to synthesize one molecule of glucose?
options: 8 bonds
4 bonds
6 bonds
10 bonds
2 bonds
correctOption: 6 bonds
optionExplanations: Eight bonds is not the standard stoichiometric requirement for the conversion of pyruvate to glucose.
Four bonds would be insufficient to overcome the three irreversible steps of glycolysis.
The synthesis of one glucose from two pyruvates requires 4 ATP (2 at pyruvate carboxylase, 2 at phosphoglycerate kinase) and 2 GTP (at PEP-carboxykinase), totaling 6 high-energy bonds.
Ten bonds exceeds the biochemical requirement identified in the established pathway for gluconeogenesis from pyruvate.
Two bonds is the net gain of anaerobic glycolysis, but the reversal (gluconeogenesis) is much more energetically expensive due to the bypass reactions.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 113 (Book Page): The stoichiometry of gluconeogenesis from pyruvate couples the cleavage of six high-energy phosphate bonds... with the formation of each molecule of glucose.

category: Define Malnutrition
coreConcept: Mechanism of Fatty Liver in Malnutrition
statement: In the pathological progression of kwashiorkor, an enlarged fatty liver is frequently identified. What is the mechanistic step that explains why lipids accumulate specifically in the liver during protein deprivation?
options: Inhibition of the TCA cycle resulting in citrate shunting to the cytoplasm
Increased synthesis of fatty acids from excess dietary carbohydrates
Accelerated breakdown of adipose tissue lipids specifically by the liver
Decreased synthesis of visceral proteins required for lipoprotein assembly and export
Impaired β-oxidation of fatty acids due to carnitine deficiency
correctOption: Decreased synthesis of visceral proteins required for lipoprotein assembly and export
optionExplanations: The text links the enlarged fatty liver in kwashiorkor to the visceral protein deficiency, not to a primary metabolic blockage of the TCA cycle.
While high carbohydrates can drive lipogenesis, the specific accumulation of fat (fatty liver) in kwashiorkor is due to the inability to export fats, not just their synthesis.

Fatty liver in kwashiorkor results from the liver's failure to export its own lipid stores due to protein lack, rather than an accelerated uptake from adipose tissue, which is actually more characteristic of marasmus-level wasting.

Hepatocytes require apolipoproteins (visceral proteins) to package and export triacylglycerols as VLDL. In kwashiorkor, the severe lack of protein inhibits visceral protein synthesis, trapping lipids in the liver and causing hepatomegaly.
Carnitine deficiency can affect fatty acid transport, but it is not the primary diagnostic mechanism mentioned for the enlarged fatty liver seen in kwashiorkor.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 361 (Book Page): Kwashiorkor occurs when protein deprivation is relatively greater than the reduction in total calories. Protein deprivation is associated with severely decreased synthesis of visceral protein.

category: Explain the significance of Cori cycle and glucosealanine cycle
coreConcept: Nitrogen transport significance of the Glucose-Alanine cycle
statement: In the glucose-alanine cycle, the transfer of alanine from the skeletal muscle to the liver serves a critical dual purpose. Beyond providing a carbon skeleton for gluconeogenesis, what is the physiological significance of this transport?
options: It increases the rate of ketone body synthesis in the liver to provide brain fuel.
It acts as a buffer to maintain muscle pH by removing excess carbonic acid.
It facilitates the direct oxidation of alanine in the hepatic TCA cycle to generate 38 ATP.
It provides a safe vehicle for the transport of muscle nitrogen to the liver for urea synthesis.
It triggers the release of insulin from the pancreatic beta cells.
correctOption: It provides a safe vehicle for the transport of muscle nitrogen to the liver for urea synthesis.
optionExplanations: The glucose-alanine cycle provides glucose, which actually suppresses ketogenesis; ketone bodies are derived from fatty acid oxidation or ketogenic amino acids like leucine/lysine, not primarily from the alanine cycle.
Alanine transport is not a primary buffer for carbonic acid; the bicarbonate and phosphate systems, along with hemoglobin, handle pH buffering in muscle.
While alanine can be converted to pyruvate and enter the TCA cycle, its primary significance in the 'cycle' named is to be converted into glucose (gluconeogenesis) to be sent back to the muscle.

The glucose-alanine cycle is essential for transporting the amino groups (nitrogen) derived from muscle protein catabolism to the liver. Alanine is a non-toxic nitrogen carrier; in the liver, it is transaminated to pyruvate, and the nitrogen enters the urea cycle for excretion.

Alanine can stimulate some insulin release, but in the physiological context of the glucose-alanine cycle (starvation/fasting), insulin levels are actually low to favor gluconeogenesis and muscle protein breakdown.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 114 (Book Page): Decreased levels of insulin favor mobilization of amino acids from muscle protein, and provide the carbon skeletons for gluconeogenesis. Page 109 (Book Page): It is the final pathway where the oxidative metabolism of carbohydrates, amino acids, and fatty acids converge... The cycle occurs totally in the mitochondria.

category: Clearly differentiate between substrate level phosphorylation and oxidative phosphorylation
statement: Which of the following characteristics is uniquely definitive of substrate-level phosphorylation (SLP) compared to oxidative phosphorylation (OxPhos)?
options: The direct transfer of a high-energy phosphate group from a metabolic intermediate to ADP or GDP.
The requirement of a functional electron transport chain to create a chemiosmotic gradient.
The dependence on the reduction of nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD+) as a prerequisite for phosphate transfer.
The utilization of the F1/Fo ATP synthase complex to dissipate a transmembrane proton motive force.
The necessity of molecular oxygen acting as the final electron acceptor in the mitochondrial matrix.
correctOption: The direct transfer of a high-energy phosphate group from a metabolic intermediate to ADP or GDP.
optionExplanations: Substrate-level phosphorylation is defined by the direct, enzyme-catalyzed transfer of a phosphoryl group from a high-energy metabolic intermediate (like phosphoenolpyruvate or 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate) directly to ADP or GDP, occurring independently of the ETC.

This describes oxidative phosphorylation. OxPhos relies on the electron transport chain (ETC) to pump protons across the inner mitochondrial membrane, creating a gradient that subsequently drives ATP synthesis via ATP synthase.

While many pathways containing SLP (like glycolysis) involve NAD+ reduction, the phosphorylation event itself in SLP does not depend on NAD+. Conversely, OxPhos is strictly dependent on the oxidation of NADH or FADH2 to provide electrons for the proton pump.

The F1/Fo ATP synthase (Complex V) is the molecular machine of oxidative phosphorylation. It uses the energy from the reentry of protons into the matrix to synthesize ATP; SLP does not involve this complex.

This is a characteristic of oxidative phosphorylation (aerobic respiration). Oxygen is the final electron acceptor in the respiratory chain, whereas substrate-level phosphorylation can occur in the absence of oxygen (anaerobic conditions).
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 94 (Book Page): This is an example of substrate-level phosphorylation, in which the energy needed for the production of a high-energy phosphate comes from a substrate rather than from the electron transport chain.

category: Define basal metabolic rate (BMR)
statement: A sedentary individual has a total daily energy expenditure (TDEE). If their physical activity accounts for 30% of this total and the thermic effect of food accounts for 10%, which of the following is true regarding their Resting Metabolic Rate (RMR)?
options: The RMR is calculated by subtracting the physical activity from the thermic effect of food.
The RMR is negligible compared to the caloric cost of physical activity.
The RMR is equal to the energy expended during physical activity.
The RMR accounts for 100% of the total caloric requirement in this sedentary state.
The RMR accounts for approximately 60% of their total energy expenditure.
correctOption: The RMR accounts for approximately 60% of their total energy expenditure.
optionExplanations: RMR is an independent component of the energy budget; it is not derived by subtracting TEF and activity from each other, but rather they are all added to reach the TDEE.
In sedentary individuals, the RMR is actually the dominant component (50-70%), making physical activity the smaller contributor by comparison.
In this profile, RMR (60%) is twice as large as physical activity (30%), not equal to it.
RMR is never 100% of TDEE because even sedentary individuals have some physical activity and a thermic response to the food they must eat to survive.
Correct. In a typical energy budget (as shown for a 50kg woman), RMR (60%) plus TEF (10%) plus Physical Activity (30%) equals the 100% total expenditure.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 359 (Book Page): Resting metabolic rate 1300 kcal = 60% ... Thermic effect of food 210 kcal = 10% ... Physical activity 630 kcal = 30%.

category: Describe the reactions, regulation, and biomedical importance of uronic acid pathway and sorbitol pathway
statement: Which of the following describes the correct metabolic sequence for the production of fructose from glucose in the liver?
options: Glucose -> Glyceraldehyde 3-P -> Dihydroxyacetone-P -> Fructose
Glucose -> Glucose 6-P -> Fructose 6-P -> Fructose
Glucose -> Glucuronate -> Xylulose -> Fructose
Glucose -> UDP-Glucose -> UDP-Fructose -> Fructose
Glucose -> Sorbitol -> Fructose
correctOption: Glucose -> Sorbitol -> Fructose
optionExplanations: This represents the middle of the glycolytic pathway; while DHAP can be converted to fructose 1,6-bisphosphate in gluconeogenesis, it is not the polyol pathway.
This sequence describes parts of glycolysis or gluconeogenesis; however, the direct conversion of glucose 6-P to fructose 6-P is an isomerization, not the polyol pathway.
This represents parts of the uronic acid pathway (forming xylulose) but xylulose is not a standard precursor for direct fructose production in humans.
UDP-glucose is used in glycogen synthesis and the uronic acid pathway; it is not converted into a 'UDP-fructose' intermediate for fructose synthesis.
The polyol pathway is a two-step process: First, glucose is reduced to sorbitol (by aldose reductase), and second, sorbitol is oxidized to fructose (by sorbitol dehydrogenase).
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 131 (Book Page): The two-reaction pathway from glucose to fructose... aldose reductase reduces glucose, producing sorbitol... sorbitol dehydrogenase... can oxidize the sorbitol to produce fructose.

category: Define energy balance
statement: When analyzing the caloric density of different dietary components for an energy balance study, which nutrient provides the highest amount of energy per gram upon metabolic combustion?
options: Fats
Proteins
Ethanol
Monosaccharides
Polysaccharides
correctOption: Fats
optionExplanations: Fats are the most energy-dense macronutrient, yielding 9 kcal/g. This high energy yield is due to their reduced chemical state, which allows for more extensive oxidation compared to the more oxidized states of carbohydrates and proteins.
Proteins yield approximately 4 kcal/g, similar to carbohydrates. While essential for structure and nitrogen balance, they are not the most concentrated source of metabolic energy compared to lipids.
Ethanol has an intermediate energy density of 7 kcal/g. While higher than carbohydrates and proteins, it is still lower than the 9 kcal/g provided by lipids.

Monosaccharides, like all carbohydrates, provide 4 kcal/g. They are essential for rapid energy but cannot match the caloric concentration of triacylglycerols which serve as the primary long-term energy reservoir.
Polysaccharides are carbohydrates and yield approximately 4 kcal/g. This is significantly less than the 9 kcal/g yielded by fats, making them less energy-dense for storage or intake purposes.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 359 (Book Page): Note that the energy content of fat is more than twice that of carbohydrate or protein, whereas the energy content of ethanol is intermediate between those of fat and carbohydrate.

category: Delineate special nutritional requirements during pregnancy, lactation, growth, and old age
statement: Which Dietary Reference Intake (DRI) standard is defined as the average daily nutrient intake level estimated to meet the requirement of one-half of the healthy individuals in a particular life stage and gender group?
options: Estimated Average Requirement (EAR)
Estimated Energy Requirement (EER)
Adequate Intake (AI)
Tolerable Upper Intake Level (UL)
Recommended Dietary Allowance (RDA)
correctOption: Estimated Average Requirement (EAR)
optionExplanations: The EAR specifically represents the median requirement of a population, serving as the foundation to calculate the RDA by adding two standard deviations.
The EER is the average dietary energy intake predicted to maintain energy balance in a healthy adult based on specific physical variables.
The AI is set only when sufficient scientific evidence is unavailable to calculate an EAR or RDA, based on observed estimates of intake.
The UL is the highest average daily intake likely to pose no risk of adverse health effects, intended to prevent toxicity rather than define requirements.
The RDA is the average daily dietary intake level sufficient to meet the nutrient requirements of nearly all (97–98%) individuals, not just 50%.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 357 (Book Page): Estimated Average Requirement (EAR): The EAR is the average daily nutrient intake level estimated to meet the requirement of one half of the healthy individuals in a particular life stage and gender group.

category: Delineate special nutritional requirements during pregnancy, lactation, growth, and old age
statement: To support the rapid rate of growth and tissue accretion during infancy, what is the recommended daily protein intake for infants?
options: 2.0 g/kg/day
0.5 g/kg/day
3.5 g/kg/day
0.8 g/kg/day
1.2 g/kg/day
correctOption: 2.0 g/kg/day
optionExplanations: The requirement of 2.0 g/kg/day in infants reflects the intensive protein synthesis required for skeletal, muscular, and organ development during the first year of life.
An intake of 0.5 g/kg/day is well below the adult RDA and is insufficient to support the high anabolic demands of infant development.
3.5 g/kg/day is excessively high and could place an unnecessary solute load on the developing renal system of a young infant.
0.8 g/kg/day is the RDA for healthy adults in maintenance mode, which does not account for the additional nitrogen needed for rapid growth in infants.
1.2 g/kg/day may be appropriate for some athletes, but infants require a higher relative concentration of protein per kilogram of body weight to support doubling their size.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 360 (Book Page): To support growth, infants should consume 2 g/kg/day.

category: Suggest dietary advice for patients suffering from diabetes mellitus, hypertension, obesity, renal disease, lactose intolerance, gluten enteropathy, hypercholesterolemia, and hemorrhoids
statement: A patient with gluten enteropathy must strictly avoid wheat-based products. When planning a balanced diet for this patient, which combination of plant-based proteins would provide the highest biologic value by compensating for individual amino acid deficiencies?
options: Corn and rice, as both are rich in lysine.
Gelatin and wheat, because they provide all essential amino acids.
Soybean protein alone, as it already has a PDCAAS of 1.00.
Wheat and kidney beans, though wheat must be replaced with another methionine-rich grain for this patient.
Corn and gelatin, because they are both low in sulfur-containing amino acids.
correctOption: Soybean protein alone, as it already has a PDCAAS of 1.00.
optionExplanations: Corn and rice are generally deficient in lysine, so they do not complement each other well; they require a lysine-rich source like beans.
Gelatin is an animal protein of very low biologic value (0.08) and is deficient in several essential amino acids; wheat is excluded in gluten enteropathy.
Soybean protein is a unique plant protein that contains a balanced profile of all nine essential amino acids, giving it a score equivalent to animal proteins (1.00).
The wheat/bean combination is a classic example of complementarity, but since the patient has gluten enteropathy (Celiac disease), they must use gluten-free grains to provide the methionine.
A combination of two proteins both low in the same amino acids (sulfur-containing) would not improve the biologic value; complementarity requires different deficiencies.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 359 (Book Page)-368: Soybean protein [has a] PDCAAS value [of] 1.00. ... wheat (lysine-deficient but methionine-rich) may be combined with kidney beans (methionine-poor but lysine-rich) to produce an improved biologic value.

category: Explain how ethanol consumption causes hypoglycemia and fatty liver
statement: A medical student is studying the metabolic consequences of alcohol ingestion. What is the immediate effect of ethanol oxidation by alcohol dehydrogenase on the hepatic coenzyme pool?
options: Increase in the NADH/NAD+ ratio in the cytosol
Selective depletion of the NADPH pool in the mitochondria
Decrease in the NADH/NAD+ ratio in the cytosol
Increase in the NAD+/NADH ratio in the cytosol
Increase in the FAD/FADH2 ratio in the mitochondria
correctOption: Increase in the NADH/NAD+ ratio in the cytosol
optionExplanations: Correct. The oxidation of ethanol by alcohol dehydrogenase in the cytosol results in the reduction of NAD+ to NADH, thereby increasing the NADH/NAD+ ratio, which has profound effects on downstream metabolic pathways.
Incorrect. Alcohol dehydrogenase is specific for NAD+ as a coenzyme in the cytosol, and while ethanol can affect NADPH via the microsomal system, the primary immediate effect is on the NADH pool.
Incorrect. The ratio of NADH to NAD+ increases because the enzyme alcohol dehydrogenase generates NADH as it oxidizes ethanol to acetaldehyde.
Incorrect. Ethanol metabolism by alcohol dehydrogenase actually reduces NAD+ to NADH, which decreases the NAD+/NADH ratio, rather than increasing it.
Incorrect. While ethanol metabolism eventually affects mitochondrial redox states, the primary and direct effect of the alcohol dehydrogenase reaction is the reduction of NAD+ to NADH in the cytosol.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 143 (Book Page): The metabolism of ethanol by alcohol dehydrogenase (ADH) produces NADH. ... The increase in NADH as ethanol is oxidized, will decrease the availability of OAA because the reversible oxidation of malate to OAA by malate dehydrogenase of the TCA cycle is driven in the reverse direction by the high availability of NADH.

category: Elaborate the reaction catalyzed by pyruvate dehydrogenase complex (PDH) along with regulation and significance
statement: A patient with chronic alcoholism presents with ataxia and confusion. The physician diagnoses Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome, noting that the brain's inability to produce sufficient ATP is due to an inactive PDH complex. Which specific enzyme component and its associated vitamin-derived coenzyme are primarily affected by this patient's nutritional deficiency?
options: E1 (Pyruvate decarboxylase) and Thiamine.
Pyruvate carboxylase and Biotin.
E2 (Dihydrolipoyl transacetylase) and Riboflavin.
E3 (Dihydrolipoyl dehydrogenase) and Niacin.
E1 (Pyruvate decarboxylase) and Pantothenic acid.
correctOption: E1 (Pyruvate decarboxylase) and Thiamine.
optionExplanations: Thiamine is the precursor for TPP, which is the essential coenzyme for the E1 (decarboxylase) component; its deficiency is classic in alcoholic patients.
Pyruvate carboxylase is a different enzyme that converts pyruvate to oxaloacetate; while it is important, it is not the 'decarboxylase' component of PDH.
E2 requires lipoic acid and CoA (Pantothenic acid); Riboflavin is the precursor for FAD used in E3.
Niacin is the precursor for NAD+, and while E3 uses it, the primary 'bottleneck' in thiamine deficiency is the E1 decarboxylation step.
Pantothenic acid is the precursor for Coenzyme A, which is used by E2, not the E1 decarboxylase component.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 102 (Book Page): Wernicke-Korsakoff, an encephalopathy-psychosis syndrome due to thiamine deficiency, may be seen with alcohol abuse. [Note: E1 requires thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP)]

category: Discuss the importance of HMP shunt
statement: A 26-year-old male of African descent is prescribed primaquine for malaria prophylaxis. Five days later, he presents with dark, tea-colored urine and scleral icterus. A blood smear reveals cells with insoluble inclusions of denatured hemoglobin. What is the fundamental biochemical defect leading to this presentation?
options: Inability to maintain the reduced glutathione pool required to detoxify reactive oxygen species.
Deficiency in 6-phosphogluconate dehydrogenase leading to ribose accumulation and osmotic lysis.
Failure of the cytochrome P450 system to metabolize primaquine into a non-toxic form.
Impaired synthesis of N-acetyllactosamine on the erythrocyte membrane.
Inability of the erythrocyte to generate ATP through the mitochondrial electron transport chain.
correctOption: Inability to maintain the reduced glutathione pool required to detoxify reactive oxygen species.
optionExplanations: G6PD deficiency prevents the generation of NADPH, which is necessary for glutathione reductase to reduce oxidized glutathione (GSSG) back to GSH. Without GSH, glutathione peroxidase cannot neutralize peroxides, leading to Heinz body formation and hemolysis.
The primary issue is the failure to produce NADPH at the G6PD step, not an accumulation of ribose or failure at the second dehydrogenase step.
While P450 is involved in drug metabolism, the hemolytic crisis in G6PD deficiency is specifically due to the erythrocyte's inability to handle oxidative stress caused by the drug.
N-acetyllactosamine synthesis is related to galactose metabolism and protein A, not the oxidative stress response of the HMP shunt.
Mature erythrocytes lack mitochondria and depend on glycolysis for ATP, but this is not the defect in G6PD deficiency.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 152 (Book Page): Diminished G6PD activity impairs the ability of the cell to form the NADPH that is essential for the maintenance of the reduced glutathione pool. This results in a decrease in the cellular detoxification of free radicals and peroxides formed within the cell.

category: Outline treatment strategies
coreConcept: Therapeutic Mechanism of Cornstarch in Von Gierke Disease
statement: What is the biochemical rationale for the administration of uncooked cornstarch as a treatment strategy for patients with Type Ia Glycogen Storage Disease?
options: It serves to increase the synthesis of glycogen branches by activating the 4:6 transferase enzyme.
It inhibits glucose 6-phosphatase, preventing excessive glycogen breakdown in the liver.
It provides a slow-release source of glucose to maintain euglycemia during fasting.
It facilitates the transport of glucose 6-phosphate across the endoplasmic reticulum membrane.
It acts as an allosteric activator of glycogen phosphorylase to bypass the metabolic block.
correctOption: It provides a slow-release source of glucose to maintain euglycemia during fasting.
optionExplanations: The treatment aims to manage blood glucose levels, not to alter the structure of glycogen branches. Branching enzymes are typically normal in Type Ia GSD.
Von Gierke disease is defined by a deficiency or lack of glucose 6-phosphatase. Inhibiting it further would be counterproductive and medically dangerous.

Correct. Uncooked cornstarch is a complex carbohydrate that is digested slowly in the gut. This provides a steady, sustained release of glucose into the bloodstream, preventing the severe fasting hypoglycemia characteristic of Type Ia GSD.
This describes the function of glucose 6-phosphate translocase. A deficiency in that translocase causes Type Ib GSD, and cornstarch does not restore its transport activity.

Activating glycogen phosphorylase would increase the production of glucose 1-phosphate and then glucose 6-phosphate, but without the phosphatase enzyme, this glucose cannot be released into the blood.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 122 (Book Page): Treatment: Nocturnal gastric infusions of glucose or regular administration of uncooked cornstarch

category: Elaborate key features of various transport systems for entry of glucose into cells
statement: GLUT-2 possesses a unique bidirectional capability in hepatocytes. How does this transporter behave during the fasting state in a healthy individual?
options: It couples with sodium to pull glucose from the bile duct.
It translocates to intracellular vesicles to prevent glucose loss.
It increases its affinity for glucose to capture trace amounts from blood.
It switches its specificity to transport ketone bodies instead of glucose.
It facilitates the efflux of glucose from the liver into the portal circulation.
correctOption: It facilitates the efflux of glucose from the liver into the portal circulation.
optionExplanations: Sodium-coupled transport (SGLT) is used for glucose reabsorption in the kidney and uptake in the intestine, not for the facilitated efflux of glucose from the liver via GLUT-2.
Unlike GLUT-4, GLUT-2 is constitutively expressed on the plasma membrane and does not rely on insulin-mediated translocation for its functional presence.
GLUT-2 has a high KM (low affinity), which is a fixed kinetic property; it does not increase its affinity during fasting, which actually aids in glucose release.
GLUT transporters are specific to hexoses; ketone body transport is handled by different specialized monocarboxylate transporters.
During fasting, liver glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis raise intracellular glucose levels; GLUT-2 facilitates the movement of this glucose down its gradient out of the hepatocyte.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 89 (Book Page): GLUT-2, which is found in the liver and kidney, can either transport glucose into these cells when blood glucose levels are high, or transport glucose from these cells when blood glucose levels are low (for example, during fasting).

category: Compare key features of aerobic and anaerobic glycolysis
statement: A 58-year-old male is brought to the emergency department with severe chest pain and signs of systemic shock. Labs reveal a significantly elevated plasma lactate level and a blood pH of 7.21. Which cellular event best explains this patient's metabolic state?
options: Impaired oxidative phosphorylation due to inadequate oxygen delivery
Increased activity of the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex
Upregulation of the malate-aspartate shuttle in cardiac tissue
Inhibition of the lactate dehydrogenase enzyme by low pH
Excessive transport of reducing equivalents into the mitochondrial matrix
correctOption: Impaired oxidative phosphorylation due to inadequate oxygen delivery
optionExplanations: Systemic shock reduces oxygen delivery to tissues, impairing oxidative phosphorylation. Cells shift to anaerobic glycolysis to produce ATP, leading to excessive lactate production and lactic acidosis.
In shock, the PDH complex is often bypassed or inhibited by high NADH levels because the lack of oxygen prevents the further oxidation of acetyl CoA.
The malate-aspartate shuttle requires a functional electron transport chain to maintain the NAD+/NADH gradient; in shock, this process is stalled rather than upregulated.
Lactate dehydrogenase remains active in low pH states; in fact, its continued operation is what produces the lactic acid that lowers the pH in the first place.
In anoxic or shock states, the mitochondria cannot accept reducing equivalents because the electron transport chain is backed up due to a lack of oxygen.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 96 (Book Page): The failure to bring adequate amounts of oxygen to the tissues results in impaired oxidative phosphorylation and decreased ATP synthesis. To survive, the cells use anaerobic glycolysis as a backup... producing lactic acid.

category: Define energy balance
statement: Which component of the diet is considered a non-essential nutrient because its carbon skeletons can be synthesized from the metabolism of certain amino acids?
options: Minerals
Essential fatty acids
Vitamins
Carbohydrate
Protein
correctOption: Carbohydrate
optionExplanations: Minerals are inorganic elements that are essential for various body functions and must be ingested.
Essential fatty acids (like linoleic and alpha-linolenic acid) cannot be synthesized by the body and must be obtained from the diet.
Vitamins are organic compounds required in small amounts that the body cannot synthesize in sufficient quantities, making them essential.
Carbohydrates are technically non-essential because the body can produce glucose from glucogenic amino acids and glycerol through gluconeogenesis.
While the body can recycle amino acids, it cannot synthesize 'essential' amino acids, meaning dietary protein is an absolute requirement.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 369 (Book Page): Carbohydrates are not essential nutrients, because the carbon skeletons of most amino acids can be converted into glucose (see Page 110 (Book Page)).

category: Delineate special nutritional requirements during pregnancy, lactation, growth, and old age
statement: A woman who is currently breastfeeding her 3-month-old infant asks about her own dietary protein needs. Beyond the standard adult RDA, what additional daily amount of protein is recommended to support the metabolic demands of lactation?
options: 60 g/day
30 g/day
10 g/day
5 g/day
No additional protein is required if she is sedentary.
correctOption: 30 g/day
optionExplanations: 60 g/day in addition to the base RDA (56g) would be over 115g total, which is generally excessive unless the woman is a heavy athlete.
The guidelines specify an additional 30 g of protein per day to ensure the mother can produce high-quality milk without depleting her own lean tissue stores.
10 g/day is still below the established guidelines for lactating women.
5 g/day is insufficient to cover the protein secreted in breast milk and the metabolic costs of its production.
Even sedentary lactating women have significantly increased protein needs to provide the necessary amino acids for the infant's growth via milk.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 360 (Book Page): Women who are pregnant or lactating require up to 30 g/day in addition to their basal requirements.

category: Describe the TCA cycle along with regulation & significance
statement: In the TCA cycle, most energy is captured as reduced coenzymes. However, one specific step produces a high-energy phosphate compound directly. Which of the following is true regarding this reaction?
options: It produces ATP via the Electron Transport Chain
It is the primary rate-limiting step of the cycle
It is catalyzed by the enzyme Succinate Thiokinase
It involves the condensation of acetyl CoA with oxaloacetate
It requires the reduction of FAD to FADH2
correctOption: It is catalyzed by the enzyme Succinate Thiokinase
optionExplanations: The question specifies direct production; ATP produced via the ETC is 'oxidative phosphorylation', whereas this reaction happens directly in the matrix.
Isocitrate dehydrogenase, not succinate thiokinase, is the primary rate-limiting and highly regulated step of the TCA cycle.
Succinate thiokinase catalyzes the cleavage of the succinyl-CoA thioester bond, providing sufficient energy to phosphorylate GDP to GTP, an example of substrate-level phosphorylation.
The condensation of acetyl CoA and oxaloacetate (citrate synthase) is highly exergonic but does not produce a high-energy phosphate directly.
The reduction of FAD to FADH2 occurs in the subsequent step catalyzed by succinate dehydrogenase, not in the succinate thiokinase reaction.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 105 (Book Page): Succinate thiokinase (also called succinyl CoA synthetase—named for the reverse reaction) cleaves the high-energy thioester bond of succinyl CoA. This reaction is coupled to phosphorylation of guanosine diphosphate (GDP) to guanosine triphosphate (GTP).

category: Differentiate between Kwashiorkor and Marasmus based on the given data
statement: In comparing the psychological and behavioral profiles of patients with Protein-Energy Malnutrition (PEM), which of the following best describes the contrast between Kwashiorkor and Marasmus?
options: Marasmus patients are usually unresponsive, whereas Kwashiorkor patients are highly reactive.
Kwashiorkor patients are vigorously hungry, while Marasmus patients are anorexic.
Both conditions consistently present with a profound lack of interest in the environment.
Kwashiorkor patients are alert and irritable, while Marasmus patients are lethargic.
Kwashiorkor patients display apathy, while Marasmus patients are typically alert.
correctOption: Kwashiorkor patients display apathy, while Marasmus patients are typically alert.
optionExplanations: Kwashiorkor patients are notoriously unresponsive and lethargic, whereas Marasmus patients are reactive and often cry or demand attention when hungry.
The opposite is true: Marasmus patients generally have a good appetite, whereas Kwashiorkor patients suffer from anorexia, making feeding more difficult.
Only Kwashiorkor is primarily associated with apathetic behavior; Marasmus patients are usually very engaged, though irritable, due to their intense hunger.
This is a reversal: Marasmus patients are characterized by an alert but irritable state, whereas Kwashiorkor patients exhibit significant apathy.
Apathy is a hallmark of Kwashiorkor, reflecting the metabolic down-regulation and protein deficit, while Marasmus patients usually remain alert and highly focused on obtaining food.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 360 (Book Page): Mood [Kwashiorkor]: Irritable when picked up; apathetic when left alone. Mood [Marasmus]: Alert, irritable.

category: Elaborate key features of various transport systems for entry of glucose into cells
statement: The transport of glucose from the intestinal lumen into the mucosal cells occurs against a concentration gradient. Which of the following best describes the energy-coupling mechanism utilized in this process?
options: Direct hydrolysis of ATP by the glucose carrier protein
Facilitated diffusion through a family of 14 GLUT isoforms
Coupling of glucose movement to the sodium ion concentration gradient
Exchange transport where one glucose enters as one pyruvate exits
Passive diffusion through the lipid core of the cell membrane
correctOption: Coupling of glucose movement to the sodium ion concentration gradient
optionExplanations: SGLT-1 is a secondary active transporter; it does not hydrolyze ATP directly. The energy is derived from the Na+ gradient maintained by the Na+/K+ ATPase.
Facilitated diffusion via GLUT transporters only moves glucose down its concentration gradient and cannot transport it from low to high concentrations.

SGLT-1 (sodium-dependent glucose transporter) utilizes the electrochemical gradient of sodium (moving from high extracellular to low intracellular concentration) to 'drag' glucose into the cell against its own concentration gradient.
There is no known glucose-pyruvate exchanger for cellular entry; glucose enters via SGLT (with sodium) or GLUT (facilitated diffusion).
Glucose is a polar molecule and cannot diffuse through the hydrophobic lipid core of the cell membrane; it requires specific transmembrane proteins.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 89 (Book Page): This system is a carrier-mediated process in which the movement of glucose is coupled to the concentration gradient of Na+, which is transported into the cell at the same time. The carrier is a sodium-dependent–glucose transporter or SGLT.

category: Describe the TCA cycle along with regulation & significance
statement: Fluoroacetate is a potent toxin often used as a rodenticide. Which of the following best describes the mechanistic step in the TCA cycle that is inhibited after fluoroacetate is metabolically converted to fluorocitrate?
options: The isomerization of citrate to isocitrate by aconitase
The condensation of oxaloacetate and acetyl CoA
The oxidation of succinate to fumarate via FAD reduction
The oxidative decarboxylation of alpha-ketoglutarate
The hydration of fumarate to malate
correctOption: The isomerization of citrate to isocitrate by aconitase
optionExplanations: Fluorocitrate acts as a competitive inhibitor of aconitase, the enzyme responsible for converting citrate into isocitrate, leading to a toxic buildup of citrate.
Fluoroacetyl CoA actually successfully undergoes condensation with oxaloacetate to form the toxic intermediate fluorocitrate; the inhibition occurs after this step.
Succinate dehydrogenase (Complex II) is responsible for succinate oxidation; it is not the target of fluorocitrate or fluoroacetate poisoning.
The oxidative decarboxylation of alpha-ketoglutarate is inhibited by arsenic/arsenite, not fluorocitrate, which targets an earlier step in the cycle.
Fumarase catalyzes the hydration of fumarate; it remains functional in fluoroacetate poisoning, though the entire cycle eventually stalls due to the block at aconitase.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 104 (Book Page): Fluoroacetate is converted to fluoroacetyl CoA, which condenses with oxaloacetate to form fluorocitrate—a potent inhibitor of aconitase—resulting in citrate accumulation.

category: Suggest dietary advice for patients suffering from diabetes mellitus, hypertension, obesity, renal disease, lactose intolerance, gluten enteropathy, hypercholesterolemia, and hemorrhoids
statement: A 54-year-old male with long-standing, poorly controlled diabetes mellitus presents with blurred vision and early cataract formation. He has been consuming a high-calorie diet rich in simple sugars. Which intracellular biochemical mechanism, occurring in the absence of insulin-dependent glucose entry, is primarily responsible for the osmotic damage in his ocular lenses?
options: Excessive production of sorbitol by aldose reductase that remains trapped in the lens.
Accumulation of fructose 1-phosphate due to a deficiency in aldolase B.
Increased glycation of hemoglobin leading to reduced oxygen delivery to the retina.
Osmotic swelling caused by the conversion of sorbitol to fructose by sorbitol dehydrogenase.
Competitive inhibition of hexokinase by high intracellular glucose concentrations.
correctOption: Excessive production of sorbitol by aldose reductase that remains trapped in the lens.
optionExplanations: In the lens, glucose is reduced to sorbitol by aldose reductase. Because the lens lacks significant sorbitol dehydrogenase to convert it further, sorbitol remains trapped, exerting an osmotic pull that causes cataracts.
Fructose 1-phosphate accumulation is the mechanism for Hereditary Fructose Intolerance, not diabetic cataracts.
While HbA1c is a marker of diabetes, glycation is a non-enzymatic process and is not the 'osmotic' mechanism responsible for lens swelling.
The conversion of sorbitol to fructose actually helps prevent its accumulation; the damage occurs in tissues like the lens and retina precisely because they lack or are low in sorbitol dehydrogenase.
Glucose is the substrate for hexokinase; it does not inhibit it competitively in this context. The pathology is driven by the bypass into the polyol pathway.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 132 (Book Page): Elevated intracellular glucose concentrations and an adequate supply of NADPH cause aldose reductase to produce a significant increase in the amount of sorbitol, which cannot pass efficiently through cell membranes... sorbitol accumulates in these cells, causing strong osmotic effects and, therefore, cell swelling.

category: Compare the energy content of macro nutrients and alcohol
statement: A 45-year-old male with a sedentary lifestyle is monitored for his daily intake. He consumes a meal containing 100g of carbohydrate, 20g of protein, and 10g of fat. Which macronutrient provides the majority of the calories in this specific meal?
options: Fat
The calories from Fat and Protein are equal
The calories from Fat and Carbohydrate are equal
Carbohydrate
Protein
correctOption: Carbohydrate
optionExplanations: Fat provides 10g x 9 kcal/g = 90 kcal, which is significantly less than the 400 kcal provided by carbohydrates.
Fat (90 kcal) and Protein (80 kcal) are close but not equal in this specific meal composition.
Carbohydrate (400 kcal) is much higher than Fat (90 kcal) in this meal, representing different caloric proportions despite fat's higher density per gram.
Carbohydrate provides 100g x 4 kcal/g = 400 kcal. Compared to 80 kcal from protein and 90 kcal from fat, it is the largest contributor.
Protein provides 20g x 4 kcal/g = 80 kcal, which is the smallest contribution in this meal.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 359 (Book Page): Carbohydrate 4 [kcal/g], Protein 4 [kcal/g], Fat 9 [kcal/g].

category: Enlist causes and types of Protein Energy Malnutrition (PEM)
statement: The enlarged fatty liver observed in patients with Kwashiorkor is a consequence of which physiological defect?
options: Accumulation of sorbitol within hepatocytes causing osmotic swelling
Excessive intake of dietary fat leading to hepatic storage
Inhibition of beta-oxidation by high insulin levels
Failure of the liver to convert glucose into glycogen
Decreased synthesis of apolipoproteins required for VLDL assembly and export
correctOption: Decreased synthesis of apolipoproteins required for VLDL assembly and export
optionExplanations: Sorbitol accumulation is a feature of hyperglycemia in diabetes, not Protein Energy Malnutrition (PEM).
Kwashiorkor diets are typically low in fat; the liver fat is endogenous, not directly from high fat intake.
Beta-oxidation may be limited by cofactor availability in malnutrition, but the primary reason for 'fatty' liver is export failure, not just oxidation failure.
Glycogen synthesis is not the primary issue; rather, it is the accumulation of lipids (triacylglycerols) due to transport failure.

Due to protein energy malnutrition, the liver cannot synthesize enough apolipoproteins (visceral proteins). Without these, triacylglycerols cannot be exported as VLDL, causing hepatic accumulation (steatosis).
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 361 (Book Page): Typical symptoms include... enlarged fatty liver... [Kwashiorkor] is associated with severely decreased synthesis of visceral protein.

category: Describe the TCA cycle along with regulation & significance
statement: The conversion of pyruvate to acetyl CoA is carried out by a massive multienzyme aggregate. Which of the following catalytic subunits are recognized as the primary enzymatic components of this complex?
options: Isocitrate dehydrogenase, fumarase, and malate dehydrogenase
Acetokinase, dihydrolipoyl dehydrogenase, and succinate thiokinase
Pyruvate dehydrogenase, dihydrolipoyl transacetylase, and dihydrolipoyl dehydrogenase
Pyruvate carboxylase, lactate dehydrogenase, and thiolase
Pyruvate decarboxylase, citrate synthase, and aconitase
correctOption: Pyruvate dehydrogenase, dihydrolipoyl transacetylase, and dihydrolipoyl dehydrogenase
optionExplanations: These are individual enzymes of the TCA cycle that are not physically associated in the PDH multimolecular aggregate.
Succinate thiokinase is a TCA cycle enzyme that performs substrate-level phosphorylation, unrelated to the catalytic subunits of PDH.
The PDH complex consists of E1 (Pyruvate dehydrogenase/decarboxylase), E2 (Dihydrolipoyl transacetylase), and E3 (Dihydrolipoyl dehydrogenase).
Pyruvate carboxylase is a mitochondrial enzyme that converts pyruvate to oxaloacetate; lactate dehydrogenase is cytosolic.
Citrate synthase and aconitase are separate enzymes of the TCA cycle, not part of the PDH aggregate.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 102 (Book Page): Component enzymes: The pyruvate dehydrogenase complex (PDH complex) is a multimolecular aggregate of three enzymes, pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDH or E1, also called a decarboxylase), dihydrolipoyl transacetylase (E2), and dihydrolipoyl dehydrogenase (E3).

category: Enlist inherited and acquired causes of lactic acidosis and give biochemical explanation for lactic acidosis in each condition
statement: A 65-year-old male is admitted with a massive pulmonary embolism. He is hypotensive (BP 80/40 mmHg) and tachypneic. Arterial blood gas shows a pH of 7.21, pCO2 of 28 mmHg, and a plasma lactate of 12 mmol/L. Which statement most accurately explains the biochemical etiology of his acidosis?
options: Increased TCA cycle activity is producing excess CO2, leading to respiratory acidosis.
The pulmonary embolism has blocked the liver's ability to perform the Cori cycle.
The patient has an inherited mutation in his mitochondrial DNA affecting Complex IV.
Reduced oxygen delivery has halted the electron transport chain, causing NADH to accumulate and LDH to reduce pyruvate to lactate.
A rise in ATP levels in his tissues has activated the enzyme lactate dehydrogenase.
correctOption: Reduced oxygen delivery has halted the electron transport chain, causing NADH to accumulate and LDH to reduce pyruvate to lactate.
optionExplanations: In shock, the TCA cycle activity decreases due to lack of oxidized cofactors (NAD+). The acidosis is metabolic (lactic), not respiratory (pCO2 is actually low due to compensation).
While the liver may be poorly perfused, the primary cause of the massive lactate rise is the global tissue hypoxia causing anaerobic glycolysis in all peripheral tissues.
The scenario describes an acute, acquired clinical event (pulmonary embolism), not a lifelong inherited mitochondrial disease.

Hypoxia prevents the ETC from accepting electrons. This causes the mitochondrial and cytosolic NADH/NAD+ ratios to rise. To maintain glycolysis for minimal ATP, the cell uses LDH to oxidize NADH to NAD+ by reducing pyruvate to lactate.
ATP levels drop precipitously during circulatory collapse; furthermore, LDH is not activated by ATP.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 96 (Book Page): Elevated concentrations of lactate in the plasma, termed lactic acidosis, occur when there is a collapse of the circulatory system, such as in myocardial infarction, pulmonary embolism... The failure to bring adequate amounts of oxygen to the tissues results in impaired oxidative phosphorylation.

category: Elaborate key features of various transport systems for entry of glucose into cells
statement: A researcher is investigating the kinetics of sugar absorption in the small intestine. He notes that the uptake of glucose into the enterocyte from the intestinal lumen continues even as intracellular glucose concentrations exceed luminal levels, provided that a specific ion gradient is maintained. Which transport system is responsible for this secondary active transport?
options: Facilitated diffusion via GLUT-2
Passive diffusion through lipid bilayers
Basolateral facilitated diffusion via GLUT-1
Sodium-independent transport via GLUT-5
Sodium-dependent glucose cotransporter 1 (SGLT-1)
correctOption: Sodium-dependent glucose cotransporter 1 (SGLT-1)
optionExplanations: GLUT-2 is located on the basolateral membrane of the enterocyte and facilitates the exit of glucose into the portal circulation via facilitated diffusion, which cannot move glucose against a concentration gradient.
Glucose is a polar molecule and cannot cross the hydrophobic core of the lipid bilayer by passive diffusion; it requires specific membrane proteins for entry.
GLUT-1 is involved in basal uptake in tissues like the blood-brain barrier and is not the primary apical transporter used for active absorption against a gradient in the intestine.
GLUT-5 is a sodium-independent transporter specifically for fructose; it does not transport glucose and does not utilize an ion gradient.

SGLT-1 (Sodium-dependent glucose cotransporter 1) uses the electrochemical gradient of sodium (maintained by the Na+/K+ ATPase) to pull glucose into the cell against its concentration gradient from the intestinal lumen.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 89 (Book Page): This system is a carrier-mediated process in which the movement of glucose is coupled to the concentration gradient of Na+, which is transported into the cell at the same time. The carrier is a sodium-dependent–glucose transporter or SGLT.

category: Compare the energy content of macro nutrients and alcohol
coreConcept: Carbohydrate energy yield and unit conversion (kcal to kJ)
statement: A 30-year-old athlete consumes a meal containing 100 grams of carbohydrates. According to the standard metabolic conversion factors used in nutritional science, what is the equivalent energy value in kilojoules (kJ)?
options: 900 kJ
400 kJ
optionExplanations: 900 kJ is not a standard conversion for 100g of carbohydrate; this value is closer to the kcal content of 100g of fat.
2940 kJ would be the energy value for 100g of alcohol (700 kcal * 4.2).
100g of carbohydrate yields 400 kcal (4 kcal/g). To convert to kJ, 400 kcal is multiplied by 4.2 kJ/kcal, resulting in 1680 kJ.
400 is the energy value in kcal (100g * 4 kcal/g), not in kJ.
3780 kJ would be the energy value for 100g of fat (900 kcal * 4.2).
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 351 (Book Page): [Carbohydrate 4 kcal/g... One cal = 4.2 J; 1 Cal (1 kcal, 1 food calorie) = 4.2 kJ.]

category: Define Marasmus and Kwashiorkor
coreConcept: Differential Diagnosis of PEM based on Weight and Edema
statement: A 2-year-old child is evaluated for malnutrition. The child’s weight-for-age is 75% of the expected value, and physical examination reveals pitting edema in the lower extremities and a distended 'pot belly'. What is the most likely diagnosis based on these specific metrics?
options: Marasmus
Scurvy
Kwashiorkor
Rickets
Beri-beri
correctOption: Kwashiorkor
optionExplanations: Marasmus is characterized by a weight-for-age less than 60% and the absence of edema.
Scurvy involves bleeding gums and subperiosteal hemorrhage, not the protein-deficiency edema seen in Kwashiorkor.
A weight-for-age between 60-80% combined with the presence of edema (which accounts for some of the weight) is characteristic of Kwashiorkor.
Rickets presents with skeletal deformities and would not explain the edema or weight-for-age metric specifically.
Beri-beri does not typically present with this specific combination of weight-for-age and protein-deficiency edema.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 360 (Book Page): Table 27.21 Weight for age (% expected): Kwashiorkor: 60–80. Edema: Kwashiorkor: Present. ... Page 361 (Book Page): Edema results from the lack of adequate plasma proteins... typical symptoms [of Kwashiorkor] include... edema.

category: Enlist the components of balanced diet and elaborate the importance of each component
statement: A nutrition student is planning a vegetarian diet and decides to combine kidney beans with whole wheat bread. Which concept of protein quality is being applied to ensure all essential amino acids are provided?
options: The protein-sparing effect of alcohol-derived calories.
Protein complementarity to overcome individual amino acid deficiencies.
Protein Digestibility-Corrected Amino Acid Score (PDCAAS) of zero.
Exclusive reliance on high-quality animal-source visceral proteins.
Positive nitrogen balance induction via gelatin supplementation.
correctOption: Protein complementarity to overcome individual amino acid deficiencies.
optionExplanations: Alcohol is not a 'protein-sparing' carbohydrate and does not assist in amino acid balance.

Plant proteins are often 'incomplete.' By combining a grain (low lysine) with a legume (low methionine), the strengths of one mask the weaknesses of the other, providing a complete amino acid profile.
A PDCAAS of zero would mean the protein has no nutritional value. The goal is to reach a score closer to 1.00.
The scenario describes a vegetarian approach, which specifically avoids animal-source proteins.
Positive nitrogen balance is a state of growth, but gelatin is a low-quality protein deficient in several essential amino acids.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 360 (Book Page): For example, wheat (lysine-deficient but methionine-rich) may be combined with kidney beans (methionine-poor but lysine-rich) to produce an improved biologic value.

category: Infer the consequences of deficiency and excess of these hormones
statement: In the lactating mammary gland, the hormone prolactin stimulates the synthesis of a specific protein that alters the substrate specificity of galactosyltransferase. What is the inferred consequence of a deficiency in this prolactin-induced protein?
options: Overproduction of milk with low glucose content
Failure to produce UDP-galactose from UDP-glucose
Inability to synthesize N-acetyllactosamine
Inability to synthesize lactose from UDP-galactose and glucose
Accumulation of free galactose in the mammary cytosol
correctOption: Inability to synthesize lactose from UDP-galactose and glucose
optionExplanations: A deficiency in alpha-lactalbumin would result in a failure to produce lactose, which is a primary osmotic component of milk, thus decreasing milk production rather than producing 'low glucose' milk.
UDP-galactose is produced by an epimerase; this process is independent of the prolactin-induced alpha-lactalbumin protein.
Protein A (galactosyltransferase) alone synthesizes N-acetyllactosamine; therefore, a deficiency in the prolactin-induced Protein B would actually leave N-acetyllactosamine synthesis intact.

Prolactin induces alpha-lactalbumin (Protein B), which binds to Protein A to form the lactose synthase complex. Without Protein B, Protein A will not use glucose as an acceptor, and lactose cannot be synthesized.
Galactose accumulation is usually related to GALT or galactokinase deficiencies, not a failure of the terminal transferase complex in the Golgi.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 143 (Book Page): [Protein B is alpha-lactalbumin, and its synthesis is stimulated by the peptide hormone, prolactin. Protein B forms a complex with the enzyme, protein A, changing the specificity of that transferase so that lactose, rather than N-acetyllactosamine, is produced.]

category: Enlist the hormones that play important roles in regulating carbohydrate metabolism
statement: Which endocrine cells are responsible for the secretion of the hormone that inhibits hepatic phosphofructokinase-1 (PFK-1) indirectly by lowering fructose 2,6-bisphosphate levels?
options: Beta cells of the pancreatic islets
Adrenal cortical cells
Anterior pituitary somatotrophs
Chromaffin cells of the adrenal medulla
Alpha cells of the pancreatic islets
correctOption: Alpha cells of the pancreatic islets
optionExplanations: Beta cells secrete insulin, which increases Fructose 2,6-bisphosphate and stimulates PFK-1.
Adrenal cortical cells secrete steroid hormones like cortisol, which have slower, transcriptional effects on carbohydrate metabolism.
Somatotrophs secrete growth hormone, which has anti-insulin effects but is not the primary regulator of the PFK-2/FBP-2 bifunctional enzyme in the liver.
Chromaffin cells secrete epinephrine, which can have similar metabolic effects to glucagon but is not the hormone specified as being from 'pancreatic islets'.
Alpha cells secrete glucagon, which triggers the reduction of Fructose 2,6-bisphosphate, thereby removing the activation of PFK-1 and favoring gluconeogenesis.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 114 (Book Page): Glucagon... This hormone from the α cells of pancreatic islets... lowers the level of fructose 2,6-bisphosphate, resulting in activation of fructose 1,6-bisphosphatase and inhibition of phosphofructokinase-1.

category: Infer the key biochemical and clinical features of various GSDs from the respective enzyme deficiencies
coreConcept: Biochemical basis of limit dextrins in Cori disease
statement: In a patient diagnosed with GSD Type III (Cori disease), the biochemical analysis of hepatic glycogen reveals an abnormal structure characterized by highly shortened outer branches. This structural pathology is a direct consequence of the cell's inability to perform which of the following enzymatic steps?
options: Phosphorolytic cleavage of α(1→4) glycosidic bonds at the nonreducing ends.
Transfer of a six-to-eight glucosyl residue chain to a non-terminal residue.
Synthesis of a short α(1→4)-linked glucosyl primer on glycogenin.
Hydrolytic removal of the single glucose residue at the α(1→6) branch point.
Conversion of glucose 1-phosphate to glucose 6-phosphate.
correctOption: Hydrolytic removal of the single glucose residue at the α(1→6) branch point.
optionExplanations: Phosphorolytic cleavage is performed by glycogen phosphorylase. This enzyme is functional in Cori disease; it degrades glycogen until it reaches the 'limit' of four residues before a branch point.
Transfer of a six-to-eight glucosyl residue chain is the function of the branching enzyme (4:6 transferase). Deficiency in this enzyme causes Type IV GSD (Andersen disease), not Type III.
Synthesis of the primer on glycogenin is the initial step of glycogenesis and is not related to the debranching deficiency seen in Type III.

In GSD Type III, the debranching enzyme is deficient. Specifically, the amylo-α(1→6)-glucosidase activity is required to hydrolytically remove the final glucose residue at a branch point after the transferase has moved the other three residues. Without it, glycogen remains as a 'limit dextrin' with abnormal short branches.
The conversion of glucose 1-phosphate to glucose 6-phosphate is catalyzed by phosphoglucomutase, which is not deficient in Cori disease; this step is downstream of the debranching process.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 121 (Book Page): Type III: Cori Disease (4:4 TRANSFERASE and/or 1:6 GLUCOSIDASE DEFICIENCY)... Glycogen has abnormal structure with four or one glucosyl residues at branch points

category: Infer the key biochemical and clinical features of various GSDs from the respective enzyme deficiencies
coreConcept: Clinical Presentation and Biochemistry of McArdle Syndrome
statement: A 19-year-old male presents with severe muscle cramping and fatigue following high-intensity weightlifting. Laboratory findings indicate myoglobinuria and a notable absence of the expected rise in blood lactate during the ischemic exercise test. Which feature is most consistent with the underlying metabolic defect?
options: The patient possesses a deficiency in the liver isozyme of glycogen phosphorylase.
The accumulated glycogen in myocytes has an abnormally high number of α(1→6) branches.
The condition is relatively benign and characterized by high levels of normal-structured muscle glycogen.
Blood glucose levels will be severely depressed during the episodes of muscle cramping.
The primary defect is a lack of glucose 6-phosphate translocase in the endoplasmic reticulum.
correctOption: The condition is relatively benign and characterized by high levels of normal-structured muscle glycogen.
optionExplanations: Liver isozyme deficiency is GSD VI (Hers disease), which presents with mild hypoglycemia and hepatomegaly, not exercise-induced muscle cramps.
The glycogen structure in McArdle syndrome is normal; abnormal structure with many branches is characteristic of other defects like GSD III.
McArdle syndrome is a deficiency in myophosphorylase. It leads to muscle-specific symptoms and is considered a relatively benign condition with high levels of normal-structure glycogen.
In McArdle syndrome, blood glucose is usually normal because the liver's ability to maintain glucose via glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis is intact.
A lack of glucose 6-phosphate translocase is GSD Ib, which presents with severe hypoglycemia and neutropenia, not isolated muscle cramping.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 121 (Book Page): [TYPE V: McARDLE SYNDROME (SKELETAL MUSCLE GLYCOGEN PHOSPHORYLASE OR MYOPHOSPHORYLASE DEFICIENCY)] ... No rise in blood lactate during strenuous exercise ... Relatively benign, chronic condition ... High level of glycogen with normal structure in muscle.

category: Diagnose G6PD (glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase) deficiency based on given data
coreConcept: Tissue-Specific Metabolic Vulnerability in G6PD Deficiency
statement: A 26-year-old male from the Mediterranean region presents to a clinic in Lahore with sudden onset of jaundice and dark, tea-colored urine. He was recently started on Primaquine for malaria prophylaxis. Laboratory results show a significant drop in hematocrit, elevated unconjugated bilirubin, and the presence of Heinz bodies on a peripheral film. Which of the following best explains why this patient is experiencing hemolysis while his liver cells remain relatively unaffected?
options: Liver cells have a higher concentration of glucose 6-phosphatase which bypasses the G6PD step.
RBCs contain higher levels of glutathione peroxidase which accelerates the destruction of the cell membrane.
Erythrocytes lack mitochondria and have no alternative sources of NADPH other than the pentose phosphate pathway.
The patient likely has a Class IV mutation which only affects the hematopoietic lineage.
The microsomal cytochrome P450 system in the liver consumes all available oxidant drugs before they reach other tissues.
correctOption: Erythrocytes lack mitochondria and have no alternative sources of NADPH other than the pentose phosphate pathway.
optionExplanations: Glucose 6-phosphatase is involved in releasing free glucose from G6P in gluconeogenesis; it does not provide NADPH or bypass the need for the pentose phosphate pathway.
Glutathione peroxidase is protective, not destructive. Higher levels would be beneficial, not a cause of hemolysis.

Erythrocytes are unique because they lack a nucleus (cannot synthesize more enzyme) and mitochondria (lack alternate NADPH-producing enzymes like malic enzyme). Thus, they are entirely dependent on G6PD for NADPH, making them the primary site of clinical disease.

Class IV mutations are clinically silent (normal activity). This patient has classic symptoms of Class II or III deficiency. The X-linked nature means the mutation is in all cells, but the metabolic consequences are tissue-specific.

The microsomal system uses NADPH for detoxification; it doesn't prevent oxidant drugs from reaching RBCs, and in fact, its usage of NADPH might compete for the coenzyme in other tissues, but it doesn't explain RBC-specific hemolysis.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 144 (Book Page): Although G6PD deficiency occurs in all cells of the affected individual, it is most severe in erythrocytes, where the pentose phosphate pathway provides the only means of generating NADPH. Other tissues have alternative sources for NADPH production (such as NADP+-dependent malate dehydrogenases).

category: Define Marasmus and Kwashiorkor
coreConcept: Pathophysiology of Fatty Liver in Kwashiorkor
statement: A 14-month-old male infant presents to the UHS teaching hospital with generalized edema, 'flaky paint' skin lesions, and an enlarged liver. Laboratory findings reveal a serum albumin of 1.8 g/dL. The infant’s weight is 70% of the expected weight for his age. Which mechanism explains the hepatomegaly observed in this specific condition?
options: Congestion of the liver due to right-sided heart failure
Decreased synthesis of apolipoproteins required for VLDL transport
Increased cholesterol synthesis in the liver
Accumulation of unconjugated bilirubin in the hepatocytes
Excessive glycogen storage due to high carbohydrate intake
correctOption: Decreased synthesis of apolipoproteins required for VLDL transport
optionExplanations: There is no evidence of congestive heart failure in this primary protein-malnutrition presentation.
In Kwashiorkor, protein deficiency leads to decreased synthesis of apolipoproteins (like Apo B-100), preventing the liver from exporting triacylglycerols as VLDL, resulting in a fatty liver.
Cholesterol synthesis is not the primary driver; the issue is the export of triacylglycerols from the liver.
Bilirubin accumulation causes jaundice, but the massive hepatomegaly in Kwashiorkor is specifically due to steatosis (fatty change).
While carbohydrate intake is high, the hepatomegaly is caused by fat accumulation, not glycogen storage.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 361 (Book Page): Typical symptoms [of Kwashiorkor] include... enlarged fatty liver, and decreased plasma albumin concentration.

category: Elaborate the effect of various physiological and pathological factors on BMR
statement: A 20-year-old female medical student (Height: 165 cm, Weight: 50 kg) is analyzed for her total daily energy expenditure. She is classified as having a 'light' physical activity level. Which distribution of her estimated energy expenditure components is most consistent with standard physiological models?
options: RMR: 1,800 kcal; Thermic effect of food: 100 kcal; Physical activity: 240 kcal.
RMR: 1,300 kcal; Thermic effect of food: 400 kcal; Physical activity: 440 kcal.
RMR: 1,300 kcal; Thermic effect of food: 210 kcal; Physical activity: 630 kcal.
RMR: 1,500 kcal; Thermic effect of food: 150 kcal; Physical activity: 490 kcal.
RMR: 1,100 kcal; Thermic effect of food: 500 kcal; Physical activity: 540 kcal.
correctOption: RMR: 1,300 kcal; Thermic effect of food: 210 kcal; Physical activity: 630 kcal.
optionExplanations: An RMR of 1,800 kcal is standard for a 70 kg man, not a 50 kg woman.
While the RMR is correct, the thermic effect of food (400 kcal) is overestimated for this individual's total energy profile.
For a 50 kg woman, the RMR is approximately 1,300 kcal (60%). The thermic effect of food is 10% (210 kcal), and light physical activity adds 30% (630 kcal).
An RMR of 1,500 kcal is too high for a standard 50 kg female; the baseline for a 50 kg woman is specifically 1,300 kcal in this model.
The thermic effect of food is typically around 10% of total expenditure; 500 kcal would be roughly 25%, which is physiologically unrealistic.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 359 (Book Page): Figure 27.6 Estimated total energy expenditure in a typical 20-year-old woman, 165 cm... weighing 50 kg... Resting metabolic rate 1300 kcal = 60%; Thermic effect of food 210 kcal = 10%; Physical activity 630 kcal = 30%.

category: Differentiate between Kwashiorkor and Marasmus based on the given data
statement: In the pathophysiology of Kwashiorkor, what is the primary mechanism leading to the characteristic clinical finding of peripheral and abdominal edema?
options: Reduced lymphatic drainage due to parasitic infection
Decreased synthesis of visceral proteins like albumin
